# Roadmap: arithmetic dynamics

**Summary.** This roadmap builds the arithmetic of iterated self-maps: deciding when an orbit is finite, measuring its growth by canonical heights, relating global small points to local invariant measures, and studying the Galois action on iterated preimages. Its endpoints include dynamical equidistribution on the projective line, explicit rational-cycle and preperiodic-point problems, selected arboreal image theorems, canonical-height specialization, uniform common torsion images in the Legendre family, and étale dynamical Mordell–Lang. The concrete maps z↦z^d, z↦z²+c, and the Lattès maps provide checks across these theories.

## Scope and ownership

This roadmap owns the arithmetic of self-maps, the dynamical canonical-height
adapters, local escape functions, Fatou and Julia sets, dynamical equilibrium
measures, dynatomic equations, iterated preimage actions, and the stated family
and orbit-intersection results. General algebraic geometry, curve theory, heights,
potential theory and Galois theory are consumed through the contracts in the indicated layers.

- ModularCurves §4C owns the universal Legendre family, and MordellLawrenceVenkatesh §6.4 its native Weierstrass coefficient model, discriminant and j-invariant. The variants in §§6.35 and 6.111 are their specializations for Lattès dynamics and projected torsion sets.
- Mathlib supplies iteration, positive periods, minimal periods and semiconjugacy;
  polynomials, projective points and resultants; native Weil heights and field
  Northcott; field extensions, finite polynomial Galois actions and Krull topology.
  These notions retain their library meanings.
- Tau Ceti's EllipticCurves supplies elliptic geometry and the elliptic height.
  The new target is its comparison with the dynamical Tate limit and with Lattès
  maps. General abelian Néron–Tate heights come from
  HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §0.19.
- The native analytic line, local potential theory, mutual energy and their
  dynamical maps, invariant measures and Julia-support comparisons are built in
  Layer 2. General projective analytification, local curvature measures and all-place
  equidistribution are treated in Layer 4; hybrid spaces and their measures are built in Layer 6.
- HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §0.18 owns the arbitrary-set Tate series,
  convergence, bounded-distance estimate, scaling, bounded-perturbation invariance
  and uniqueness, with argument order `tateLimit φ α h`. Section 1.1 compares its
  series with normalized iterates; the dynamical height adapters, semiconjugacy,
  iteration and applications belong here.
- HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §§5.17a–f owns arbitrary-dimensional
  arithmetic divisor actions, projective adelic metrized line bundles and
  intersections, normalized cycle heights, Bouche–Tian estimates, arithmetic
  Hilbert–Samuel and successive minima. Layer 4 uses those carriers and absolute
  normalizations; its additional targets are arithmetic Siu, all-place Yuan
  equidistribution, quasi-projective boundary completion, dynamical metrics,
  bifurcation theory and the P¹ energy comparisons. The supplier's archimedean
  abelian equidistribution proof is independent of these additional targets.
- AlgebraicCurves owns function fields, regular projective models, divisors,
  the different and Hurwitz. SchemeAndStackFoundations, §§0.3, 0.9 and Layer 5, supplies
  schemes, spreading out and intersection degrees. The dynatomic coordinate
  rings and dynamical ramification calculations belong here.
- EffectiveDiophantineMethods §0.11 and Layers 3–4 supply certified height
  candidates, Mordell–Weil calculations and rational-point certificates.
  The dynamical equations, projective chart comparisons, finite candidate sets
  and orbit-repetition criteria belong here.
- ConformalMapping supplies local complex analysis and analytic continuation;
  Tau Ceti supplies the sphere atlas used by ComplexManifolds, Milestone 3;
  Layer 2 constructs the meromorphic comparison on that atlas;
  FuchsianOrbifolds supplies compact-surface finite-degree theory. Spherical
  omitted-value normality is the value-distribution extension specified below.
  Dynamical rays, kneading and parabolic transversality belong here.
- PolynomialGaloisGroups and LocalGaloisGroups supply finite Galois and local
  infrastructure; InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups, IG.2, supplies
  Hilbert irreducibility. The preimage tower and arboreal action belong here.
- General GIT quotients, all-place adelic equidistribution, bifurcation currents,
  Banach-contraction decomposition and generic measure entropy require the
  explicit additional contracts in the indicated layers. They are distinct from set quotients,
  local measures, Hilbert-space spectral theory and Birkhoff's theorem.

Uniform boundedness, dynamical Lehmer and unrestricted dynamical Mordell–Lang
are conjectural statements, used only under explicitly stated hypotheses. The
selected rational-cycle theorems retain their rank assumptions. Generic rational-map arboreal
surjectivity is stated in every characteristic; generic monic polynomials retain
the exceptional quadratic characteristic-two image theorem.

- Northcott on projective space, including ℙ¹, is supplied by HeightsAndUnits §1.1; its projective finiteness theorem is not a separate target here.

- The projective absolute Weil height is `projectiveWeilHeight` of ClassicalArithmeticCompletion §6.37; this roadmap uses that definition rather than a second chart construction.

- The Layer 3 number-field finiteness and period-reduction statements use Layer 1 Northcott and Layer 2 good-reduction period classification. The whole-field Lech–Cassels theorem supplies its integral assembly form. The weaker coefficient-height extension bound in Layer 6 is supplied by the equality in §1.3, which also gives its normalized constant.
- Power-orbit classification retains arbitrary characteristic; ClassicalArithmeticCompletion §6.37 supplies its characteristic-zero specialization.
- RestrictedPowerSeries §2.4 owns the general restricted-series zero bound;
  the orbit-interpolation argument consumes its unit-disc specialization.
- The sphere charts, their transition formulas and the chartwise holomorphy
  criterion are supplied by Tau Ceti's `Geometry/Manifold/Instances/OnePoint.lean`,
  as consumed by ComplexManifolds, Milestone 3. No second atlas or chart API is a
  target here. The meromorphic-extension comparison retains its additional
  pole and removable-value content.

## Conventions

For a self-map f, f^[n] denotes n-fold composition, including the identity at n=0. A preperiodic point has a finite forward orbit; an exact period is positive. Equality of iterates means equality of maps. The projective line has coordinates [x₀:x₁], affine coordinate x₀/x₁ and infinity [1:0]. Binary forms have their specified formal degrees even when dehomogenization drops the actual degree. The resultant orientation gives Res(X₀^d,X₁^d)=1, Res(X₁^d,X₀^d)=(−1)^d and Res(aX₀+bX₁,cX₀+eX₁)=ae−bc. Conjugation is the left action γ∘f∘γ⁻¹; a source using f^γ=γ⁻¹∘f∘γ uses the inverse group element.

Maps of degree at least two are required wherever a canonical dynamical limit, Julia-support theorem or entropy log d is asserted. Targets state stronger field or characteristic conditions individually. Pullbacks of measures and divisors count local algebraic degrees, including inseparable multiplicity. This degree is not the separable degree or the number of distinct points in a fibre. Good reduction and potential good reduction are separate conditions; arbitrary PGL₂ conjugation need not preserve good reduction in the chosen coordinates.

Arithmetic heights are absolute unless explicitly called **native relative**. Over a number field K of degree q, the absolute logarithmic height is the native logarithmic height divided by q. Thus an absolute bound B gives native multiplicative radius exp(qB), while a native logarithmic bound B gives exp(B). A finite superset supplied by EffectiveDiophantineMethods §0.11 is used with infinity included; the orbit criterion below is a mathematical statement about that set.

At a finite place v above p, distinguish the native Mathlib absolute value
`v(x) = N(v)^(-ord_v(x))` from the standard local absolute value extending
`|p| = 1/p`, used with weights `r_v = [K_v : ℚ_p]/[K : ℚ]` in Layer 4.
Prove the native-to-standard finite-place comparison: the native value is the standard
value raised to `[K_v : ℚ_p]`. Consequently escape rates and local energies
scale by this local degree when passing from native sums to weighted absolute
sums (Mathlib `FinitePlace.norm_embedding'`; baker-rumely-2006, §2, pp. 4–5).
The witness is the inert prime 3 in ℚ(i): its native value at 3 is 1/9,
its standard value is 1/3 and its local degree is 2. At a split prime the local
degree is 1. Every finite-set probability average assumes a nonempty set.

For the elliptic adapter, `Point.canonicalHeight` is the full native limiting
x-coordinate doubling height, associated to 2(O). Over a number field of degree q,
its quotient by 2q is the absolute Néron–Tate height for (O). Thus the raw Tate limit
is `Point.canonicalHeight`, and the absolute Lattès height is its quotient by q.
The dynamical height associated to 2(O) is twice the height associated to (O).

For a projective number-field variety X of dimension n and an ample bundle L,
write ĉ₁(L̄)^(n+1) for the absolute intersection I of
HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §5.17b, already divided by [K:ℚ], and
h_L̄(X)=I/((n+1)deg_L X). The same normalization gives point heights.
**Normalization check.** On ℙ¹, scaling every archimedean metric by e^(−c) adds c
to point and normalized curve heights and 2c to self-intersection: starting from the standard metric at
c=1 gives height 1 and self-intersection 2. A second division by [K:ℚ] or omission
of n+1 would change these values.

Over ℂ, the Riemann sphere has the topology of `OnePoint ℂ`, its compatible compact uniformity and the supplied `OnePoint.instChartedSpace` complex atlas. Over a complete algebraically closed nontrivially valued nonarchimedean field K, the Berkovich line is the multiplicative-seminorm space of §2.2 with the **weak** topology. Type-I points have their classical chordal topology; the strong hyperbolic-tree topology is different. No one-point compactification of K is a replacement for this analytic line. The exceptional set means classical points with finite backward orbit. A finite-grand-orbit predicate on all analytic points is distinct. Pure Frobenius can have infinitely many classical exceptional points.

For singular logarithmic potentials use log 0 = −∞ in the extended-real subharmonic sense, with their locally integrable representatives defining distributions. Poincaré–Lelong is stated for nonzero rational functions. The nonarchimedean sign is μ_f=Δĝ_F+δ_G, with Δlog⁺|T|=δ_G−δ∞. It is opposite to Baker–Rumely's convention. The complex sign is μ_f=Δg_F+ω, with normalized unit-circle angular probability ω and Δlog⁺|z|=ω−δ∞; on C, Δ is 1/(2π) times the Euclidean Laplacian and Δlog|z|=δ₀. The sphere's measure-valued Laplacian is defined on differences of subharmonic potentials with Radon Riesz measures, including the actual escape potential. Arbitrary continuous functions do not have measure-valued Laplacians. Continuous dynamical potentials rule out type-I atoms; they permit the Gauss atom. Measure support and topological entropy use the native library notions; Layer 2 constructs measure entropy on native measurable carriers.

Y₁(n) is the affine dynatomic scheme, X₁(n) its regular projective characteristic-zero model, and X₀(n) the quotient by cycle rotation. Formal period need not be exact period at a root-of-unity multiplier. The period-three parametrization and the assertion of at most one rational three-cycle are separate targets: the latter uses Morton's elliptic reduction. Poonen type-(3,2) and its dependent exclusions and bounds retain rank J(C₁(3₂))(Q)≤1. The type-(1,3) and type-(2,3) exclusions and the bounds using them also retain rank E11(ℚ)=0 for E11:y²+y=x³−x², independently of the genus-two rank bound. Stoll's six-cycle exclusion retains its genus-four rank hypothesis. No conjecture becomes an unconditional theorem merely by being named as a proposition.

In the Lech presentation A=Z[T₁,…,Tₙ], F=Frac(A), and the primitive variable Y is separate from the parameters. Marked expressions U(y,t)/V(t) have V in A, nonzero. Marks can include zero and need not generate the field. The primitive equation is generically separable and can be nonmonic over A. The parameter map is extended to the entire field before marked evaluation identities are used.

## Exact supplier contracts

Each contract specifies the mathematical output consumed by its linked targets.
An extension named here requires the full stated output; a theorem with a weaker
conclusion does not discharge that contract. Arithmetic point lists retain every
rank, saturation, local-data and finite-certificate hypothesis.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.ModularCurves — §4C

Consume the universal Legendre family and its field fibres, with its chosen x-coordinate.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.MordellLawrenceVenkatesh — §6.4

Consume the universal Legendre family and its field fibres from ModularCurves §4C, and the native Weierstrass coefficient model y²=x(x−1)(x−t) over every commutative ring and its discriminant 16t²(t−1)² from MordellLawrenceVenkatesh §6.4. Over a field of characteristic ≠2 with t≠0,1, consume its j-invariant formula 256(t²−t+1)³/(t²(t−1)²). Section 6.35 specializes this model for its Lattès map; §6.111 specializes the coefficient tuple inside `legendreTorsionImages` to state the projected-torsion theorem on native points.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence — §§0.2, 0.3, 2.4

Consume §0.2 `prod_infinitePlace_comap_pow_mult`, `mulHeight_algebraMap`, `absMulHeight₁_eq_rpow`, `absMulHeight₁_eq_of_minpoly_eq`, and §0.3 `finite_setOf_absMulHeight₁_le` with their number-field degree normalizations. For affine-orbit intersections use §2.4: over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, a finite-rank subgroup of (K×)^n has finitely many nondegenerate solutions of Σ a_i x_i=1 with every a_i nonzero. ### From TauCetiRoadmap.HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions — §0.18

Consume `tateLimit φ α h`, `tendsto_tateLimit`, `abs_tateLimit_sub_le`, `tateLimit_comp`, `tateLimit_unique` and `congr_bounded` on an arbitrary type S with φ:S→S, α>1 and a global bound |h(φP)−αh(P)|≤C. ### From TauCetiRoadmap.HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions — §§5.17a–f

Consume §5.17a `metrizedDivisorAction`, `arithmeticDegree` and `arithmeticIntersection` for projective arithmetic models in every dimension; §5.17b `AdelicMetrizedLineBundle`, `SemipositiveAdelic`, `IntegrableAdelic`, `adelicIntersection_uniformBound`, `adelicCycleHeight` and `cycleProbabilityMeasure`; §5.17c `BergmanDensity` and `bergmanDensity_uniform` with its positive smooth metric and curvature-volume hypotheses; §5.17d `AdelicSectionLattice`, `arithmeticEulerCharacteristic` and the arithmetic Hilbert–Samuel asymptotic; §5.17e section lifting and arithmetic Nakai; and §5.17f `AdelicSuccessiveMinimum` and `successiveMinima_inequality`. Intersections are symmetric, multilinear, compatible with pullback and field extension, and continuous for uniform changes with a fixed model outside finitely many places. The integrable continuity bound uses fixed differences of semipositive factors. For a nonzero effective pure n-cycle Z and ample L, the supplied absolute height is I(L̄^(n+1),Z)/((n+1)deg_L Z), where I is divided by [K:ℚ]; for semipositive L̄ the local probability measure is c₁(L̄_v)^n/deg_L Z. The zero cycle has no such normalization. These inputs do not assert the all-place equidistribution or quasi-projective completion targets of this roadmap.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions — §0.16

For a global height field K with its chosen product-formula structure, a smooth projective variety V/K and η ∈ Pic(V) ⊗ ℝ, consume the Weil height class with a representative h(V,η):V(K̄)→ℝ. It is ℝ-linear in η up to bounded functions, depends only on the line-bundle class, and satisfies h(V,η)∘φ=h(W,φ*η)+O(1) for a morphism φ:W→V. For ample η its representatives are bounded below. Use the supplier's relative height normalization from §§0.9–0.16: on ℙᴺ(K), O(1) gives the chosen relative projective height h_K; under finite extension L/K the relative height scales by [L:K], and division by [L:K] gives the extension-independent representative on K̄ relative to the chosen structure on K.

For number fields, use the absolute representative instead: on ℙᴺ it is Projectivization.logHeight_L(x)/[L:ℚ] for any number field L containing the coordinates. The supplier's number-field contract, from ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeights §§1.12–1.14, supplies Northcott separately: for ample η, B∈ℝ and D≥1, the points P∈V(K̄) with [K(P):K]≤D and absolute h(V,η)(P)≤B form a finite set. The same holds for the relative number-field normalization after rescaling B. Over a general global height field this conclusion requires an additional bounded-degree Northcott hypothesis; the height-machine identities alone do not imply it (Call–Silverman §1, input (2) and Corollary 1.1.1).

**Checks.**

- On ℙ¹(ℚ), h([2:1])=log 2 and an O(2)-height is 2log 2; tensor powers scale the height class.
- Over L=ℚ(√2), the native relative height of [2:1] is 2log 2 and its absolute height is log 2, agreeing with the value over ℚ.
- For K=ℚ(t) with the geometric degree height, every [a:1] with a∈ℚ has height 0 and K-degree 1. Thus B=0,D=1 gives infinitely many points, while the corresponding set in ℙ¹(ℚ) for the absolute number-field height is {0,1,−1,∞}.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions — §0.19

For an abelian variety A over a number field K and a symmetric line bundle L ([−1]*L ≅ L): [m]*L ≅ `L^{⊗m²}` for every integer m, and the Néron–Tate height `ĥ_{A,L}` : A(K̄) → ℝ with `ĥ_{A,L}` − `h_{A,L}` bounded and `ĥ_{A,L}(mP)` = `m²·ĥ_{A,L}(P),` compared with Tau Ceti's elliptic canonicalHeight for dim A = 1 and L = O((O)).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.EffectiveDiophantineMethods — §0.11

Consume `ED0.boundedHeightPoints`, its completeness theorem `ED0.mem_boundedHeightPoints_of_mulHeight₁_le`, and `ED0.boundedHeightProjectivePoints` with `ED0.mem_boundedHeightProjectivePoints`. The inputs are a number field L, a power basis over ℚ with integral generator, a complete collection of [L:ℚ] archimedean embedding data with pairwise disjoint root boxes as in §0.4, and rationals D≥1 and 0<τ≤1. The union S_<∪S_≈ contains every x with native multiplicative height at most D; its projective counterpart includes ∞ and every P with native logarithmic height at most log D. A native bound B uses D≥exp(B); an absolute bound B_abs uses D≥exp([L:ℚ]B_abs). Both lists are retained. Sections 3.47 and 3.53 apply this supplied completeness to the dynamical height bound and projective evaluation; they do not construct another bounded-height enumeration.

Mordell–Weil certificates for two genus-2 Jacobians: (a) for C₀(5): y² = x⁶ + 8x⁵ + 22x⁴ + 22x³ + 5x² + 6x + 1, the FPS Theorem 3 rank-one result and explicit generator data, with the finite descent and local certificates required by ED.3/fps-genus-two-mordell-weil; (b) for C₁(3₂): y² = x⁶ − 2x⁴ + 2x³ + 5x² + 2x + 1, ED.3/poonen-genus-two-mordell-weil supplies the torsion/rank-lower-bound and 3-saturation contracts for [∞₊ − ∞₋]. ### From TauCetiRoadmap.EffectiveDiophantineMethods — Layer 3

Consume EffectiveDiophantineMethods §3.26 (ED.3/rank-zero-curves) with its explicit arithmetic-data hypotheses. For E11: y² + y = x³ − x² the supplied torsion subgroup is {O, (0, 0), (0, −1), (1, 0), (1, −1)} ≅ ℤ/5; the additional premise rank E11(ℚ)=0 makes this the complete list E11(ℚ). This rank premise is independent of rank J(C₁(3₂))(ℚ)≤1. ### From TauCetiRoadmap.EffectiveDiophantineMethods — Layer 3

Complete lists of rational points of three genus-2 curves with rank-zero Jacobians (models of X₁(13), X₁(16), X₁(18)): y² = x⁶ + 2x⁵ + x⁴ + 2x³ + 6x² + 4x + 1 and y² = x⁶ + 2x⁵ + 5x⁴ + 10x³ + 10x² + 4x + 1 each have exactly the six rational points (−1, ±1), (0, ±1) and the two points at infinity; v² = u(u² + 1)(1 + 2u − u²) has exactly (0, 0), (±1, ±2) and the point at infinity. ### From TauCetiRoadmap.EffectiveDiophantineMethods — Layer 3

For Stoll's genus-4 curve X₀^dyn(6): the Jacobian J, its Mordell–Weil group, and a saturation certificate showing that, if rank J(ℚ) = 3, the subgroup G generated by differences of the ten known rational points has finite index and its saturation at the relevant primes is computed (Stoll 2008, §3).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.EffectiveDiophantineMethods — Layer 4

Chabauty–Coleman certificates with every residue disc treated: (a) C₀(5): y² = x⁶ + 8x⁵ + 22x⁴ + 22x³ + 5x² + 6x + 1 has exactly the six rational points (0, ±1), (−3, ±1), ∞± (FPS 1995, Theorem 6, p = 3, given J(ℚ) ≅ ℤ); (b) C₁(3₂): y² = x⁶ − 2x⁴ + 2x³ + 5x² + 2x + 1 has exactly (−1, ±1), (0, ±1), (1, ±3), ∞± (Poonen 1995, Proposition 2, p = 3, including the variant embedding P ↦ [P + S₊] on the disc of the Weierstrass point (1, 0) mod 3); (c) under rank J(ℚ) = 3, X₀^dyn(6) has exactly its ten known rational points (Stoll 2008, p = 5 with a differential annihilating G).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.RestrictedPowerSeries — §2.4

Consume RestrictedPowerSeries §2.4: a nonzero restricted power series over a complete nonarchimedean field has at most N distinct closed-unit-disc zeros, where N is its last coefficient index attaining the Gauss norm. In the orbit argument the field is ℚ_p, the coefficients tend to zero, and the evaluated variable ranges over ℤ_p. Thus infinitely many distinct integral zeros force every coefficient to vanish. Use the evaluation interface of RestrictedPowerSeries §2.1.

*Needs:* RestrictedPowerSeries §§2.1, 2.4; `PowerSeries.IsRestricted`; `PadicInt`.

([bell-ghioca-tucker-2010](#bell-ghioca-tucker-2010), §1, p. 2; proof of Theorem 4.1, p. 14 (arXiv v1): the closed-disc zero theorem is the final analytic step after interpolation. [Flynn–Poonen–Schaefer](#fps95), §8, Theorem 4, p. 21, states this general bound.)

**Endpoint checks.** The polynomial z(z−1) has last dominant index 2 and exactly two integral zeros. For odd p, the analytic function (1+p)^z−1 has only the zero z=0; at p=2 use 5^z−1. These follow from the injectivity of the exponential on pℤ_p for odd p and on 4ℤ₂. The expansion Σ binom(z,i)p^i is a Mahler expansion, so its binomial coefficients are not the monomial coefficients to which Strassmann applies. At p=2 the continuous function 3^z instead has a parity factor and requires two analytic residue classes.

Consume `IsInvariant`, `IsCategoricalQuotient` and `IsGeometricQuotient` for the SL₂ action groupoid on Rat_d. These predicates do not assert the existence of a reductive quotient; the GIT existence and dynamical application are targets of §0.28.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.SchemeAndStackFoundations — Layer 5

For a projective variety X of dimension n over a field and a line bundle L on X, the degree deg_L X = (c₁(L)^n · [X]) as an intersection number, positive when L is ample, and equal to deg X ⊂ P^N for L = O(1).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.ModularCurves — 0d-finite-étale-schemes-and-galois-actions

Over a field K with separable closure K^s: the equivalence X ↦ X(K^s) between finite étale K-schemes and finite continuous Gal(K^s/K)-sets, functorial in K-morphisms, together with its value on the monogenic case: for a separable g ∈ K[x], Spec K[x]/(g) ↦ the Gal(K^s/K)-set of roots of g in K^s, and for polynomials g, h and p ∈ K[x] with g ∣ h ∘ p, the morphism Spec K[x]/(g) → Spec K[y]/(h) induced by y ↦ p(x) ↦ the map of roots β ↦ p(β).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.NumberFieldArithmetic — layer-3-the-index-dedekindkummer-and-dedekinds-theorem

For a monic separable f ∈ ℤ[x] and a rational prime p with p ∤ disc(f): p is unramified in the splitting field of f over ℚ, i.e. Algebra.IsUnramifiedIn (𝓞 L) (Ideal.span {p}) for L = the splitting field (equivalently: p is unramified in every root field ℚ(θ) (layer 3.5–3.6) and unramified in each of two number fields implies unramified in their compositum (layer 1.5)).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.AlgebraicCurves — layer-6-extensions-of-function-fields

For a finite separable extension F'/F of function fields over an algebraically closed k of any characteristic and a place P of F with a local integral generator y whose minimal polynomial φ has 𝒪_P[y] = 𝒪'_P (monogenic case): the places over P, their ramification indices and residue degrees are read off the factorization of φ mod P (Kummer's theorem, Stichtenoth Cor. 3.3.8), and the discriminant ideal of 𝒪'_P over 𝒪_P is generated by disc φ.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.AlgebraicCurves — layer-7-the-different-and-the-hurwitz-genus-formula

Consume AlgebraicCurves Layer 7 over exact constant field k in every characteristic for finite separable F′/F: the different divisor, d(P′|P)≥e(P′|P)−1, tower transitivity, and Hurwitz 2g′−2=[F′:F](2g−2)+deg Diff. With separable residue extension, d=e−1 precisely at tame places. The discriminant valuation is Σ d(P′|P)f(P′|P); replace d by e−1 only in the tame case. For the Juul application pass to algebraically closed k, where residue extensions are separable. The genus-zero base is k(t).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.AlgebraicCurves — layer-8-constant-field-extensions-galois-ramification-and-inseparability-

For a finite Galois extension M/F of function fields over an algebraically closed k of any characteristic, a place q of M over p, and an intermediate field L = M^H: decomposition and inertia groups with |I(q|p)| = e(q|p); the Galois action on places and its decomposition/inertia stabilizers; §5.7 derives the root-permutation orbit comparison of Juul Lemma 2.4 from this input. Consume also the statement that unramified in each of two subfields implies unramified in their compositum (Stichtenoth Cor. 3.9.3).

### From TauCetiRoadmap.AlgebraicCurves — Layer 9

Consume the formal derivative calculus and the Kähler/Weil differential comparison for separably generated function fields, applied to k(t) and k(f(t)) with f separable. Layer 7 supplies the different exponent used to identify the local multiplicities of §5.6a's critical divisor. These rational function fields are separably generated over k even when k is imperfect.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.InverseGaloisAndArithmeticFundamentalGroups — IG.2

Hilbert's irreducibility theorem for number fields in the form: for a number field K, independent indeterminates s = (s_0, …, `s_{d−1})` and a finite Galois extension M/K(s) split by a monic separable P ∈ K[s][x], there is a thin set E ⊆ K^d such that for a ∈ K^d ∖ E the specialized polynomial P_a is separable and Gal(P_a/K) ≅ Gal(M/K(s)) compatibly with the root actions.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.SchemeAndStackFoundations — Layer 0

(1) Quasi-projective varieties over a field K: schemes admitting an immersion into ℙ^N_K = Proj K[x₀, …, x_N], their closed subvarieties and K-points, with étale and unramified endomorphisms as Mathlib AlgebraicGeometry.Etale / FormallyUnramified morphisms of finite type. (2) Spreading out: for smooth geometrically irreducible X, an étale Φ, V and α over ℂ defined over a finitely generated ℤ-algebra R ⊂ ℂ, a model X_R → Spec R such that, over a dense open U ⊆ Spec R, X_U is smooth and quasi-projective, Φ extends to an unramified endomorphism, fibres are geometrically irreducible, and α extends to a section (EGA IV §§8–9, 12; Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Proposition 4.3). (3) Base change of smoothness, unramifiedness and quasi-projectivity along Spec ℤ_p → Spec R.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions — §§0.16, 0.30

For a projective variety X over ℚ̄ with an ample line bundle L, the Weil height `h_{X,L}` : X(ℚ̄) → ℝ (well defined up to bounded functions), with pullback functoriality `h_{Y,φ*M}` = `h_{X,M}` ∘ φ + O(1) for morphisms φ : Y → X, restriction to closed subvarieties, commensurability `c₁h_{X,L}` − c₂ ≤ `h_{X,L′}` ≤ `c₃h_{X,L}` + c₄ of two ample heights, and HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §0.30 `weilHeight_dominant_lower_bound` for a generically finite morphism on a dense open; the extension to its whole finite-fibre locus is a Layer 6 target; applied to a projective compactification of the moduli space M_d of degree-d rational maps, giving the ample moduli height `h_{M_d}.`

### From TauCetiRoadmap.FuchsianOrbifolds — layer-5-compact-surface-degree-theory-and-fuchsian-applications

Finite nonconstant holomorphic sphere maps: local analytic normal forms, positive local multiplicities, finite fibres with degree sum, critical values, inverse branches off critical values, composition. Use the FuchsianOrbifolds independent lower compact-surface degree module; do not reconstruct it in arithmetic dynamics.

### From TauCetiRoadmap.ConformalMapping — Layers, L0 (the local mapping engine)

Import ConformalMapping L0 Hurwitz and its local open-mapping and degree consequences. A nonconstant locally uniform inverse-branch limit then yields a common image neighborhood.

`OnePoint.instIsManifold`, `OnePoint.chartAt_coe`, `OnePoint.chartAt_infty`,
`OnePoint.affineChart_coe`, `OnePoint.invChart_coe`, `OnePoint.invChart_infty`,

and `OnePoint.mdifferentiableAt_iff_of_eq_infty` from

uses the existing compact Hausdorff topology. These are the inputs of

Genus 0 of the rational function field, rational differential coefficient and places.

Degree of a finite extension of function fields, the places above a given place and the fundamental identity Σe·f=[F′:F], for the rotation quotient.

Extend the supplied height machine by `h_{T,D}(t)/h_{T,A}(t)→deg` D for every real divisor class D on a smooth projective curve and deg A=1, as `h_{T,A}→∞,` with compatible algebraic-extension normalization. Supply the generic intersection-degree identity and the uniform relative height bound used by Call–Silverman Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 for global height fields, not only number fields.

Consume §6.37, `projectiveWeilHeight`, `projectivePowerMap`, their affine and infinity computation rules, the compositional iterate formula and `powerMapCanonicalHeight_eq`. ### From Mathlib and Tau Ceti

`WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.xRep` in `Mathlib/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/Affine/Point.lean` supplies the normalized x-coordinate representatives (1,0) at zero and (x,1) at a nonsingular affine point (x,y). The point type includes only nonsingular affine points and the point at infinity; ellipticity is a separate condition, not a field of that type. The Legendre bound explicitly excludes t = 0,1.

`Equiv.conj` (`Mathlib/Logic/Equiv/Defs.lean`) supplies conjugation of self-maps as h∘f∘h⁻¹. Use `Equiv.divRight₀` and `Equiv.addRight` for the rational scaling and translation convention Checks in §§0.36, 2.16 and 3.3; their backward-orbit transport follows from conjugacy transport in §2.17.

Consume `Polynomial.dickson 1 a n` over a commutative ring, together with `Polynomial.map_dickson`, `Polynomial.dickson_add_two`, `Polynomial.dickson_one_one_eval_add_inv` and `Polynomial.dickson_one_one_mul`, from `Mathlib/RingTheory/Polynomial/Dickson.lean`. These supply the carrier, coefficient transport, recurrence, parameter-one evaluation and composition identities used in §6.25. Consume also `Polynomial.dickson_sq_mul_eval_mul` from `TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Dickson.lean`: over a commutative ring, `(dickson k (b^2*a) n).eval (b*t) = b^n*(dickson k a n).eval t`, for every k,n and a,b,t. Applying it over R[X] at X gives D_n(bX,b²a)=bⁿD_n(X,a), the parameter scaling used in §6.25.

## How to read the build

Layer 0 fixes iteration, homogeneous rational maps, conjugacy, moduli and
reduction. Layer 1 applies the Tate limit to heights. Layer 2 constructs local
escape functions and measures before proving the transfer, support and entropy
comparisons. Layer 3 develops formal periods, affine dynatomic rings, projective
models, analytic comparisons and certified rational-point reductions. Layer 4
passes from local energies to adelic heights, pairings and equidistribution.
Layer 5 builds the preimage tower and its Galois action. Layer 6 develops power
and Lattès examples, families, specialization and orbit intersections.

`Suggested.lean` states the headline theorems whose objects can be expressed at the pinned libraries: rational three-cycle uniqueness and the four- and five-cycle exclusions (§§3.57, 3.58, 3.88), Stoll's integer-family finite-level Galois theorem (§5.64), Ritt's classification (§6.23), the full affine-line orbit-intersection theorem (§6.84), the whole-field Lech–Cassels embedding (§6.86), polynomial-line return times (§6.90), infinitely many algebraic torsion specializations of a constant mark (§6.87), the uniform common Legendre torsion bound (§6.111), and its extension to two standard projections with three common branch values (§6.112). Its real-bodied definitions are `forwardOrbit`, `IsFiniteUnionAP`, `ellipticStandardProjection` and `legendreTorsionImages`. The module docstring identifies the other headline theorems and the carriers they lack at the pins; the layers below specify their full statements, APIs and Checks.

Within a layer the targets follow their prerequisites. Layer 0 constructs the
power map and the rational-function-field height used by Layers 1–2. The
period-three parametrization precedes the two-cycle reduction and the final
rational preperiodic bound. The Lech argument constructs the whole-field
embedding before transporting any marked expression.

## Layer 0: Iteration, maps and moduli

### 0.1 The forward orbit of a point under a self-map

For a type α, a self-map f : α → α and x : α, the forward orbit of x is O_f(x) = {f^n(x) : n ∈ ℕ} (with f^0(x) = x), the range of the orbit map ℕ → α, n ↦ f^[n] x (Mathlib's iterate `Nat.iterate`).

α any type; no structure on α is used. n = 0 is included, so x ∈ O_f(x).

Define O_f(x) as Set.range (n ↦ f^[n] x). Membership: y ∈ O_f(x) iff y = f^[n] x for some n (definition of range). Forward invariance f(O_f(x)) ⊆ O_f(x) and O_f(x) = {x} ∪ O_f(f x) from f^[n+1] x = f (f^[n] x) (Function.iterate_succ_apply'); iteration also commutes with f. Functoriality: if g ∘ fa = fb ∘ g (Function.Semiconj g fa fb) then g ∘ fa^[n] = fb^[n] ∘ g (Function.Semiconj.iterate_right), so g(O_fa(x)) = O_fb(g x).

*Needs:* `Nat.iterate`; `Function.iterate_succ_apply'`; `Function.Semiconj`; `Function.Semiconj.iterate_right`.

([silverman-aws-2010](#silverman-aws-2010), §1, p. 2 — Exactly the definition (with ϕ^0(x) = x, stated on the same page); [call-silverman-1993](#call-silverman-1993), §1, p. 168 — The orbit whose finiteness defines preperiodicity.)

Prove the following basic API.

- `forwardOrbit`: O_f(x) = {f^[n] x : n ∈ ℕ} ⊆ α.
- y ∈ O_f(x) ↔ ∃ n, f^[n] x = y.
- x ∈ O_f(x).
- f maps O_f(x) into itself.
- O_f(x) = insert x (O_f(f x)).
- If Function.Semiconj g fa fb then g '' O_fa(x) = O_fb(g x).
- If y ∈ O_f(x) then O_f(y) ⊆ O_f(x).

**Checks.**

- The forward orbit of 0 under n ↦ n + 1 on ℕ is all of ℕ.
- For the identity map, forwardOrbit id x = {x}.
- Under z ↦ z² − 1 on ℤ, the forward orbit of 1 is {1, 0, −1}.
- Under n ↦ n + 1 on ℤ, 1 ∉ O(2): the forward orbit is not the orbit of the ℤ-action generated by f.

**Endpoint checks.** Under n ↦ n + 1 on ℕ the orbit of 0 is ℕ; under the identity every orbit is a singleton. Under z ↦ z² − 1 on ℤ the orbit of 1 is {1, 0, −1} (Silverman, AWS notes, Example 2).

Applications include Silverman, AWS notes, §1 — preperiodic and wandering points are those with finite and infinite orbit; Call–Silverman, Corollary 1.1.1(a) — the orbit of a point of canonical height zero has bounded height, hence is finite; Preperiodic iff the forward orbit is finite — the finite-orbit characterisation of preperiodic points; Zero Tate limit and Northcott give preperiodicity — Northcott applied to the forward orbit; ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIBifurcation (DeMarco–Mavraki–Ye §2.2) — a map is PCF when every critical point has a finite forward orbit.

### 0.2 Preperiodic points of a self-map

For f : α → α, a point x is preperiodic (IsPreperiodicPt f x) if some iterate f^[m] x lies in Mathlib's periodicPts f, i.e. f^[m + n] x = f^[m] x for some m and some n ≥ 1. The preperiodic points form preperiodicPts f ⊇ periodicPts f.

α any type. Period n ≥ 1 (a periodic point of period 0 is excluded, as in Mathlib's periodicPts).

Define IsPreperiodicPt f x := ∃ m, f^[m] x ∈ Function.periodicPts f and preperiodicPts f := {x | IsPreperiodicPt f x}. Periodic points are preperiodic (m = 0); x preperiodic iff f x preperiodic (shift m by one, using Function.IsPeriodicPt.apply_iterate). On a finite type every point is preperiodic, by pigeonhole on the orbit map (Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite). For g ↦ g^d on a group with d ≥ 2: `g^{d^{m+n}}` = `g^{d^m}` with n ≥ 1 gives `g^{d^m(d^n − 1)}` = 1, so g has finite order; conversely if g has order N the powers d^m mod N repeat.

*Needs:* `Function.periodicPts`; `Function.IsPeriodicPt`; `Finite.exists_ne_map_eq_of_infinite`; `IsOfFinOrder`.

([silverman-aws-2010](#silverman-aws-2010), §1, p. 3 — The notion; the equivalence with the iterate form is Preperiodic iff the forward orbit is finite; [call-silverman-1993](#call-silverman-1993), §1, p. 168 — The defining form chosen here; [silverman-aws-2010](#silverman-aws-2010), §1, p. 4, Exercise A — The compatibility test with Mathlib's IsOfFinOrder.)

Prove the following basic API.

- IsPreperiodicPt f x :↔ ∃ m, f^[m] x ∈ periodicPts f.
- The set {x | IsPreperiodicPt f x}.
- IsPreperiodicPt f x ↔ ∃ m n, 0 < n ∧ f^[m + n] x = f^[m] x.
- A periodic point of positive period (Mathlib's IsPeriodicPt f n x, n > 0) is preperiodic.
- periodicPts f ⊆ preperiodicPts f.
- IsPreperiodicPt f (f x) ↔ IsPreperiodicPt f x.
- Preperiodicity is preserved along the orbit: f^[m] x is preperiodic.
- On a finite type every point is preperiodic.
- For k ≥ 1, x is preperiodic for f^[k] iff it is for f.

**Checks.**

- 1 is preperiodic but not periodic for z ↦ z² − 1 on ℤ; the starting point is not periodic.
- 2 is not preperiodic for z ↦ z² − 1 on ℤ (its orbit tends to ∞).
- For g ↦ g^d with d ≥ 2 on a group, IsPreperiodicPt ↔ Mathlib's IsOfFinOrder g.
- Every point is preperiodic for the identity.

**Endpoint checks.** 1 is preperiodic but not periodic for z ↦ z² − 1 on ℤ; 2 is wandering (Silverman, AWS notes, Example 2). For g ↦ g^d (d ≥ 2) on a group the preperiodic points are the torsion elements (AWS notes, Exercise A).

Applications include Call–Silverman, Corollary 1.1.1 — preperiodic points are exactly the points of canonical height zero, and form a set of bounded height; Silverman, AWS notes, Theorem 15 (Northcott) — PrePer(ϕ, K) is finite for a number field K; ĥ_f(P) = 0 iff P is preperiodic (ℙ¹) — the target predicate of the zero-height criterion; Layer 3 — finiteness of preperiodic points of bounded degree for a fixed polarized morphism; Layer 6 and ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIBifurcation — PCF maps: all critical points preperiodic; ĥ_crit = 0.

### 0.3 Iterates of an endomorphism act on points by its powers

Let C be a category, X, T objects and φ ∈ End X (Mathlib's monoid CategoryTheory.End X). For every T-point P : T ⟶ X and n ∈ ℕ, (Q ↦ Q ≫ φ)^[n] P = P ≫ φ^n. Consequently P is periodic of period n for Q ↦ Q ≫ φ iff P ≫ φ^n = P: the iterates of a morphism of schemes (C = schemes over S, T = Spec K) are the powers φ^n in End X, and equality of iterates is equality of morphisms.

Any category; φ^n is the power in CategoryTheory.End X, whose product is xs * ys = ys ≫ xs (CategoryTheory.End.mul_def).

Induct on n. The zero case is P ≫ 𝟙 = P. For n + 1 use Function.iterate_succ_apply', φ^(n+1) = φ * φ^n = φ^n ≫ φ (pow_succ' and CategoryTheory.End.mul_def), and associativity. The periodicity statement is the case of Function.IsPeriodicPt unfolded with the first identity.

*Needs:* `CategoryTheory.End`; `CategoryTheory.End.mul_def`; `Function.iterate_succ_apply'`; `Function.IsPeriodicPt`.

([silverman-aws-2010](#silverman-aws-2010), §1, p. 2 — Iteration of a self-map; here the self-map is postcomposition with a morphism; [silverman-aws-2010](#silverman-aws-2010), §6.1, p. 19, Supplementary Material — Dynamical systems given by morphisms of schemes, whose iterates are compositions of morphisms.)

**Endpoint checks.** For C = Type and T = a point, the statement is Mathlib's Function.End pow = iterate. For X = P¹_K the powers of the scheme morphism of a rational map f are the morphisms of f^n (Rational maps as endomorphisms of the scheme ℙ¹_K).

### 0.4 The resultant of a pair of binary forms

For a commutative ring R, binary forms F, G ∈ R[X₀, X₁] and formal degrees m, n ∈ ℕ, `Res_{m,n}(F,` G) := Polynomial.resultant F(X, 1) G(X, 1) m n, Mathlib's (m + n) × (m + n) Sylvester determinant of the dehomogenisations F(X, 1) = aeval ![X, 1] F. For a homogeneous lift (F₀, F₁) of a degree-d rational map the resultant is Res_d(F₀, F₁) := `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁); since `Res_{d,d}(cF₀,` cF₁) = `c^{2d}` `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁), the resultant of the map is defined up to `(K^×)^{2d},` and its valuation on a normalised lift is well defined. Orientation (pinned): `Res_{d,d}(X₀^d,` X₁^d) = 1 and `Res_{d,d}(X₁^d,` X₀^d) = (−1)^d; for m = n = d this is the determinant of Silverman (AWS notes, Example 23), Rumely ((1)) and Milnor (Appendix A).

R commutative; F, G arbitrary (in applications homogeneous of degrees m, n, so that F(X, 1), G(X, 1) have degree ≤ m, n). Formal degrees are explicit: they matter when a leading coefficient vanishes (a root at ∞).

Define binaryResultant m n F G := Polynomial.resultant (aeval ![X, 1] F) (aeval ![X, 1] G) m n. Compatibility with Mathlib's homogenisation: aeval ![X, 1] (homogenize f m) = f when deg f ≤ m (Polynomial.aeval_homogenize_X_one), so `Res_{m,n}(homogenize` f m, homogenize g n) = resultant f g m n. Scaling: `Res_{m,n}(cF,` G) = c^n Res and `Res_{m,n}(F,` cG) = c^m Res (Polynomial.resultant_C_mul_left, Polynomial.resultant_C_mul_right); symmetry (Polynomial.resultant_comm); base change (Polynomial.resultant_map_map); `Res_{m,n}(0,` G) = 0 for n ≠ 0 (Polynomial.resultant_zero_left). `Res_{d,d}(X₀^d,` X₁^d) = resultant (X^d) 1 d d = 1 (Polynomial.resultant_X_pow_left); for a polynomial p of degree n, `Res_{n,n}` of Mathlib's toTupleMvPolynomial p is lead(p)^n (repeat Polynomial.resultant_succ_left_deg on the constant second form).

### 0.5 Binary forms split into linear forms over an algebraically closed field

Let K be algebraically closed and G ∈ K[X₀, X₁] nonzero and homogeneous of degree n. There are c ∈ K^× and n nonzero linear forms ℓ_i = a_i X₀ + b_i X₁ such that G = c·∏_i ℓ_i. The points [−b_i : a_i] are its zeros with multiplicity; ∞ occurs n − deg G(X, 1) times. When n = 0 the product is empty and the scalar c is the constant form itself.

K algebraically closed; G ≠ 0 homogeneous of degree n.

g = G(X, 1) is nonzero of degree k ≤ n, and G = homogenize g n (Polynomial.homogenize_eq_of_isHomogeneous). g splits (IsAlgClosed.splits_domain): g = lead(g) `∏_{r ∈ roots g}` (X − r) (Polynomial.C_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_multiset_X_sub_C). Homogenising the product with degree 1 for each root factor and degree n − k for the leading coefficient gives G = `lead(g)·X₁^{n−k}·∏(X₀` − rX₁). Retain lead(g) as the nonzero scalar; this also covers n = 0.

### 0.6 Reduction of points of ℙ¹ modulo the maximal ideal

For a valuation ring R with fraction field K and residue field k, projReduction R : ℙ¹(K) → ℙ¹(k) sends [x] to [x̃], where x is scaled to have coordinates in R with at least one unit coordinate and x̃ is its coordinatewise residue. It is surjective and sends ∞ to ∞.

R a valuation ring, K = Frac R.

Every x ≠ 0 in K² can be scaled into R² with a unit coordinate (valuation ring: divide by a coordinate of minimal valuation); two such scalings differ by a unit of R, so [x̃] is well defined (Projectivization.lift). x̃ ≠ 0 because a unit coordinate has nonzero residue (IsLocalRing.residue_ne_zero_iff_isUnit). Surjectivity: lift a representative with a nonzero coordinate from k to R (IsLocalRing.residue is surjective).

### 0.9 Bimultiplicativity of the binary resultant

For binary forms over a commutative ring with F₁, F₂, G homogeneous of degrees m₁, m₂, n: `Res_{m₁+m₂,n}(F₁F₂,` G) = `Res_{m₁,n}(F₁,` G) · `Res_{m₂,n}(F₂,` G); symmetrically `Res_{m,n₁+n₂}(F,` G₁G₂) = `Res_{m,n₁}(F,` G₁) · `Res_{m,n₂}(F,` G₂).

Homogeneity gives deg F_i(X, 1) ≤ m_i and deg G(X, 1) ≤ n (MvPolynomial.IsHomogeneous.totalDegree_le).

Dehomogenisation is a ring homomorphism, so (F₁F₂)(X, 1) = F₁(X, 1)F₂(X, 1). With k_i = m_i − deg F_i(X, 1), Polynomial.resultant_add_left_deg moves the formal degree m_i to the actual degree at the cost of the factor `(−1)^{n k_i}` `g_n^{k_i},` where g_n is the coefficient of X^n in G(X, 1). Polynomial.resultant_mul_left already places the product at the sum of the two input natDegrees, without assuming the product has that natDegree. Apply resultant_add_left_deg to raise those formal degrees by k₁ and k₂; the sum k₁ + k₂ raises the product degree to m₁ + m₂. The signs and g_n powers then multiply. This remains valid over rings with zero divisors, where natDegree of a product can drop. The second formula follows from the first by Polynomial.resultant_comm (or directly from Polynomial.resultant_mul_right and Polynomial.resultant_add_right_deg).

*Needs:* [The resultant of a pair of binary forms](#04-the-resultant-of-a-pair-of-binary-forms); `Polynomial.resultant_mul_left`; `Polynomial.resultant_mul_right`; `Polynomial.resultant_add_left_deg`; `Polynomial.resultant_add_right_deg`; `Polynomial.natDegree_mul_le`; `MvPolynomial.IsHomogeneous.totalDegree_le`; `Polynomial.resultant_comm`.

### 0.10 The resultant under a linear change of the pair of forms

For a commutative ring R, a matrix A ∈ M₂(R) and binary forms F₀, F₁ homogeneous of degree d: `Res_{d,d}(A₀₀F₀` + A₀₁F₁, A₁₀F₀ + A₁₁F₁) = det(A)^d · `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁).

R commutative; F_j homogeneous of degree d.

The Sylvester matrix is linear in the coefficient vectors of both polynomials (Polynomial.sylvester): its first d columns carry shifts of the second form, its last d columns shifts of the first. Hence Syl(A·F) = Syl(F) · M where M is, after reindexing Fin (d + d) ≃ Fin 2 × Fin d, the Kronecker product of the 2 × 2 matrix of A (with rows and columns ordered as in the Sylvester blocks) with the d × d identity. det M = det(A)^d (Matrix.det_kronecker, Matrix.det_reindex_self), and Matrix.det_mul gives the claim.

*Needs:* [The resultant of a pair of binary forms](#04-the-resultant-of-a-pair-of-binary-forms); `Polynomial.sylvester`; `Matrix.det_mul`; `Matrix.det_kronecker`; `Matrix.det_reindex_self`.

([milnor-1993](#milnor-1993), Appendix A, p. 39 (arXiv v1) — The diagonal and swap cases; the general linear case is their common extension; [rumely-2013](#rumely-2013), §1, p. 5 (arXiv v2) — The scalar case A = cI.)

### 0.11 The zeros of a binary form in ℙ¹, with multiplicity

For a field K, n ∈ ℕ and a binary form G, binaryRoots n G ∈ Multiset ℙ¹(K) consists of [r : 1] for each root r of G(X, 1) (with multiplicity) and ∞ = [1 : 0] with multiplicity n − deg G(X, 1); for G = 0 it is empty. For G ≠ 0 homogeneous of degree n its underlying set is the zero set of G in ℙ¹(K), and it has n elements when K is algebraically closed.

K a field; n is the formal degree (the multiplicity of ∞ depends on it).

Define binaryRoots n G := ((G(X, 1)).roots.map (r ↦ [r : 1])) + (n − deg G(X, 1)) • {∞} (Polynomial.roots), and 0 for G = 0. Membership: for x = (x₀, x₁) with x₁ ≠ 0, G(x) = x₁^n G(x₀/x₁, 1) (Polynomial.eval_homogenize); at ∞, G(1, 0) is the coefficient of X₀^n, zero iff deg G(X, 1) < n. Cardinality n over an algebraically closed field: deg G(X, 1) roots (IsAlgClosed.card_roots_eq_natDegree) plus n − deg at ∞. Multiplicativity under products (roots of a product, Polynomial.roots_mul) and invariance under scaling.

### 0.12 The resultant vanishes exactly at a common zero

Let K be a field, d ≥ 1 and F₀, F₁ ∈ K[X₀, X₁] homogeneous of degree d. Then `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁) = 0 iff F₀ and F₁ have a common zero x ∈ K̄² ∖ {0} (K̄ = AlgebraicClosure K), i.e. a common zero in ℙ¹(K̄).

d ≥ 1 (in degree 0 the resultant is 1 for every pair). Homogeneity of degree exactly d with formal degrees d, d.

Base change to K̄ does not change whether the resultant vanishes (Polynomial.resultant_map_map, injectivity of K → K̄). If F₀ = 0 (or F₁ = 0) the resultant is 0 (Polynomial.resultant_zero_left) and the other form has a zero in ℙ¹(K̄) by Binary forms split into linear forms over an algebraically closed field (d ≥ 1). Otherwise factor F₀ = ∏ ℓ_i and F₁ = ∏ m_j into linear forms (Binary forms split into linear forms over an algebraically closed field) and expand by Bimultiplicativity of the binary resultant: Res = `∏_{i,j}` `Res_{1,1}(ℓ_i,` m_j). `Res_{1,1}(aX₀` + bX₁, cX₀ + eX₁) = ae − bc (2 × 2 Sylvester determinant, Matrix.det_fin_two) vanishes iff the two linear forms are proportional iff they have the same zero; so Res = 0 iff some ℓ_i and m_j share a zero.

### 0.13 The resultant under a linear substitution of the variables

For a commutative ring R, A ∈ M₂(R) and binary forms F₀, F₁ homogeneous of degree d, write F∘A for the substitution X_i ↦ Σ_j A_ij X_j (linearSubst A). Then `Res_{d,d}(F₀∘A,` F₁∘A) = `det(A)^{d²}` · `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁).

R commutative; F_j homogeneous of degree d.

For d = 0 both resultants equal the determinant of the empty Sylvester matrix, namely 1, including when either form is zero; det(A)^0 = 1. In the remaining steps d > 0. Universal identity: both sides are integer polynomials in the entries of A and the coefficients of F; by Polynomial.resultant_map_map it suffices to prove it for the universal forms over ℤ[a, b, A], hence over the algebraic closure of its fraction field (an injective ring map). Over an algebraically closed field factor F₀ = c₀∏_i ℓ_i and F₁ = c₁∏_j m_j with c₀,c₁ nonzero into linear forms (Binary forms split into linear forms over an algebraically closed field; if a form is 0 both sides vanish by Polynomial.resultant_zero_left); then F_k∘A factor as ∏ (ℓ_i∘A) and ∏ (m_j∘A). Expand both sides by Bimultiplicativity of the binary resultant into d² factors `Res_{1,1}(ℓ_i∘A,` m_j∘A) and `Res_{1,1}(ℓ_i,` m_j). For linear forms, `Res_{1,1}(ℓ∘A,` m∘A) = det(A) · `Res_{1,1}(ℓ,` m): the coefficient matrix of (ℓ∘A, m∘A) is that of (ℓ, m) times A (Matrix.det_fin_two, Matrix.det_mul).

### 0.14 The resultant of a conjugated lift

For A ∈ M₂(R) and binary forms F₀, F₁ of degree d, Rumely's homogeneous conjugate F^A := adj(A) ∘ F ∘ A, (F^A)_i = Σ_j adj(A)_ij (F_j∘A), satisfies `Res_{d,d}(F^A_0,` F^A_1) = `det(A)^{d²+d}` · `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁).

### 0.15 The resultant as a Nullstellensatz certificate

For a commutative ring R, d ≥ 1 and binary forms F₀, F₁ homogeneous of degree d, there are binary forms `G_{k,j}` (k, j ∈ {0, 1}) homogeneous of degree d − 1 with `G_{k,0}F₀` + `G_{k,1}F₁` = `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁) · `X_k^{2d−1}` for k = 0, 1. In particular, over a field, if Res ≠ 0 then F₀(x) = F₁(x) = 0 forces x = 0, and `q_{k,j}` = `G_{k,j}/Res` is the certificate consumed by Mathlib's Height.logHeight_eval_ge with M = d − 1, N = d.

d ≥ 1; R commutative (no domain hypothesis).

Apply Polynomial.exists_mul_add_mul_eq_C_resultant to f = F₀(X, 1), g = F₁(X, 1) with formal degrees d, d (natDegree ≤ d by homogeneity): f·p + g·q = C(Res) with deg p, deg q < d. Homogenise to degree 2d − 1 = d + (d − 1): F₀·homogenize p (d−1) + F₁·homogenize q (d−1) = `Res·X₁^{2d−1}` (Polynomial.homogenize_mul, Polynomial.homogenize_eq_of_isHomogeneous, Polynomial.homogenize_C); this is the case k = 1. For k = 0 apply the case k = 1 to F∘σ with σ the swap of variables and substitute σ back; The resultant under a linear substitution of the variables gives Res(F∘σ) = `det(σ)^{d²}` Res(F) = `(−1)^{d}` Res(F), absorbed into the `G_{0,j}.` If Res ≠ 0 over a field and F₀(x) = F₁(x) = 0 then `Res·x_k^{2d−1}` = 0 for both k, so x = 0.

### 0.18 Rational self-maps of ℙ¹ over a field

For a field K, RationalMap K is the quotient of Σ_d HomogeneousLift K d by the relation 'same degree and proportional forms'. Its degree is the degree of any lift. Composition of lifts makes RationalMap K a monoid (unit: the class of (X₀, X₁)), with deg(f g) = deg f · deg g, so f^n is the n-th iterate as a map (not merely on points). Polynomial maps p ↦ z ↦ p(z) embed K[X] (under composition) via Mathlib's toTupleMvPolynomial, and f ↦ F₀(X, 1)/F₁(X, 1) ∈ RatFunc K is injective on the maps of positive degree. The total toRatFunc sends both constant 0 and constant ∞ to 0, so it is not injective on all maps.

K a field. Maps of degree 0 are the constants, one for each point of ℙ¹(K); Rat_d(K) is {f | deg f = d}.

Define the setoid on Σ_d HomogeneousLift K d and RationalMap K as its quotient; mk F is the class of F and degree is the first component (well defined). Monoid: mul on representatives is Composition of homogeneous lifts; well defined because (cF) ∘ G = c(F ∘ G) and F ∘ (cG) = c^d (F ∘ G) (homogeneity); associativity and units from the corresponding lift identities. ofPolynomial p is mk (HomogeneousLift.ofPolynomial p) (for p = 0 the lift (0, 1) is the constant 0); ofPolynomial (p ∘ q) = ofPolynomial p * ofPolynomial q because the composite of the lifts (homogenize p m, X₁^m) and (homogenize q n, X₁^n) is (homogenize (p ∘ q) (mn), `X₁^{mn})` (Polynomial.homogenize_mul). toRatFunc f := F₀(X, 1)/F₁(X, 1) in RatFunc K (well defined on the class). For deg f ≥ 1, F₁(X, 1) ≠ 0 and Res ≠ 0 makes F₀(X, 1), F₁(X, 1) coprime with max(deg F₀(X, 1), deg F₁(X, 1)) = deg f, so f is recovered from the fraction; the constant map ∞ goes to Mathlib's junk value 0 = (1 : RatFunc K)/0, which is why injectivity is stated on {f | 1 ≤ deg f}.

### 0.19 The action of a rational map on ℙ¹(K)

RationalMap.toEnd : RationalMap K →* Function.End (ℙ¹(K)) sends f = mk F to [x] ↦ [F(x)] on Mathlib's ℙ K (Fin 2 → K). It is a monoid homomorphism, so toEnd (f^n) = (toEnd f)^[n]. It is injective when K is infinite and not injective over finite fields.

K a field; ℙ¹(K) = Mathlib's Projectivization ℙ K (Fin 2 → K), with [x : 1] = mk ![x, 1] and ∞ = [1 : 0].

Well defined on points: F(x) ≠ 0 for x ≠ 0 (Homogeneous lifts of a degree-d self-map of ℙ¹, eval_ne_zero) and F(cx) = c^d F(x), so Projectivization.lift applies; scaling F does not change [F(x)] (Projectivization.mk_eq_mk_iff). Multiplicativity from (F ∘ G)(x) = F(G(x)) (Composition of homogeneous lifts); powers are iterates since Function.End's power is iteration. Injectivity for infinite K: if f, g of degrees d, e act identically then F₀G₁ − F₁G₀ vanishes on K², hence is 0 (MvPolynomial.IsHomogeneous.funext), so F₀G₁ = F₁G₀; as F₀, F₁ have no common factor (Res ≠ 0) the lifts are proportional and d = e. Over 𝔽_p, z^p fixes every point of ℙ¹(𝔽_p) (Fermat), so toEnd (z^p) = toEnd 1 while z^p ≠ 1.

### 0.20 Good reduction of a rational map

Let R be a valuation ring with fraction field K and residue field k. A rational map f over K has good reduction (over R) if it has a lift (F₀, F₁) with coefficients in R, at least one unit coefficient, and whose resultant `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁) is a unit of R. Its reduction f̃ is then the class over k of the reduced lift (F̃₀, F̃₁), a rational map of the same degree d.

R a valuation ring (e.g. ℤ_(p), ℤ_p, the valuation ring of a complete nonarchimedean field), K = Frac R, k = R/𝔪.

Define HasGoodReduction R f by the existence of an integral homogeneous lift with a unit coefficient and unit resultant. The normalization condition prevents the degree-zero pair from reducing to (0, 0); for positive degree it already follows from a unit resultant. Reduce a normalized integral lift coefficientwise. Its residue pair is nonzero because a unit coefficient survives, and its resultant is nonzero because it is the residue of a unit. Normalized lifts of the same map differ by an R-unit, so their reduced classes agree; the degree remains d. For an integral polynomial p ∈ R[X] of positive degree n, the standard lift is normalized because its second form is X₁^n, and its resultant is lead(p)^n. Thus, under the integral-coefficient hypothesis, good reduction is equivalent to a unit leading coefficient. Constants, including nonunits and zero, have good reduction via a normalized constant pair. Degree-one maps from GL₂(R): resultant det γ ∈ R^×.

- The reduced map over the residue field.
- deg (reduction f) = deg f.

- Maps given by γ ∈ GL₂(R) have good reduction.

- (z² + 2)/z has good reduction over ℤ_[3].
- z² + c with c ∈ ℤ has good reduction over every ℤ_[p].
- z²/2 is conjugate over ℚ_[2] to z², which has good reduction, while z²/2 does not.

### 0.21 Units of the monoid of rational maps: PGL₂

The units of RationalMap K are exactly the maps of degree 1, and unitsEquivPGL : (RationalMap K)ˣ ≃* PGL(2, K) (Mathlib's Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup) sends the class of the linear lift of γ ∈ GL₂(K) to the class of γ; the action of a unit on ℙ¹(K) is Mathlib's action of PGL(2, K) on ℙ K (Fin 2 → K).

K a field.

deg is multiplicative with deg 1 = 1, so a unit has degree 1; a degree-1 lift (a X₀ + b X₁, c X₀ + e X₁) has resultant ae − bc ≠ 0 (The resultant of a pair of binary forms, linear case), i.e. is ofGL of an invertible matrix, with inverse the class of ofGL γ⁻¹. The map GL₂(K) → (RationalMap K)ˣ, γ ↦ mk (ofGL γ) is a surjective homomorphism with kernel the scalars, which is the kernel of Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup.mk; this gives the MulEquiv. ### 0.22 Base change of rational maps and points

For a field homomorphism σ : K → L, RationalMap.map σ : RationalMap K →* RationalMap L applies σ to the coefficients of a lift, and projMap σ : ℙ¹(K) → ℙ¹(L) applies σ to coordinates; both are injective, deg is preserved, and toEnd (map σ f) (projMap σ P) = projMap σ (toEnd f P). Over a field F algebraic over ℚ every rational map is the base change of a map over a number field L ⊆ F.

σ a ring homomorphism of fields (injective).

map on lifts is HomogeneousLift.map (Homogeneous lifts of a degree-d self-map of ℙ¹); it respects proportionality and composition (MvPolynomial.map commutes with aeval), giving a monoid homomorphism. projMap σ [x] = [σ x] via Projectivization.lift (σ injective keeps σ x ≠ 0); compatibility with toEnd because MvPolynomial.eval (σ ∘ x) (map σ F) = σ (eval x F). Field of definition: the finitely many coefficients of a lift generate L = ℚ(coefficients) (IntermediateField.adjoin), finite-dimensional because F is algebraic over ℚ (IntermediateField.finiteDimensional_adjoin); the lift has coefficients in L.

### 0.23 Good reduction is read off a normalised lift

Let R be a valuation ring with fraction field K and f a rational map of degree d over K. For any integral lift F of f that is normalised (some coefficient is a unit of R): f has good reduction iff `Res_{d,d}(F₀,` F₁) ∈ R^× iff the reduced forms F̃₀, F̃₁ over k have nonzero resultant (the reduction still has degree d).

R a valuation ring, K = Frac R; F integral and normalised.

Normalised lifts exist and are unique up to R^×: scale any lift by the inverse of a coefficient of minimal valuation (valuation ring property); two normalised lifts differ by c ∈ K^× with c and `c^{-1}` integral. For d ≥ 1, an integral lift c·F of a normalized lift has c ∈ R and resultant `c^{2d}Res(F);` this is a unit exactly when both c and Res(F) are units. For d = 0 the resultant is always 1, and the normalized nonzero constant pair directly supplies good reduction. IsUnit x ↔ residue x ≠ 0 in a local ring (IsLocalRing.residue_ne_zero_iff_isUnit), and the residue of Res(F) is the resultant of the reduced forms (Polynomial.resultant_map_map). For d ≥ 1, the reduced resultant is nonzero iff the reduced forms have no common zero over k̄ (The resultant vanishes exactly at a common zero), i.e. no common factor, i.e. the reduced map has degree d.

**Endpoint checks.** (X₀² + 2X₁², X₀X₁) is normalised with resultant 2: good reduction at p iff p ≠ 2. The non-normalised lift (2X₀² + 4X₁², 2X₀X₁) has resultant 32 at every p, which is why normalisation is required.

### 0.24 Reduction commutes with evaluation

Let R be a valuation ring with fraction field K and f a rational map with good reduction. For every P ∈ ℙ¹(K): projReduction (f(P)) = f̃(projReduction P).

R a valuation ring; f with good reduction.

Take an integral lift F with unit resultant and a representative x ∈ R² of P with a unit coordinate. F(x) ∈ R² reduces to F̃(x̃), which is nonzero because x̃ ≠ 0 and F̃ is a lift over k (Homogeneous lifts of a degree-d self-map of ℙ¹, eval_ne_zero); so F(x) has a unit coordinate and projReduction [F(x)] = [F̃(x̃)] (Reduction of points of ℙ¹ modulo the maximal ideal).

### 0.25 Conjugation of rational maps by PGL₂

PGL(2, K) acts on RationalMap K by γ • f = γ ∘ f ∘ γ⁻¹ (the action of the unit group through unitsEquivPGL and Mathlib's ConjAct); two maps are conjugate iff they are IsConj in the monoid RationalMap K. Conjugation preserves degree, intertwines the actions on ℙ¹(K) (toEnd (γ • f) ∘ γ = γ ∘ toEnd f), and on lifts is γ ∘ F ∘ adj(γ), whose resultant is `det(γ)^{d²+d}` Res(F). Convention: Silverman's and Rumely's f^γ = γ⁻¹ ∘ f ∘ γ is γ⁻¹ • f.

K a field.

Define the action as the pullback along unitsEquivPGL.symm of Mathlib's MulDistribMulAction of ConjAct (RationalMap K)ˣ on the monoid (ConjAct.units_smul_def). IsConj f g ↔ ∃ γ, γ • f = g by definition of IsConj (a unit c with c * f = g * c). Degree: deg (γ f γ⁻¹) = 1·d·1; points: toEnd is a monoid homomorphism (The action of a rational map on ℙ¹(K)) and units act by PGL(2, K) (Units of the monoid of rational maps: PGL₂). Lift formula: γ⁻¹ is the class of adj(γ); the resultant of the lift γ ∘ F ∘ adj(γ) is given by The resultant of a conjugated lift (applied to adj γ, whose adjugate is γ). Preperiodic points correspond under the bijection γ of ℙ¹(K) (Semiconjugacies preserve preperiodic points).

### 0.26 Rational maps as endomorphisms of the scheme ℙ¹_K

For a field K there is an injective monoid homomorphism RationalMap K → End(ℙ¹_K) into the K-endomorphisms of the projective line ℙ¹_K = Proj K[X₀, X₁], sending mk F to the morphism [F₀ : F₁]; its action on K-points is RationalMap.toEnd and every K-endomorphism of ℙ¹_K is in the image. Hence f^n corresponds to the n-th power of a scheme morphism, and by Iterates of an endomorphism act on points by its powers iterate equality is equality of morphisms of schemes.

K a field; SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.3 supplies ℙ¹_K, its charts and O(n). This target constructs the morphism from a base-point-free homogeneous pair and classifies all K-endomorphisms, including degree-zero constants.

First prove the Picard classification of the projective line: every line bundle on ℙ¹_K is O(d) for a unique integer d, and the global-section formula for O(d): global sections of O(d), for d≥0, identify with degree-d binary forms, compatibly with evaluation on both standard charts. Prove the description of projective-line morphisms by generating sections: morphisms to ℙ¹ correspond to an invertible sheaf with two generating sections up to isomorphism; its pullback of O(1) is that sheaf. A globally generated O(d) has d≥0. Construct the map to scheme endomorphisms by gluing the chart ratios F₀/F₁ and F₁/F₀ on their nonvanishing loci. Prove agreement on points, compatibility with composition, invariance under scaling the lift, and bijectivity. For surjectivity apply the three preceding projective-line targets; for injectivity compare over K̄, an infinite field, then descend morphism equality. These prerequisites are owned here (Silverman AWS §6.1, p.19; Stacks §27.13, Lemma 27.13.1 (Tag 01NE), Picard calculation Lemma 31.29.5 (Tag 0BXJ), and section calculation Lemma 30.8.1 (Tag 01XT)).

- (X₀²,X₀X₁) fails to generate O(2) at [0:1]; a pair with a common zero cannot define this degree-two morphism.

### 0.27 Reduction commutes with composition and iteration

Let R be a valuation ring with fraction field K. If f and g have good reduction then so does f g, and (f g)~ = f̃ g̃; in particular f^n has good reduction and (f^n)~ = (f̃)^n.

R a valuation ring; f, g with good reduction.

Take integral lifts F, G with unit resultants. F ∘ G has integral coefficients and reduces to F̃ ∘ G̃ (reduction is a ring homomorphism, compatible with MvPolynomial.aeval). F̃ and G̃ have nonzero resultant over k, so F̃ ∘ G̃ is a lift over k (Composition of homogeneous lifts), i.e. its resultant — the residue of Res(F ∘ G) — is nonzero; hence Res(F ∘ G) is a unit (IsLocalRing.residue_ne_zero_iff_isUnit) and f g has good reduction with reduction mk(F̃ ∘ G̃) = f̃ g̃. ### 0.27a The power map z ↦ z^d on the projective line

Let K be a field and d ≥ 1 an integer. The power map P_d : ℙ¹_K → ℙ¹_K is the rational map (Rational self-maps of ℙ¹ over a field) given by the pair of homogeneous forms (X^d, Y^d): [x : y] ↦ [x^d : y^d]. In the affine coordinate z = x/y it is z ↦ z^d, with P_d(0) = 0 and P_d(∞) = ∞ (∞ = [1 : 0]). It has degree d, and Res(X^d, Y^d) = 1 in the normalisation of The resultant of a pair of binary forms. Iterates P_dⁿ are composites of morphisms.

K is any field; the definition needs no characteristic hypothesis. d ≥ 1; the dynamical statements (canonical height, preperiodic points, multipliers) assume d ≥ 2, where P_d is polarised: P_d^*O(1) ≅ O(d). The multiplier d at a fixed root of unity and the critical-point count use char K ∤ d (in characteristic p | d, P_d is inseparable and every affine point is critical).

X^d and Y^d are homogeneous of degree d; over an algebraic closure their only common zero is (0, 0), since x^d = y^d = 0 forces x = y = 0. Hence (X^d, Y^d) is a Layer 0 rational map of degree d. Resultant: dehomogenising, Res(X^d, 1) = 1 (Mathlib Polynomial.resultant; the Sylvester matrix of (X^d, 1) is the identity), so Res(X^d, Y^d) = 1 and P_d has good reduction at every nonarchimedean place (Good reduction of a rational map). Composition: (X^d, Y^d) ∘ (X^e, Y^e) = ((X^e)^d, (Y^e)^d) = `(X^{de},` `Y^{de})` as forms, so P_d ∘ P_e = `P_{de}` as rational maps and P_dⁿ = `P_{dⁿ}` by induction on n.

### 0.27b Admissible absolute values and heights on a rational function field

Let k be a field and k(t) = RatFunc k. For each monic irreducible π ∈ k[t] let |g|_π := exp(−deg π · ord_π g), and let |g|_∞ := exp(deg num(g) − deg denom(g)) (Mathlib RatFunc.inftyValuation), for g ≠ 0. These are nonarchimedean absolute values; for g ≠ 0 almost all of them equal 1 at g; and ∏_v |g|_v = 1. They form an instance of Mathlib's Height.AdmissibleAbsValues on k(t) with no archimedean absolute values. The resulting logarithmic height is the degree height: Height.logHeight₁ g = max(deg num g, deg denom g), and for coprime p, q ∈ k[t] not both zero the height of [p : q] ∈ ℙ¹(k(t)) is Height.logHeight ![p, q] = max(deg p, deg q) =: `h_{k(t)}(`[p : q]).

k any field (finite or infinite, any characteristic). The absolute values are normalised so that log|t|_∞ = 1: this is the height relative to the divisor (∞) of degree 1 on ℙ¹_k.

Each |·|_π and |·|_∞ comes from a discrete valuation (IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation on k[t], RatFunc.inftyValuation) composed with x ↦ exp(−c·x); ultrametric, hence nonarchimedean. Finiteness of support: g ≠ 0 has finitely many zeros and poles among the monic irreducibles. Product formula: Σ_π deg π · ord_π(g) = deg num(g) − deg denom(g) by unique factorisation in k[t], which is log|g|_∞. Thus Σ_π log|g|_π+log|g|_∞=0. For g=t the finite degree sum and log|t|_∞ both equal 1, fixing the infinity sign. Height: Σ_v log⁺|g|_v = Σ_π deg π · max(0, −ord_π g) + max(0, deg num g − deg denom g) = deg denom g + max(0, deg num g − deg denom g) = max(deg num g, deg denom g); the vector formula follows in the same way with max over coordinates.

**Endpoint checks.** h((t² + 1)/(t − 1)) = 2 and h(![t², t + 1]) = 2. Constants have height 0, so Northcott fails when k is infinite: the set {g : h(g) ≤ 0} contains k. For g ∉ k, h(g) = [k(t) : k(g)] (Mathlib RatFunc.finrank_eq_max_natDegree).

### 0.29 The moduli space M_d(K) of degree-d maps

For a field K and d ∈ ℕ, ModuliSpace K d is the set of conjugacy classes (Mathlib's ConjClasses of the monoid RationalMap K) of maps of degree d, i.e. Rat_d(K)/PGL₂(K). For d ≥ 2 and K algebraically closed it is the set of K-points of Silverman's geometric quotient M_d = Rat_d/SL₂ (whose scheme structure is specified below as a required construction); for non-closed K it separates twists. Base change K → L induces M_d(K) → M_d(L).

K a field; no algebraic closedness in the definition. The scheme structure, affineness and dimension 2d − 2 for d ≥ 2 are separate GIT targets. Degree 0 and 1 here refer only to the orbit set; the degree-one GIT quotient does not separate all conjugacy classes.

Degree is a conjugacy invariant (Conjugation of rational maps by PGL₂), so it descends to ConjClasses (RationalMap K) (conjDegree); ModuliSpace K d is the fibre over d. mk f = mk g iff IsConj f g (ConjClasses.mk_eq_mk_iff_isConj); every class has a representative. Base change: IsConj is preserved by the monoid homomorphism map σ (Base change of rational maps and points).

### 0.30 The fixed points of a rational map, with multiplicity

For f = mk F of degree d, the fixed-point form is X₁F₀ − X₀F₁ (degree d + 1), and fixedPoints f := binaryRoots (d + 1) (X₁F₀ − X₀F₁). For d ≥ 2 the form is nonzero, P ∈ fixedPoints f iff toEnd f P = P, the multiset has d + 1 elements over an algebraically closed field, and conjugation transports it: fixedPoints (γ • f) = γ · fixedPoints f.

K a field; d ≥ 2 for the nonvanishing of the form (for the identity map the form is 0).

Well defined on the class: scaling F scales the form (The zeros of a binary form in ℙ¹, with multiplicity, binaryRoots_smul). Nonvanishing for d ≥ 2: if X₁F₀ = X₀F₁ then X₀ | F₀ and X₁ | F₁ with F₀ = X₀H, F₁ = X₁H, and H of degree d − 1 ≥ 1 is a common factor, contradicting Res ≠ 0 (The resultant vanishes exactly at a common zero). Membership: [x] is fixed iff F(x) is proportional to x iff x₁F₀(x) − x₀F₁(x) = 0 (The zeros of a binary form in ℙ¹, with multiplicity, mem_binaryRoots_iff). Conjugation: the fixed-point form of γ ∘ F ∘ adj(γ) is the fixed-point form of F composed with adj(γ) (the 2 × 2 determinant det[y, γF(adj(γ)y)] with y = γx/det γ), whose roots are γ applied to those of F.

- The multiset of fixed points of f.
- For deg f ≥ 2: P ∈ fixedPoints f ↔ toEnd f P = P.

- fixedPoints (γ • f) = (fixedPoints f).map (γ • ·).

- fixedPoints (z²) = {0, 1, ∞}.
- z ↦ z + 1 has the single fixed point ∞ with multiplicity 2.
- Over ℚ, fixedPoints (z² + 1) = {∞}: the K-points of the multiset miss the irrational fixed points.

### 0.31 The critical points of a rational map, with multiplicity

For f = mk F of degree d, the Jacobian form Jac(F) = ∂₀F₀·∂₁F₁ − ∂₁F₀·∂₀F₁ is a binary form of degree 2d − 2, and criticalPoints f := binaryRoots (2d − 2) (Jac F). In characteristic 0 and d ≥ 1, at a finite point [z : 1] with F₁(z, 1) ≠ 0 membership is equivalent to f'(z) = 0. In characteristic 0 and d ≥ 1 there are 2d − 2 critical points with multiplicity over an algebraically closed field (Riemann–Hurwitz), each of multiplicity at most d − 1; conjugation transports them.

K a field; the affine derivative and ramification interpretations below require characteristic 0 and positive degree. In characteristic p the Jacobian can vanish even for separable degree-p maps (for example z^p + z), so this total definition is not the critical divisor in that generality.

Jac(cF) = c² Jac(F), so the roots depend only on f (The zeros of a binary form in ℙ¹, with multiplicity, binaryRoots_smul); Jac(F) is homogeneous of degree 2(d − 1) (MvPolynomial.pderiv lowers degree by 1). Affine characterisation: with f_i = F_i(X, 1), Euler's identity z∂₀F_i + ∂₁F_i = d F_i at (z, 1) gives Jac(F)(z, 1) = d·(f₀'f₁ − f₀f₁')(z); in characteristic 0, for F₁(z, 1) ≠ 0 the point is critical iff the derivative of f₀/f₁ vanishes at z. Nonvanishing and count in characteristic 0: f₁ ≠ 0 (otherwise F₁ = 0 and Res = 0), and d·f₁²·(f₀/f₁)' ≠ 0 because a map of degree d ≥ 1 is not constant; so Jac(F) ≠ 0 and it has 2d − 2 roots (card_binaryRoots). Conjugation: Jac(γ ∘ F ∘ adj γ) = det(γ)^2 · (Jac F) ∘ adj(γ) by the chain rule, so criticalPoints (γ • f) = γ · criticalPoints f; chain rule for composites gives the critical points of f ∘ g.

Prove the following basic API.

- The multiset of critical points.
- Characteristic 0, algebraically closed, d ≥ 1: 2d − 2 critical points.
- criticalPoints (γ • f) = (criticalPoints f).map (γ • ·).
- Characteristic 0: each critical point has multiplicity ≤ d − 1.
- Characteristic 0, d ≥ 1: at [x : 1] with F₁(x, 1) ≠ 0, critical iff (f₀'f₁ − f₀f₁')(x) = 0 for f_i = F_i(X, 1).
- Chain rule: P is critical for f ∘ g iff P is critical for g or g(P) is critical for f.
- Chain rule: for rational maps f, g of degree ≥ 1 in characteristic 0, local degrees multiply, `e_{f∘g}(c)` = e_g(c)·e_f(g(c)), where the critical multiplicity at c is e(c) − 1; so c is critical for f ∘ g iff c is critical for g or g(c) is critical for f.
- The local degree of the n-th iterate at c is the product of the local degrees of f at c, f(c), …, `f^{n−1}(c);` hence the critical points of fⁿ are the points whose orbit meets a critical point of f within n − 1 steps, with critical multiplicity that product minus one.

**Checks.**

- z³ over ℚ has critical points 0, 0, ∞, ∞.
- In characteristic p, z^p has no critical points in the sense of the Jacobian form (it vanishes identically).
- For Milnor's normal form, [ω : 1] is critical iff μ₂ω² + 2ω + μ₁ = 0.

**Endpoint checks.** z³ over ℚ: 0 and ∞, each twice. z^p over 𝔽_p: Jac = 0 and the definition returns no critical points. Milnor's normal form z(z + μ₁)/(μ₂z + 1): Jac = 2(μ₂X₀² + 2X₀X₁ + μ₁X₁²).

### 0.33 The multiplier of a rational map at a fixed point

For f with lift F and a fixed point P: if P = [z : 1] then μ_P(f) = f'(z), the derivative at z of the rational function F₀(X, 1)/F₁(X, 1) (F₁(z, 1) ≠ 0 at a finite fixed point); if P = ∞ then μ_∞(f) = μ_0(ι • f) with ι(z) = 1/z. Coordinate-free (all characteristics): if F(x) = c·x with c ≠ 0 then `μ_{[x]}(f)` = (∂₀F₀(x) + ∂₁F₁(x))/c − d. The value at a non-fixed point is unspecified (junk).

K a field; P fixed by f for the value to be meaningful.

Finite fixed point: with f(z) = F₀(z,1)/F₁(z,1) and F₁(z, 1) ≠ 0 (since f(z) = z is finite), μ = (F₀'F₁ − F₀F₁')(z)/F₁(z, 1)² (Polynomial.derivative). At ∞ use the unit ι = [z ↦ 1/z] of Units of the monoid of rational maps: PGL₂ and the finite formula for ι • f at 0. Trace formula: Euler's identity x₀∂₀F_i + x₁∂₁F_i = d F_i for forms of degree d (MvPolynomial.pderiv) gives, at a finite fixed point [z : 1] with F(z, 1) = c(z, 1), ∂₀F₀ − z∂₀F₁ = tr DF − dc, and f'(z) = (∂₀F₀ − z∂₀F₁)/c. Polynomial maps: `μ_{[z:1]}` = p'(z); μ_∞ = 0 when deg p ≥ 2 (ι • p = 1/p(1/w) = w^n/(...) vanishes to order n at 0). For a fixed point of a map of degree at least 2, μ_P = 1 iff P is a multiple root of the nonzero fixed-point form: its chart derivative is c(μ_P − 1). The identity is excluded, since its fixed-point form is zero and fixedPoints returns the empty multiset.

### 0.34 Critically marked maps and their moduli M_d^cm(K)

A critically marked map of degree d is (f, c) with deg f = d and c : Fin (2d − 2) → ℙ¹(K) listing criticalPoints f with multiplicity; PGL(2, K) acts on (f, c) by γ • (f, c) = (γ • f, γ ∘ c), and CriticallyMarkedModuliSpace K d is the orbit quotient. That scheme-level cover belongs to the geometric-invariant-theory contract. It is not identified with this orbit quotient and no fine-moduli universal property is asserted: critical marking alone can leave automorphisms.

Define CriticallyMarkedMap K d as the subtype and the action through Conjugation of rational maps by PGL₂ and The critical points of a rational map, with multiplicity (criticalPoints_smul keeps the marking valid). Quotient by MulAction.orbitRel; forget (f, c) = mk f is well defined. Surjectivity: over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 the multiset has 2d − 2 elements (card_criticalPoints), so it can be listed. Fibres: two markings of the same f differ by a permutation; conjugacies of the map act compatibly.

### 0.35 Multipliers are conjugation invariant

For γ ∈ PGL(2, K), f a rational map and P a fixed point of f: `μ_{γ•P}(γ` • f) = μ_P(f).

Homogeneity gives G(y) = t^d·c·y and DG(y) = `t^{d−1}·γ·DF(x)·adj(γ).` Its trace is t^d·tr DF(x), so the trace divided by the eigenvalue, and hence the multiplier, is unchanged. Degree zero has zero derivatives and multiplier zero. ### 0.36 Milnor's normal forms for quadratic maps

Let K be algebraically closed of characteristic 0 and f of degree 2 over K. Either f has two distinct fixed points and is conjugate to z(z + μ₁)/(μ₂z + 1) with μ₁μ₂ ≠ 1, μ₁ and μ₂ the multipliers at 0 and ∞; or f has a single fixed point and is conjugate to z + 1/z. In the first case the normal form is determined by (μ₁, μ₂).

### 0.39 Milnor's relation σ₃ = σ₁ − 2

Normal form z + 1/z: the single fixed point ∞ has multiplicity 3 and multiplier 1 (multiplier_eq_one_iff), so σ₃ = 1 = σ₁ − 2.

## Layer 1: Canonical heights

Tate’s elementary limiting argument is the common engine. Separate the projective-line construction on native height carriers from the general-variety and divisorial-eigenclass endpoints, which require HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §0.16. Zero height implies preperiodicity only with the stated Northcott and field hypotheses.

### 1.1 Normalized iterates and the Tate series

Use the argument order tateLimit φ α h throughout. For any φ:S→S, h:S→ℝ, α>1, P∈S and n≥0, prove the finite identity h(P)+Σ_(0≤i<n) α^(−i−1)(h(φ^(i+1)P)−αh(φ^iP))=h(φ^nP)/α^n. Thus whenever the normalized iterates at P converge, the error series at P is summable and the supplied tateLimit φ α h P is that limit. This comparison also applies to a finite orbit without a global bounded-error assumption; it does not prescribe a second definition through a total limit (Call–Silverman §1, Proposition 1.2, (4)–(6), p.169).

Under α>1 and a global bounded-error hypothesis, derive the following refinements from the supplied convergence and uniqueness theorems.

- Multiplying h by any real c multiplies its Tate limit by c; the error bound becomes |c|C.
- Replacing (φ,α) by (φ^[k],α^k), k≥1, leaves the Tate limit unchanged; the new error bound is C(1+α+⋯+α^(k−1)).
- If h≥0, the Tate limit is nonnegative, by the normalized-iterate comparison.

**Checks.**

- For φ=id,h=1,α=2, the partial sums for n=0,1,2 are 1,1/2,1/4 and tend to 0, not to the initial height 1.
- For φ(x)=2x,h(x)=x,α=2,P=1, all errors are 0 and the normalized terms at n=0,1,2 are 1,1,1; replacing φ by φ² and α by 4 gives the same value 1.
- For the same φ and α with h(x)=−x,P=1, the limit is −1; nonnegativity needs h≥0. Taking c=−2 multiplies the original limit 1 by −2.
- On ℕ with φ(n)=n+1,h(n)=n², the global error |(n+1)²−2n²| is unbounded. On an adjoined fixed point P with h(P)=1 the normalized sequence is still 2^(−n) and the comparison gives Tate value 0 there.
