### 2.1 Meromorphic maps to the sphere

For a nonempty connected open domain Ω ⊆ ℂ and f meromorphic on Ω, prove
the meromorphic-to-sphere holomorphy comparison: the meromorphic germs of f determine a
unique holomorphic map Ω → `OnePoint ℂ`, taking the value ∞ at each pole and
the analytic extension value at every removable singularity. Conversely, a
holomorphic sphere-valued map other than the constant-infinity map determines
these meromorphic germs. Use the supplied atlas and chartwise differentiability
criteria, with Mathlib `MeromorphicOn` and `meromorphicOrderAt`. Values assigned
to a meromorphic function at isolated singularities do not determine its
extension (Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces, §§1.9, 1.12–1.16).

- The meromorphic function 1/z extends with value ∞ at 0; retaining totalized division's value 0 there gives a discontinuous map.
- The quotient z/z extends with value 1 at 0; its totalized value 0 is a removable-value error, rather than a pole.
- The zero function gives the constant finite map 0, whereas the constant-infinity map is the separate case; order ⊤ must not be treated as a negative pole order.

potential class, and define the more general curvature distribution separately.

Prove symmetry, additivity, nonnegativity of self-energy, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and the following coordinate-change formula: for mass-zero ν,η each a continuous-potential part plus finitely many type-I atoms, simultaneous Möbius transport changes their mutual energy by Σ_x ν({x})η({x})log|γ′(x)| in affine charts avoiding poles, with the reciprocal-chart version at infinity. This is zero for two continuous-potential measures, but need not vanish for empirical measures.

**Checks.**

- At two nested disc points of radii 1 and 2 the mass-zero difference has self-energy log 2; the reverse sign violates positivity.
- The zero signed measure has energy zero, while a nonzero continuous-potential mass-zero measure has positive energy; constants cannot be treated as measures of mass zero.
- At distinct type-I points x,y the mutual energy is −log|x − y|; diagonal-excluded atomic self-energy uses the empty sum for a singleton.
- Over ℂ, ν=δ₀−δ₁ has energy 0, while the pushforward under z↦2z has energy 2 log 2. In every empirical-measure coordinate change retain the atomic diagonal correction; a global cancellation requires the product formula, not local invariance.

### 2.6 Ergodic foundations for measure entropy

Use the native ergodic predicates and conditional-expectation API, and construct the additional finite-partition entropy, conditional entropy, Shannon–McMillan–Breiman and ergodic-decomposition contract specified below. Birkhoff alone does not supply measure entropy.

Use Mathlib `Ergodic`, measure-preserving transformations, conditional expectation on their native carriers. Prove the pointwise Birkhoff theorem for an integrable real function on a probability space under a measure-preserving transformation: its time averages converge almost everywhere to conditional expectation on the invariant σ-algebra, and to its integral in the ergodic case (Lyubich1983, §7, pp. 374–375, ergodic-theory inputs). The new definition is measure entropy, constructed by the partition target below.

**Checks.**

- On a one-point probability space every partition has entropy 0; the empty atom contributes 0log0 = 0.
- A two-symbol uniform Bernoulli shift has entropy log 2, distinguishing natural from base-two logarithms.
- The identity on a two-point probability space is measure preserving but not ergodic; measure preservation alone cannot discharge an ergodicity hypothesis.

### 2.7 Measure entropy and maximizing measures

Use Mathlib ergodicity and conditional expectations, with the preceding pointwise Birkhoff theorem, and extend this ergodic theory with finite measurable-partition entropy, natural logarithms and 0log0=0. Require joins, h(T,P)=lim `n⁻¹H(∨_{j<n}T⁻ʲP),` hμ(T)=sup_P h(T,P), fibre disintegration and the conditional-entropy lower bound, hμ(T)≤Dynamics.coverEntropy T univ, Shannon–McMillan–Breiman with the positive-measure Bowen-set estimate, and ergodic decomposition with integration of entropy. These are the exact entropy inputs to Lyubich §7, Lemma 1 and the maximal-entropy proof.

Applications include [Degree and topological entropy](#267-degree-and-topological-entropy); [Entropy of the canonical measure](#285-entropy-of-the-canonical-measure); [Unique maximal-entropy measure](#290-unique-maximal-entropy-measure); [`µ_{f,∞}` is Lyubich's measure of maximal entropy](#292-µ_f-is-lyubichs-measure-of-maximal-entropy).

### 2.8 Spherical meromorphic Montel

Extend the ConformalMapping local theory with normality in the compact-open spherical topology for meromorphic maps on a plane domain omitting three fixed distinct sphere values, including a constant-infinity limit. Prove its equivalence with local uniform equicontinuity by compact-domain Arzelà–Ascoli. Use the sphere charts and ConformalMapping L0 Hurwitz theorem to prove that spherical limits are holomorphic sphere maps and to obtain compact-subdomain derivative control. ConformalMapping L1's locally bounded holomorphic theorem alone has a different hypothesis (Lyubich §3).

Applications include [Classical Fatou and Julia sets](#218-classical-fatou-and-julia-sets); [Repelling periodic points are dense in Julia](#235-repelling-periodic-points-are-dense-in-julia); [Complex blowing up and inverse branches](#247-complex-blowing-up-and-inverse-branches); [Polynomial-size Bowen nets for rational sphere maps](#257-polynomial-size-bowen-nets-for-rational-sphere-maps).

### 2.9 Almost-periodic Banach contractions

For a continuous linear contraction on a complex Banach space whose every orbit is relatively compact, prove the direct-sum decomposition into the closed span of unimodular eigenvectors and the subspace on which iterates tend to zero. When the only unimodular eigenvectors are the constants at eigenvalue 1, obtain convergence to the constant projection. The proof uses the compact abelian group associated to the recurrent operator powers, Haar averaging and characters. This is the Banach/Markov extension of OperatorTheory; the dynamical inverse-branch and eigenfunction arguments are in Layer 2 (Lyubich §2, pp.352–354).

### 2.12 The homogeneous escape rate `G_{F,v}`

It is defined at every absolute value, archimedean or not, without completeness of K; for a place v of a number field K it is taken with the absolute value v itself (Mathlib's InfinitePlace, resp. normalised FinitePlace).

d ≥ 2 Res(F) ≠ 0 x ≠ 0 (the formula is extended by the junk value of limUnder at x = 0)

### 2.14 The multiplier of a periodic cycle

Let f be a rational map of degree d ≥ 1 over a field K (any characteristic; Rational self-maps of ℙ¹ over a field) and P ∈ ℙ¹(K) periodic of exact period n ≥ 1. The multiplier of the cycle of P is λ(P) = `λ_{fⁿ}(P),` the fixed-point multiplier of fⁿ at P (The multiplier of a rational map at a fixed point). With a lift F, Φ = Fⁿ and Φ(x) = μ·x for a representative x of P, Layer 0's trace formula gives λ(P) = tr(DΦ(x))/μ − dⁿ with dⁿ read in K: no division by the degree occurs, so the residue characteristic is kept (in characteristic p | d the value is still defined). In an affine chart containing the orbit, λ(P) = `∏_{i<n}` f′(fⁱ(z)) (Chain rule: the multiplier of a cycle is a product of derivatives); it is the same for all points of the cycle (All points of a cycle have the same multiplier), and for P fixed by fᵐ (n | m) the multiplier of P for fᵐ is `λ(P)^{m/n}.`

P periodic of exact period n ≥ 1 for f

Define λ(P) := `λ_{fⁿ}(P)` with n = minimalPeriod (toEnd f) P (Mathlib's Function.minimalPeriod; toEnd is The action of a rational map on ℙ¹(K)), using The multiplier of a rational map at a fixed point for fⁿ, the n-th power in Layer 0's monoid of rational maps. The trace formula is Layer 0's characterisation of the fixed-point multiplier, applied to the lift Fⁿ of fⁿ.

### 2.17 Exceptional points

For a self-map f of X, backwardOrbit(f,a)={x : ∃n≥0, f^n(x)=a} and exceptionalSet(f)={a : backwardOrbit(f,a) is finite}. The n=0 term contains a. For a surjective self-map this agrees with finite grand orbit; for rational maps of degree ≥2 take K algebraically closed, or assume surjectivity on the chosen point carrier; finiteness of a single fibre does not define exceptional. On the Berkovich line distinguish the classical exceptional set from the set computed on the full analytic carrier.

Use native Nat.iterate and Set.Finite; expose the union of iterated preimages. For a surjective self-map, each point in a finite backward orbit has a preimage in that set. Counting the available preimages forces the set to be permuted; hence it is a finite union of cycles and includes its forward orbit. A nonconstant rational map is surjective on ℙ¹(K) when K is algebraically closed; over an arbitrary field its action on K-points need not be surjective. This proves equivalence with the source’s grand-orbit convention.

### 2.20 Weighted divisibility for p-fold composition

Let p be an odd prime and H=X+∑b_iX^i be the generic polynomial over Z[b_0,…,b_D]. For 0≤β≤p−1, every monomial c∏b_i^α_i with coefficient c not divisible by p in [X^β](H^p−X) satisfies `∑_{i=0}^{p−1}α_i≥p` and 2α_0+α_1≥p−1. Every composition monomial has weight ∑(i−1)α_i=β−1. For β=0 the only monomials with α_0=1 are binom(p,l+1)b_0b_1^l; in particular the term p b_0 is distinguished. Here H^p means p-fold composition, not ordinary multiplication.

Generic finite-degree polynomial; p odd prime.

Track substitution monomials by weighted degree to obtain ∑(i−1)α_i=β−1 and the β=0 binomial exceptions (Lemma 42). Reduce modulo p; high-index coefficients i≥p cannot occur in the relevant low-degree monomials with α_0<p (Lemma 39). For total low-index degree use the substitution matrix on R[X]/(X^p), with R=F_p[`b_0,…,b_{p−1}`]`/(b_0,…,b_{p−1})^p.` The operator is I+N with N^p=0, so its p-th power is I (Lemma 40). For weighted low degree embed b_0=u b_1² modulo b_1^(p−1), invert b_2, and use nilpotent quadratic preparation to find a root δ in the ideal (b_1) after a monic quadratic extension. Translate X by δ: substitution becomes triangular with diagonal 1,(1+ε),…,(1+ε)^(p−1), ε^(p−1)=0. The cyclotomic product gives characteristic polynomial t^p−1; Cayley–Hamilton gives the required identity (Lemma 41). The exact preparation step is as a construction target of this layer.

### 2.26 Classical exceptional-set dichotomy

Over an algebraically closed field, a degree-d≥2 rational map has either at most two classical exceptional points, or characteristic p>0 and a PGL₂ conjugacy to z↦z^(p^r) for r≥1. In the latter case E is the conjugate of P¹(overline(F_p)) and is countably infinite. In particular E is Borel and countable for every valued field here; in characteristic zero it has at most two points. Every degree-at-least-two map of separable degree one belongs to the Frobenius alternative.

Algebraically closed field; the absolute value is irrelevant to classification.

Surjectivity permutes every finite backward orbit. If there are three exceptional points, a common iterate fixes all three and each has a singleton inverse fibre. Normalize them to 0,1,∞. Factorization of the zero and pole forms makes that iterate z↦z^D; its singleton fibre above 1 forces z^D−1=(z−1)^D, so D is a power of the characteristic. Write f as a separable rational map composed with a Frobenius power. Separable degrees multiply under composition, so the preceding iterate forces separable degree one. A degree-d map of separable degree one has d+1 distinct fixed points: its local derivative is zero, so each fixed-point equation has a simple zero. Normalize three fixed points to 0,1,∞. In these coordinates f=M∘Frobenius^r and M fixes 0,1,∞, hence M is the identity. For Frobenius, a finite backward orbit is equivalent to algebraicity over the finite prime field. ### 2.27 Nonclassical finite grand orbits

Two such points would bound an annulus whose logarithmic modulus is multiplied by d^n under the iterate. Fixed endpoints force its positive modulus to equal d^n times itself, a contradiction. ### 2.28 Classical invariance laws

For a nonconstant rational map on P¹(C) or P¹(K) with the corresponding chordal uniformity, F and J are open/closed complements, completely invariant: f⁻¹F=f(F)=F and f⁻¹J=f(J)=J. They are unchanged by replacing f with f^m, m≥1, and are transported by PGL₂ conjugacy. These rational-map assertions are not universal laws for arbitrary topological self-maps.

Either the complex sphere case, or the complete algebraically closed nontrivially nonarchimedean chordal case; f is nonconstant in that case.

Openness follows from the local definition. For backward invariance restrict to inverse neighborhoods; for forward invariance use openness of the finite holomorphic/rational map and its local normal form. For iterate invariance write each exponent as mn+i; the finitely many rational maps f^i have uniform Lipschitz bounds in chordal metrics. PGL₂ maps and inverses have finite chordal Lipschitz constants, so they transport the local uniform condition.

### 2.29 Disc criterion for classical stability

For a family G of rational functions on P¹(K), local chordal uniform equicontinuity at x is equivalent to the existence of a projective disc D containing x such that, for every g∈G, g(D) lies in one residue class. For the family of iterates, x∈F_I iff some sufficiently small disc has this property. Equivalently there is a disc whose forward saturation omits an infinite set of classical points.

K complete and algebraically closed with a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value; f∈K(z), degree d≥2; arbitrary characteristic unless restricted.

Normalize a target residue class. The pole-free rational expansion and ultrametric coefficient bound give a common chordal Lipschitz constant on a smaller disc. Conversely a common small chordal image bound places each image in the residue class of its center (Lemmas 4.18–4.19). For the converse omitted-value criterion, move two omitted values to a finite point and infinity. Disc images of pole-free expansions are discs; an omitted finite value gives the common Lipschitz bound of Theorem 4.27 and Corollary 4.28. Infinite omission in particular provides two distinct values. For a stable disc D, no returned image can strictly contain D: the coefficient giving strict expansion would force some further returned image to leave its residue class (Lemma 4.30). If D never meets a positive iterate, shrink to D′⊊D and the saturation omits D∖D′. Otherwise some return image is contained in D, and all forward images lie in finitely many residue classes; a different residue class is omitted. Both complements are uncountable (Theorem 4.29).

### 2.47 Complex blowing up and inverse branches

For f on P¹(C), J is nonempty, perfect and completely invariant; E has at most two points and lies in F. For every open U meeting J and every compact K⊆P¹(C)∖E, there exists N with K⊆f^n(U) for all n≥N. For each a outside E, J is contained in the closure of its backward orbit (with equality if a∈J). Any family of holomorphic inverse branches of f^m defined on a domain U is spherical normal. If U meets J, their image diameters on every V compactly contained in U tend uniformly to zero as m→∞. Write `Z_ℓ=⋃_{j=1}^ℓ` f^j(Crit f) and τ=#f(Crit f). On any simply connected U disjoint from Z_ℓ, the number σ_m(U) of inverse branches satisfies σ_m(U)≥d^m(1−2τd^(−ℓ)) for m,ℓ≥1.

f∈C(z), algebraic degree d≥2, acting holomorphically on the compact Riemann sphere with spherical topology.

Meromorphic Montel bounds the permanent omitted values of forward images of a Julia neighborhood by two; backward invariance of this finite omitted set puts it in E. Exceptional cycles are superattracting and lie in F. If J were empty, compactness would give a uniformly convergent subsequence of global iterates. Uniformly close sphere maps are homotopic, contradicting deg(f^n)=d^n. Backward density and E⊂F rule out isolated Julia points. For uniform blowing up choose a repelling periodic point in U by the density theorem. A small V⊆U satisfies f^p(V)⊃V for its period p. Enlarge K to compact L outside E with f(L)⊃L using invariant exceptional-neighborhood bases. Montel for f^p and equality of exceptional sets under iteration show `⋃_{j≥0}f^{pj}(V)` covers L. These open sets increase, so a single one covers L. Applying f(L)⊃L gives the claimed inclusion for every sufficiently large exponent. For normality of all inverse branches, locally choose a periodic orbit of at least three points avoiding the domain neighborhood. Every inverse branch omits this orbit, since its forward image is outside the orbit. Montel applies; disjointness of branch images is not the omitted-value hypothesis. If U meets J and an inverse-branch subsequence of increasing order has a nonconstant limit, Hurwitz gives a neighborhood Y of the limiting image of a Julia point with Y contained in each branch image of a smaller domain U′. Complete invariance and closedness put that limiting image in J. Thus `f^{m_j}(Y)⊆U′,` contradicting uniform blowing up to a nonexceptional point outside U′. Normality then gives uniform shrinking on compact V. There are d^m branches when m≤ℓ. At each later step at most τ of the mutually disjoint branch images contain a critical value; the rest each admit d further branches. Induction gives `d^m−σ_m≤τ∑_{i=1}^{m−ℓ}d^i≤2τd^{m−ℓ}.`

### 2.48 Periodic points and multipliers

A classical periodic point a of f over K is in J_I iff its cycle multiplier λ satisfies |λ|>1; it is in F_I iff |λ|≤1. This includes indifferent points. Through the type-I embedding the same alternatives locate a in J_Ber or F_Ber.

The Berkovich statement uses the classical-trace comparison, not a multiplier definition on nonclassical points.

### 2.51 Periods of points under good reduction (Morton–Silverman)

Setting: v is a nonarchimedean absolute value on K with valuation ring 𝒪 = {a : v(a) ≤ 1}, maximal ideal 𝔪 = {a : v(a) < 1} and residue field k = 𝒪/𝔪 (Mathlib's ValuationSubring and IsLocalRing.ResidueField), a ↦ ã the residue map; p = char k ≥ 0 is the residue characteristic. A lift F is normalised if its coefficients lie in 𝒪 and one of them is a unit; f has good reduction at v when v(Res F) = 1 for a normalised lift (Good reduction of a rational map), and then f̃ = [F̃₀ : F̃₁] is a rational map over k of the same degree d. Let f have degree d ≥ 2 and good reduction at v, and let P ∈ ℙ¹(K) be periodic of exact period n. Let m be the exact period of red(P) under f̃, λ̃ = λ_m(f̃, red P) ∈ k the multiplier of the reduced cycle, and r the multiplicative order of λ̃ in k^× (r = ∞ when λ̃ = 0 or λ̃ is not a root of unity). Then either n = m, or n = m·r·p^e for some e ≥ 0, where p = char k; if char k = 0 then e = 0. (Over ℚ_p the exponent satisfies e ≤ 1 for p odd and e ≤ 3 for p = 2 by Bound on the p-power in the period (Hutz).)

v nonarchimedean f of degree ≥ 2 with good reduction at v P ∈ ℙ¹(K) periodic of exact period n

m | n by Periodic points reduce to periodic points with dividing period. Replace f by g = f^m (good reduction and g̃ = f̃^m by Reduction commutes with composition and iteration); P has exact period N = n/m under g (Function.minimalPeriod_iterate_eq_div_gcd) and red P is fixed by g̃ with multiplier λ̃. If N = 1 then n = m. Otherwise choose A ∈ GL₂(𝒪) whose second column is a primitive representative of P (so A·[0 : 1] = P and det A is a unit) and conjugate: the conjugate has good reduction (Conjugation by GL₂(R) preserves good reduction), P moves to 0, and periods and multipliers are unchanged (Multipliers are conjugation invariant). If λ̃ ≠ 1: by The orbit congruence 1 + λ + ⋯ + `λ^{N−1}` ∈ 𝔪 λ̃ ≠ 0 and λ̃^N = 1, so r is finite and r | N. Replace g by g^r and N by N/r; the new multiplier λ̃^r = 1. If N/r = 1 then n = m·r. If λ̃ = 1 and N ≥ 2: The orbit congruence 1 + λ + ⋯ + `λ^{N−1}` ∈ 𝔪 gives N = 0 in k, so p = char k > 0 and p | N; replace g by g^p (multiplier still ≡ 1) and N by N/p, and repeat. The process stops since N decreases; it ends with N = 1, giving n = m·r·p^e (r = 1 when the reduced multiplier was already 1). ### 2.56 Lyubich transfer limit

For f on P¹(C) define the native continuous-function operator `Aψ(z)=d⁻¹∑_{f(w)=z}deg_w(f)ψ(w).` There is a Radon probability ν_f such that A^nψ converges to the constant ∫ψ dν_f uniformly on every compact subset of P¹(C)\E. It is atom-free and balanced and supp ν_f=J. In particular d⁻n(f^n)*δ_a converges weakly to ν_f for a outside E. No new transfer-operator carrier is required; use continuous linear maps on native continuous functions.

f∈C(z), algebraic degree d≥2, acting holomorphically on the compact Riemann sphere with spherical topology.

Finite local-degree branches make Aψ continuous even across critical values and give ||A||≤1, positivity and A1=1. First use a compact L⊆P¹(C)∖E with f⁻¹L⊆L. Inverse-branch counting and normality prove equicontinuity of A_L^nψ. At critical preimages use continuous roots; at a nonexceptional period-r point the return multiplicity t<d^r makes the remaining branch weight (t/d^r)^k tend to zero. Arzelà–Ascoli gives relatively compact orbits in C(L). Use the almost-periodic Banach contraction splitting of Lyubich §2. Peripheral eigenfunctions must be constant and eigenvalue 1: a modulus maximizer and backward-density force equality on J. The transient part tends to zero. The exceptional cycles have forward-invariant neighborhood bases. Every compact K outside E lies in such a compact backward-invariant L. Julia is contained in each L by backward density. The measures constructed on different L agree by evaluating the same transfer limit at a fixed Julia point, so uniform convergence descends to K. The positive normalized limit functional on C(L) is represented by a Radon probability using native Riesz–Markov. Duality gives balance and normalized preimage convergence. Construct the same limit on L=J, which is compact, backward invariant and disjoint from E. Independence of L gives ν=ν_J, hence supp ν⊆J. Conversely, for nonnegative ψ on J positive at a chosen Julia point, uniform blowing up makes A^Nψ strictly positive everywhere on J; compactness gives a positive minimum. The limit functional is therefore positive on ψ, proving J⊆supp ν. A maximal positive atom of a balanced invariant probability must have full local degree along its forward orbit; the finite critical set then forces a finite grand orbit, so the atom would belong to E, disjoint from J. Thus ν is atom-free.

### 2.57 Polynomial-size Bowen nets for rational sphere maps

For every δ>0 there is a constant C_δ>0 such that, for every integer m≥1, the compact complex sphere has a finite net in the spherical Bowen metric `max_{0≤j<m}Δ(f^j` x,f^j y), of radius δ and cardinality at most C_δ m⁵d^m. The constant may depend on f and δ, but not on m.

f∈C(z), algebraic degree d≥2, acting holomorphically on the compact Riemann sphere with spherical topology.

Fix a finite spherical net X containing the critical points and at least three distinct values. Inverse branches on discs avoiding `X_m=⋃_{j=1}^m` f^j(X) omit X. Normalize each source disc to the unit disc. The requested spherical Montel theorem gives equicontinuity on a smaller disc, hence a uniform shrink factor k for this fixed omitted net; this replaces the Koebe-based proof of Lyubich Proposition 8. Use the planar annulus-cover estimate of §6 and a finite smooth sphere atlas: outside an ε-neighborhood of a finite set Z there is a variable-radius net of size ≤C|Z|²(log(δ/ε)+A)+R, with radii bounded by k times distance to Z (Proposition 7). For Z=X_m, |X_m|=O(m), and ε_m=δ/(2L^m) for a spherical Lipschitz bound L>1, this gives O(m³) centers. For each orbit, record the last time outside the critical-net neighborhood, a center at that time, a branch of the preceding iterate, and the next nearby point of X_m. Inverse-branch equicontinuity controls the earlier orbit and the Lipschitz bound controls the later orbit. There are at most C(δ)m⁵d^m such records, hence a spherical Bowen net of that size (Theorem 7).

The fixed omitted-net branch estimate is derived here from the separately requested spherical Montel theorem.)

### 2.58 Berkovich invariance laws

On P¹,an_K the Fatou/Julia sets are open/closed complements and are completely invariant under f. PGL₂ conjugacy transports them. Every classical exceptional point is in F_Ber. The iterate law is proved separately by the canonical-measure comparison below.

K complete and algebraically closed with a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value; f∈K(z), degree d≥2; arbitrary characteristic unless restricted.

Let U be stable and A the infinite complement of its forward saturation S(U). The analytic map is open, so f(U) is open and still omits A. The set A is backward invariant. Finite fibres and surjectivity make f⁻¹(A) infinite; it misses both f⁻¹(U) and S(U), hence the whole saturation of f⁻¹(U). This proves forward and backward stability without an iterate argument. PGL₂ acts by homeomorphisms on the analytic carrier, so it transports open neighborhoods, saturations and infinite complements. If E is finite, its cycles have singleton inverse fibres and full local degree, hence zero return multiplier. The nonarchimedean periodic dichotomy and classical-trace comparison put them in F_Ber. In the Frobenius alternative every classical point is stable by the inseparable-map theorem, and the same trace comparison applies.

### 2.59 The global height limit is the sum of the escape rates

Let K be a number field with Mathlib's places: InfinitePlace K (with multiplicity mult(v)) and FinitePlace K (normalised absolute values), so that Height.logHeight x = `Σ_{v | ∞}` mult(v)·log ‖x‖_v + `Σ_{v ∤ ∞}` log ‖x‖_v for x ∈ K² ∖ {0}. ### 2.60 Bound on the p-power in the period (Hutz)

Setting: v is a nonarchimedean absolute value on K with valuation ring 𝒪 = {a : v(a) ≤ 1}, maximal ideal 𝔪 = {a : v(a) < 1} and residue field k = 𝒪/𝔪 (Mathlib's ValuationSubring and IsLocalRing.ResidueField), a ↦ ã the residue map; p = char k ≥ 0 is the residue characteristic. A lift F is normalised if its coefficients lie in 𝒪 and one of them is a unit; f has good reduction at v when v(Res F) = 1 for a normalised lift (Good reduction of a rational map), and then f̃ = [F̃₀ : F̃₁] is a rational map over k of the same degree d. Let char K = 0 and v be discrete, with additive ord(π) = 1 and p = char k > 0, and let f have good reduction. In Periods of points under good reduction (Morton–Silverman) the exponent satisfies `2^{e−1}` ≤ ord(p) if p is odd, and `F_{e−1}` ≤ ord(2) if p = 2, where F_j is the j-th Fibonacci number (Mathlib's Nat.fib). In particular over ℚ_p (ord(p) = 1): e ≤ 1 for p odd and e ≤ 3 for p = 2.

v discrete normalised p = char k > 0 f good reduction Mixed characteristic: char K = 0, so ord(p) is finite; ord is additive and ord(π) = 1, whereas v is the multiplicative absolute value.

For e = 0 the asserted inequalities hold with truncated natural subtraction: 2⁰ = 1 ≤ ord(p) and F₀ = 0 ≤ ord(2); no `b_{e−1}` or `c_{e−1}` estimate is needed. For e = 1 the bounds are again 1 ≤ ord(p) and F₀ = 0 ≤ ord(2). Assume henceforth e ≥ 2. Reduce as in Periods of points under good reduction (Morton–Silverman) to g = `f^{m r}` with 0 of exact period p^e, fixed mod 𝔪 with multiplier ≡ 1. Let k₀ be the first index k < e with b_k > ord(p), or k₀ = e if none exists. For k < k₀, Valuation recursion along p-power iterates (Hutz) gives inductively b_k ≥ 2^k and, for k ≥ 1, c_k ≥ `2^{k−1}` (p odd), respectively b_k ≥ `F_{k+1}` and c_k ≥ F_k (p = 2), starting from b₀, c₀ ≥ 1 and b₁ ≥ 2. If `b_{e−1}` ≤ ord(p) then `2^{e−1}` ≤ `b_{e−1}` ≤ ord(p) (resp. F_e ≤ ord(2)). If `b_{e−1}` > ord(p) then (p − `1)·c_{e−1}` ≤ ord(p) by Valuation recursion along p-power iterates (Hutz). The b_k increase strictly (each term of the b-recursion exceeds b_k), so b_k ≥ ord(p) + 1 for all k ≥ k₀, and the c-recursion gives `c_{k+1}` ≥ min(ord(p) + 1, p·c_k) for k₀ ≤ k ≤ e − 2. If for some such k the minimum were ord(p) + 1, then (inductively) `c_{e−1}` ≥ ord(p) + 1 > ord(p)/(p − 1), a contradiction; so `c_{k+1}` ≥ p·c_k along the chain and `c_{e−1}` ≥ `p^{e−1−k₀}·c_{k₀}` ≥ `2^{e−2}` for p odd (using `c_{k₀}` ≥ `2^{k₀−1},` or c₀ ≥ 1 if k₀ = 0), respectively ≥ `F_{e−1}` for p = 2 `(F_{i+1}` ≤ 2F_i). Hence `2^{e−1}` ≤ (p − `1)·2^{e−2}` ≤ ord(p) for p odd, and `F_{e−1}` ≤ `c_{e−1}` ≤ ord(2) for p = 2 (Mathlib's Nat.fib); in the first case likewise `F_{e−1}` ≤ F_e ≤ ord(2).

### 2.61 Polynomial realization of a rational cycle

For a mixed-characteristic DVR R and P,Q∈R[X], let h=P/Q∈Frac(R)(z). Suppose a finite cycle σ lies in R and Q(a) is a unit for every a∈σ. There exists θ∈R[X] with θ(a)=h(a) on σ and with the same reduced return multiplier when the cycle has more than one point in a residue class. For a good-reduction projective rational map, apply this to its residue-return cycle after a PGL₂(R) coordinate change or reciprocal chart. Combining the corresponding residue-period and multiplier-order factorization with sharp jet growth proves the existing parent Zieve endpoint; it is not a new copy of that endpoint.

Finite K/Q_p for the corresponding consequence; more generally a DVR and good reduction at every point in the selected projective cycle suffice.

For the finite set S={Q(a):a∈σ} of units, construct a polynomial Ψ with `1−tΨ(t)=∏_{s∈S}(1−t/s).` Then θ=P·Ψ(Q) agrees with h on σ. For two distinct points in one residue class with matching images, the first-order difference quotient shows the derivatives of the corresponding return polynomials agree modulo m. Apply it to θ’s return map and the polynomial realization of h’s return; the derivative of Ψ at a denominator value gives the rational chain-rule derivative modulo m (Lemma 46). Use the corresponding reduction of periodic points to pass to the residue-return orbit, all in one residue disc, and normalize it to m. Unit denominators follow from pointwise good reduction; reciprocal coordinates handle a disc at infinity. The corresponding period theorem supplies the order r of the reduced multiplier. Replace the return map by its r-th iterate and use the polynomial realization to reach the tangent-to-identity hypotheses of sharp jet growth. Insert p^(n−1)≤2e_K/(p−1) (and p=2 sharpening) in the corresponding zieve-period-exponent-bound. No assertion that global polynomial interpolation preserves exact characteristic-zero multipliers is needed.

### 2.68 Gauss Julia set at good reduction

A residue component either has a periodic forward itinerary, omitting all other components, or has a wandering itinerary, omitting a predecessor component. Thus every point outside Gauss has a stable neighborhood. Prove Gauss is Julia directly: a weak-open neighborhood contains all but finitely many residue components. Any components omitted by all its forward images form a finite backward-invariant residue set. ### 2.80 Complex canonical measure comparison and support

The corresponding archimedean measure `μ_{f,∞}=Δg_F+ω` equals ν_f from the complex transfer limit. Hence its native support is the classical Julia set, and it is the unique atom-free balanced Radon probability. More generally it is the unique balanced Radon probability with zero mass on E, and every nonexceptional point has normalized preimages converging to `μ_{f,∞}.`

f∈C(z), algebraic degree d≥2, acting holomorphically on the compact Riemann sphere with spherical topology. The sphere measure-valued Laplacian supplier must first construct the corresponding measure and establish its positivity, mass one, atomlessness and balance.

The corresponding measure is atom-free, hence μ(E)=0 because E is finite. For each continuous ψ, balance says ∫A^nψ dμ=∫ψ dμ. Transfer convergence holds at every point outside E and |A^nψ|≤||ψ||; dominated convergence identifies ∫ψdμ with ∫ψdν. Equality of Radon measures on continuous tests proves μ=ν. The same reasoning proves uniqueness for every exceptional-null balanced probability. Support equality and preimage convergence now transport through the equality.

### 2.87 Nonarchimedean preimage equidistribution

Let μ_f be the corresponding canonical Radon probability on P¹,an_K, and E the classical exceptional set. For every Radon probability ρ with ρ(E)=0, d^(-n)(f^n)*ρ converges weakly to μ_f. Conversely, convergence implies ρ(E)=0. Pullbacks count analytic local degrees, including inseparable multiplicity. In particular normalized preimages of any a outside E converge, and μ_f is the unique balanced probability assigning E mass zero.

Identify the corresponding Δg_F+δ_G measure with the telescoping pullback construction of FRL Proposition-Definition 3.1: their potential difference is constant by uniqueness. Represent ρ−δ_G=Δu with u≤0, possibly singular. Prove d^(-n)u∘f^n→0 on the hyperbolic line, then use Hartogs and weak Laplacian convergence. Near exceptional attracting cycles use ρ’s arbitrarily small mass in small discs. Outside those basins and for separable degree >1, pass to an iterate and use diam(fζ)≥C diam(ζ)^(d−1); the resulting (d−1)^n growth is dominated by d^n. For separable degree one normalize to a Frobenius power. The residue orbit is periodic or wanders through disjoint classes; in the latter case their ρ-masses tend to zero. This handles the infinite exceptional set without an at-most-two assertion. Any positive ρ-mass on the countable classical E gives positive mass to a finite exceptional cycle. Its periodic atomic pullback part cannot converge to the corresponding measure, which has no type-I atoms. For balanced exceptional-null ρ, convergence of its constant normalized-pullback sequence proves uniqueness.

### 2.90 Unique maximal-entropy measure

If η is any f-invariant Borel probability on P¹(C) with h_η(f)=log d, then `η=ν_f=μ_{f,∞}.` Thus the corresponding archimedean maximal-entropy endpoint is supplied by the identification, the entropy value and this uniqueness theorem.

For a distinct ergodic η, singularity with ν and local inverse branches produce a positive-η set whose preferred inverse-branch blocks occur with frequency above the uniform 1/N threshold. Apply the existing Birkhoff target to the indicator of this positive-η set. Count branch words with this excessive frequency using binomial estimates/Stirling: their growth rate is θ<N. The critical-disc Bowen-net construction contributes only a polynomial factor. Lyubich’s positive-measure-set entropy lemma, proved using Shannon–McMillan–Breiman, gives hη(f)<log d. For general invariant η use the generic ergodic decomposition and entropy integration theorem; almost every ergodic component of a maximizing η must maximize and thus equal ν.

### 2.93 Berkovich blowing up and minimality

If an open U meets J_Ber, `⋃_{n≥0}f^n(U)` contains P¹,an_K\E, with E the classical exceptional set. Consequently J_Ber is contained in every closed backward-invariant S with S\E nonempty; the Julia set is the smallest nonempty closed completely invariant set not contained in E. If J_Ber has at least two points, it has no isolated point.

K complete and algebraically closed with a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value; f∈K(z), degree d≥2; arbitrary characteristic unless restricted.

If U meets J, its forward saturation has finite complement A by the definition. Since A is backward invariant, every point of A has finite grand orbit. Classical points in A belong to E. A nonclassical point in A forces potential good reduction by finite-grand-orbit rigidity. The singleton Julia point would then lie in U, contradicting its omission. For a∈S\E every U meeting J contains a backward iterate of a. Closedness and backward invariance imply J⊆S. If a Julia point were isolated, apply blowing up to a neighborhood meeting J only there. Complete invariance then forces its backward orbit to be finite, and the nonclassical rigidity forces a singleton Julia set.

### 2.94 Berkovich canonical measure has Julia support

For every f of degree ≥2 over K, the native measure support of the corresponding canonical measure is exactly J_Ber: supp μ_f=J_Ber. The support is nonempty and compact, f⁻¹(supp μ_f)=supp μ_f=f(supp μ_f), and μ_f gives the classical exceptional set mass zero.

The previous containment theorem gives supp μ⊆J and nonempty support. Local-degree measure pullback has support f⁻¹(supp μ); balance f*μ=dμ gives backward invariance of support. Closedness comes from the native support theorem; compactness follows from the native compact analytic carrier. The corresponding canonical-measure-is-probability theorem gives no type-I atoms; E is countable, so μ(E)=0. Conull support then has a point outside E. Apply Julia minimality to S=supp μ for the reverse containment. Pushforward invariance and surjectivity give the image equality.

### 2.96 Singleton and perfect Julia sets

The following are equivalent: J_Ber is a singleton; J_Ber is at most countable; J_Ber has an isolated point; f has potentially good reduction. In that case the point is type II and μ_f is its Dirac mass. Otherwise J_Ber is nonempty, uncountable and perfect.

K complete and algebraically closed with a nontrivial nonarchimedean absolute value; f∈K(z), degree d≥2; arbitrary characteristic unless restricted.

Potential good reduction gives the transported Gauss singleton. A countable nonempty compact Hausdorff space has an isolated point by the Baire theorem: without isolated points it would be a countable union of nowhere-dense singletons. An isolated Julia point forces a singleton by blowing up. Complete invariance then gives a nonclassical finite grand orbit, since classical exceptional points are Fatou; rigidity gives potential good reduction. Alternatively singleton support of a Radon probability is Dirac, and the corresponding point-mass criterion gives the same converse.

**Endpoint checks.** Perfect means closed with no isolated points in the weak topology; no second-countability assumption is introduced.

### Examples

For z ↦ z^d over ℂ the Julia set is the unit circle and its canonical measure is angular probability. Under nonarchimedean good reduction the classical Julia set is empty, while the Berkovich Julia set is the Gauss singleton with unit mass. Pure Frobenius is a separate inseparable case and can have infinitely many classical exceptional points.

### 3.1 The order of a binary form at a point of ℙ¹

Let K be a field, F ∈ K[X, Y] a binary form and P = [a : b] ∈ ℙ¹(K), given by a nonzero vector (a, b). The order of F at P is ord_P F := the largest k ≥ 0 with (bX − aY)^k ∣ F in K[X, Y], i.e. Mathlib's multiplicity of the linear form ℓ_P = bX − aY in F (with Mathlib's junk value when F = 0). It depends only on the point: replacing (a, b) by (ca, cb), c ≠ 0, multiplies ℓ_P by the unit c. For F ≠ 0 homogeneous of degree D, ord_[a:1] F is the root multiplicity of a in the dehomogenisation F(X, 1), and ord_[1:0] F = D − deg F(X, 1). Points over an extension L of K are treated by mapping F to L[X, Y].

K is any field; F ∈ K[X, Y] = MvPolynomial (Fin 2) K with X = X 0, Y = X 1. The order is used only for F ≠ 0 and P ≠ 0; no algebraic closedness is assumed in the definition.

Define ord_P F := multiplicity(ℓ_P, F) with ℓ_P = P₁·X − P₀·Y (mathlib:multiplicity). ℓ_P has degree one, hence is irreducible and prime in the unique factorisation domain K[X, Y] (instance inference: MvPolynomial over a field is a unique factorisation monoid), so ord_P(F·G) = ord_P F + ord_P G for F, G ≠ 0. Scaling P by c ≠ 0 scales ℓ_P by c, which does not change the multiplicity. Dehomogenisation: for P = [a : 1] and F homogeneous of degree D, F = (X − aY)^k·H with H(a, 1) ≠ 0 if and only if F(X, 1) = (X − a)^k·H(X, 1) with H(a, 1) ≠ 0; hence ord_[a:1] F = rootMultiplicity a (F(X, 1)) (mathlib:MvPolynomial.aeval, mathlib:Polynomial.rootMultiplicity). At ∞ the power of Y dividing F is D − deg F(X, 1) (mathlib:MvPolynomial.IsHomogeneous).

*Needs:* `multiplicity`; `MvPolynomial.aeval`; `Polynomial.rootMultiplicity`; `MvPolynomial.IsHomogeneous`.

- ord_P F ∈ ℕ for F ∈ K[X, Y] and P : Fin 2 → K.
- For a nonzero homogeneous F and P ≠ 0: ord_P F = 0 iff F(P) ≠ 0.
- For F, G ≠ 0 and P ≠ 0: ord_P(FG) = ord_P F + ord_P G.
- `ord_{cP}` F = ord_P F for c ≠ 0: the order depends only on the point of ℙ¹.
- For F ≠ 0 homogeneous: ord_[a:1] F = rootMultiplicity a (F(X, 1)) (Mathlib's Polynomial.rootMultiplicity).
- For F ≠ 0, P ≠ 0: ℓ_P^k ∣ F iff k ≤ ord_P F.

**Checks.**

- ord_[1:0](X²Y) = 1 over ℚ (the order at ∞ counts the power of Y).

- In characteristic 2, X²−Y²=(X−Y)² and ord_[1:1](X²−Y²)=2; the characteristic restriction on the preceding check is necessary.

### 3.2 The n-th period polynomial Φₙ(φ) = Y·Fₙ − X·Gₙ

Let R be a commutative ring and φ = (F, G) a pair of forms in R[X, Y] (a lift of a self-map of ℙ¹). The composite lift of φⁿ is (F₀, G₀) = (X, Y) and `(F_{n+1},` `G_{n+1})` = (F(Fₙ, Gₙ), G(Fₙ, Gₙ)). The n-th period form is Φₙ(φ) := Y·Fₙ(X, Y) − X·Gₙ(X, Y) ∈ R[X, Y]. If F, G are homogeneous of degree d then Φₙ is homogeneous of degree dⁿ + 1; Φ₀ = 0; replacing the lift by (uF, uG), u ∈ R^×, multiplies Φₙ by `u^{1 + d + ⋯ + d^{n−1}}.` For a polynomial map f of degree d with lift (Y^d f(X/Y), Y^d), Φₙ(X, 1) = fⁿ(X) − X.

Φ₀ = Y·X − X·Y = 0. Scaling: (uF, uG) has composite lift `u^{1+d+⋯+d^{n−1}}(Fₙ,` Gₙ) by induction. For a polynomial map: Fₙ = `Y^{dⁿ}` fⁿ(X/Y) and Gₙ = `Y^{dⁿ}` by induction, so Φₙ(X, 1) = fⁿ(X) − X (mathlib:Polynomial.iterate_comp_eval).

### 3.3 The formal germ of a map at a fixed point

For a lift φ = (F, G) over a field K with F(0, 1) = 0 ≠ G(0, 1) (the point 0 = [0 : 1] is fixed), the germ of φ at 0 is g_φ := F(z, 1)·G(z, 1)⁻¹ ∈ K[[z]], a power series with constant coefficient 0 (G(z, 1) is a unit of K[[z]]). Its linear coefficient is the multiplier λ = φ′(0) of the fixed point (The multiplier of a periodic cycle). For a germ g with constant coefficient 0, gⁿ denotes the n-fold substitution iterate (g⁰ = z, `g^{n+1}` = g ∘ gⁿ, Mathlib's PowerSeries.subst). A general fixed point P ∈ ℙ¹(K) is moved to 0 by a conjugation (The period form under conjugation by GL₂), which leaves the multiplier unchanged.

K is a field; F(0, 1) = 0 and G(0, 1) ≠ 0 (for a morphism lift, F(0,1) = 0 already forces G(0,1) ≠ 0). The junk value of Mathlib's power-series inverse is irrelevant because G(0, 1) ≠ 0.

The coefficient of z in gⁿ is λⁿ (chain rule for substitution: the linear coefficient of g ∘ h is the product of those of g and h, mathlib:PowerSeries.coeff). Conjugating by z ↦ uz (u ≠ 0) replaces g(z) by u·g(z/u), leaving the linear coefficient unchanged; this is the compatibility with Layer 2's conjugation-invariant multiplier.

Let r ≥ 1, let p be a prime or 0, let B : ℕ → ℤ, and put A(k) = B(v_p(k/r)) if r ∣ k and A(k) = 1 otherwise (v₀ ≡ 0). Then for every N ≥ 1: `Σ_{k ∣ N}` μ(N/k)·A(k) = [N = 1] + [N = r]·(B(0) − 1) + `Σ_{a ≥ 1}` [N = r·pᵃ]·(B(a) − B(a − 1)).

### 3.8 Denominators of preperiodic points of z^d + c

Let K be a field with a nonarchimedean valuation v (for instance a number field and a finite place), d ≥ 2, c ∈ K and α ∈ K preperiodic for f(z) = z^d + c. Case v(c) < 0 and d·v(α) > v(c): v(f(α)) = v(c), so d·v(f(α)) = d·v(c) < v(c) and f(α) falls in the previous case; α is not preperiodic. Case v(c) ≥ 0 and v(α) < 0: v(f(α)) = d·v(α) < v(α) < 0 and inductively v(fⁿ(α)) → −∞. Hence for preperiodic α: v(c) < 0 forces d·v(α) = v(c), and v(c) ≥ 0 forces v(α) ≥ 0 (mathlib:padicValRat for K = ℚ).

### 3.11 The orbit-repetition check

For a self-map f : α → α, a finite set S ⊆ α, N ∈ ℕ and x ∈ α, define the orbit-repetition predicate for f, S, N and x to mean that there are i < j < N with f^[i] x = f^[j] x and f^[k] x ∈ S for every k ≤ j. This is a predicate on a finite initial orbit segment. Prove soundness: the predicate implies preperiodicity. Prove completeness: if S contains every preperiodic point and N ≥ |S| + 1, every preperiodic x satisfies it. Prove failure of repetition outside the candidate set: if x ∉ S the predicate fails, and prove monotonicity in S and N. No equality or computability hypothesis is needed (hutz15, §2, pp. 6–7; pigeonhole on a finite forward orbit).

**Checks.**

- The identity at 3 in S = {3}, N = 2 has i = 0, j = 1; excluding the starting point loses this witness.
- The successor orbit starting at 0 has no repetition even in S = {0, …, 4}; membership in a finite candidate set alone does not imply preperiodicity.
- A three-cycle in S = {0, 1, 2} satisfies the predicate at N = 4, with i = 0, j = 3; N = 3 does not suffice for this start.
- At N = 0 there are no i < j < N, including for a fixed point.

*Needs:* Layer 0 `forwardOrbit`, preperiodicity; Mathlib finite-set pigeonhole.

### 3.19 Divisibility of binary forms is decided by their orders on ℙ¹

(a) Let K be algebraically closed and F, G ∈ K[X, Y] nonzero binary forms. Then F ∣ G in K[X, Y] if and only if ord_P F ≤ ord_P G for every P ∈ ℙ¹(K); in particular F = c·∏_P `ℓ_P^{ord_P F}` with c ∈ K^× and Σ_P ord_P F = deg F. (b) For any field extension L/K and F, G ∈ K[X, Y], if F ∣ G in L[X, Y] then F ∣ G in K[X, Y].

(a) needs K algebraically closed; (b) holds for every field extension. F, G are homogeneous and nonzero in (a).

Write f = F(X, 1), g = G(X, 1). For F homogeneous of degree a, F = `Y^{a − deg f}·Y^{deg f}` f(X/Y), so F ∣ G iff a − deg f ≤ b − deg g and f ∣ g in K[X]. By mathlib:IsAlgClosed.dvd_iff_roots_le_roots, f ∣ g iff roots f ≤ roots g, i.e. rootMultiplicity x f ≤ rootMultiplicity x g for all x (mathlib:Polynomial.count_roots); by the affine API of The order of a binary form at a point of ℙ¹ these are ord_[x:1] F ≤ ord_[x:1] G, and a − deg f = ord_∞ F. The factorisation and Σ_P ord_P F = deg F follow from the splitting of f (mathlib:IsAlgClosed.card_roots_eq_natDegree) together with the power of Y. (b): K[X, Y] → L[X, Y] (mathlib:MvPolynomial.map) is injective and L[X, Y] = L ⊗_K K[X, Y] is free over K[X, Y] on a K-basis of L containing 1. If G = F·H with H ∈ L[X, Y], expanding H in that basis and comparing the coefficient of 1 gives G = F·H₁ with H₁ ∈ K[X, Y].

### 3.20 The zeros of Φₙ are the points of period n

Let φ be a lift of a morphism of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 1 over a field K, inducing f : ℙ¹(K) → ℙ¹(K). For n ≥ 0 and P = [v] ∈ ℙ¹(K): Φₙ(φ)(v) = 0 if and only if fⁿ(P) = P.

K is a field; φ = (F, G) is a pair of binary forms of degree d ≥ 2 over K with no common zero in ℙ¹(K̄), i.e. a lift of a morphism of ℙ¹ of degree d (Rational self-maps of ℙ¹ over a field); (Fₙ, Gₙ) is the composite lift of φⁿ, so the forms of every iterate are fixed, not only their ratio.

The composite lift of a morphism has no common zero: (Fₙ(v), Gₙ(v)) ≠ 0 for v ≠ 0 (induction, Layer 0's iterate of a morphism), and fⁿ([v]) = [Fₙ(v) : Gₙ(v)]. Φₙ(v) = v₁Fₙ(v) − v₀Gₙ(v) is minus the determinant of the vectors v and (Fₙ(v), Gₙ(v)); it vanishes iff they are proportional, i.e. iff [Fₙ(v) : Gₙ(v)] = [v₀ : v₁] (mathlib:Projectivization.mk).

### 3.22 The period form under conjugation by GL₂

Let φ be a lift over a field K and A ∈ GL₂(K). Let lin = A·(X, Y)ᵀ and let ψ = A⁻¹ ∘ φ ∘ A be the conjugate lift, ψᵢ = Σⱼ (A⁻¹)ᵢⱼ φⱼ(lin). Then for every n, Φₙ(ψ) = det(A)⁻¹·Φₙ(φ)(lin); consequently ord_P Φₙ(ψ) = `ord_{AP}` Φₙ(φ), i.e. a_P(ψ, n) = `a_{AP}(φ,` n) and a*_P(ψ, n) = `a*_{AP}(φ,` n).

A is invertible; ψ is the lift of the conjugate map α⁻¹ ∘ f ∘ α of Conjugation of rational maps by PGL₂.

The composite lift of ψ is A⁻¹ ∘ (lift of φⁿ) ∘ A: the inner A⁻¹ and A cancel between consecutive factors. For a vector v: Φ(ψ)(v) = −det(v, A⁻¹w) with w = φⁿ(Av), and det(v, A⁻¹w) = det(A)⁻¹det(Av, w), so Φₙ(ψ)(v) = det(A)⁻¹Φₙ(φ)(Av). ### 3.24 The dynatomic polynomial Φ*ₙ(φ)

Let φ be a lift of a morphism of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 2 over a field K and n ≥ 1. If it is ι(Q) for some Q, set Φ*ₙ := Q; Q is unique by mathlib:IsFractionRing.injective. Otherwise the junk value 0 (never used for morphisms of degree ≥ 2). ### 3.39 The Morton–Silverman uniform boundedness conjecture

For integers N ≥ 1, d ≥ 2 and D ≥ 1, the uniform boundedness conjecture UBC(N, d, D) is the proposition: there is a constant C(N, d, D) such that for every number field K with [K : ℚ] ≤ D and every morphism φ : ℙᴺ → ℙᴺ of degree d defined over K, #PrePer(φ, ℙᴺ(K)) ≤ C(N, d, D). Use it only as an explicit hypothesis; for each fixed φ the set is finite (Northcott), and uniformity across all maps of fixed degree is the open content.

An open conjecture; no theorem of this roadmap consumes it except as an explicit hypothesis (the Layer 6 conventions). d ≥ 2 is essential: in degree 1 the identity has every point preperiodic.

Monotonicity in D, the trivial case D = 0, and the necessity of d ≥ 2 are API/tests; the per-map finiteness is Finitely many L-rational preperiodic points (Northcott).

### 3.51 Formal period versus exact period

Let φ be a lift of a morphism of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 2 over a field K. Let φ be a lift of a morphism of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 2 over a field K of characteristic p ≥ 0, P ∈ ℙ¹(K̄) periodic of exact period m, and r the multiplicative order in K̄^× of the multiplier (φᵐ)′(P) (r = ∞ if it is 0 or not a root of unity). If P is not periodic, a*_P(n) = 0.

With N = n/m: a*_P(ψ, N) = [N = 1] + [N = r](B(0) − 1) + `Σ_{a≥1}`[N = r pᵃ](B(a) − B(a − 1)) (The Möbius transform of a multiplicity profile, The multiplicity profile k ↦ a_P(k) at a fixed point); for r = ∞ it is [N = 1]. Each displayed term is ≥ 1 exactly on its support: B(0) − 1 ≥ 1, and for p > 0, B(a) − B(a − 1) ≥ B(a − 1) − 1 ≥ `2^{a−1}(B(0)` − 1) ≥ 1 by the growth B(a + 1) ≥ 2B(a) − 1 (same profile lemma), with B(0) = a_P(mr). For r = 1 the terms at N = 1 add: a*_P(m) = 1 + (B(0) − 1) = a_P(m) ≥ 2.

### 3.65 Reduction of the dynatomic polynomial at a prime of good reduction

Let R be a discrete valuation ring with fraction field K and residue field k, and φ a lift with coefficients in R such that both φ_K and its reduction φ̃ are lifts of morphisms of degree d ≥ 2 (good reduction). Then for n ≥ 1 there is a form Q ∈ R[X, Y] with Q = u·Φ*ₙ(φ_K) for some u ∈ K^× and Q̃ = Φ*ₙ(φ̃). In the language of cycles: the reduction of Z*ₙ(φ) is Z*ₙ(φ̃) (and likewise for Zₙ).

R is a discrete valuation ring; φ has good reduction (Good reduction of a rational map): after scaling the lift so that its coefficients lie in R with one of them a unit, φ̃ has no common zero over k̄ (equivalently the resultant is a unit).

Composite lifts and period forms commute with reduction (The period form commutes with change of coefficients), and Φₙ(φ̃) ≠ 0 since φ̃ is a morphism of degree ≥ 2 (API of The n-th period polynomial Φₙ(φ) = Y·Fₙ − X·Gₙ); so Φₙ(φ) ∈ R[X, Y] has unit content. Clear denominators of each Φ*ₘ(φ_K) and divide by the lowest coefficient valuation to obtain primitive Qₘ over R. The residue polynomial of a primitive form is nonzero; since k[X,Y] is a domain, a product of primitive forms is primitive. Thus lowest coefficient valuations add under multiplication. The product identity for Φ* and the unit content of Φₙ imply `∏_{m∣n}` Qₘ = v Φₙ with v a unit of R. This supplies the content argument directly, without an uncited general Gauss-content theorem. Reducing, `∏_{m∣n}` Q̃ₘ = ṽ·Φₙ(φ̃) for all n with Q̃ₘ ≠ 0; Möbius inversion over k (as in The Möbius product ∏ `Φₘ^{μ(n/m)}` is a polynomial, applied to φ̃, and mathlib:ArithmeticFunction.prod_eq_iff_prod_pow_moebius_eq_of_nonzero) gives Q̃ₙ = w·Φ*ₙ(φ̃) with w ∈ k^×; lift w to R^× and rescale Qₙ (mathlib:IsLocalRing.residue).

### 3.67 Transitivity of unicritical marked-point monodromy

For d≥2,n≥1, remove from the parameter plane the finite branch parameters of the period-n dynatomic curve. Analytic continuation acts transitively on its generic formal period-n roots (all exact period n there). The geometric-integrality conclusion is the subsequent assembly in §3.70.

Generic parameter away from every branch value; n=1 handled by the explicit graph c=z−z^d.

For n>1 rotate a primitive periodic word to its maximal lexicographic marking. If its maximal angle fails the satellite condition, primitive monodromy raises the last digit. If it satisfies the satellite condition, use the primitive angles of Lemma 3.12 successively to reach a word whose total digit sum increases. The sum is bounded by n(d−1)−1, so the process reaches the distinguished orbit with word (d−1)…(d−1)(d−2). Use the distinguished satellite loop to connect every marking in that orbit; concatenate and reverse loops to connect any two initial roots. This proves marked-point transitivity without using global connectedness or the geometric-integrality assembly of §3.70.

### 3.69 The dynatomic curve Y₁(n) of the family x^d + c

For d ≥ 2 and n ≥ 1, the dynatomic curve Y₁(n) is the affine plane curve over ℤ defined by Φ*ₙ(x, c) = 0, i.e. Spec of the coordinate ring ℤ[c][x]/(Φ*ₙ(x, c)). Its points in a ring L are the pairs (x, c) ∈ L² with Φ*ₙ(x, c) = 0; over a field these are the pairs with x of formal period n for x^d + c (exact period n apart from the points described by Which formal periods occur: n ∈ {m, m·r, m·r·pᵉ}, e.g. (−1/2, −3/4) on Y₁(2)). The substitution σ : x ↦ x^d + c induces an automorphism of Y₁(n) whose n-th power is the identity. This target owns only the affine coordinate ring and rotation. These downstream constructions are not prerequisites of the affine curve.

### 3.72 No rational 6-cycles for z² + c, conditionally (Stoll)

Let J be the Jacobian of the genus-4 curve X₀^dyn(6) = X₁^dyn(6)/⟨σ⟩ for z² + c. If the Mordell–Weil rank of J(ℚ) is 3, then X₀^dyn(6) has exactly ten rational points and there are no c, x ∈ ℚ with x of exact period 6 for z² + c. (Stoll deduces rank J(ℚ) ≤ 3, hence = 3, from the weak Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for J together with analytic continuation and the functional equation of L(J, s); that hypothesis is not consumed here.)

f_c(z) = z² + c with c ∈ ℚ; exact period is Mathlib's Function.minimalPeriod of f_c on ℚ (0 for non-periodic points). Explicit hypothesis: rank J(ℚ) = 3. The Jacobian, its Mordell–Weil group and its rank are supplied through EffectiveDiophantineMethods:ED.3; the statement is not formalisable in Mathlib at the pinned commit, so no Lean form is suggested.

Ten known rational points of X₀^dyn(6) generate a torsion-free subgroup G of rank 3 of J(ℚ) (Stoll §3); if rank J(ℚ) = 3 then G has finite index and J(ℚ) is the saturation of G (request EffectiveDiophantineMethods:ED.3: saturation at the required primes). A Chabauty argument at p = 5 with a differential annihilating G shows that no further rational point maps into the saturation of G (request EffectiveDiophantineMethods:ED.4, Stoll's lemma before Theorem 6). None of the non-cuspidal points among the ten lifts to a rational point of X₁^dyn(6), and a rational 6-cycle gives a non-cuspidal rational point of X₁^dyn(6) (The dynatomic curve Y₁(n) of the family x^d + c, Exact period n implies formal period n).

### 3.75 Rational points of period 1, 2, 3 for z² + c

Let c ∈ ℚ and f = z² + c. (1) f has a rational fixed point iff c = 1/4 − ρ² for some ρ ∈ ℚ; the fixed points are 1/2 ± ρ. (2) f has a rational point of exact period 2 iff c = −3/4 − σ² for some σ ∈ ℚ, σ ≠ 0; they are −1/2 ± σ and form a 2-cycle. (3) f has a rational point of exact period 3 iff c = −(τ⁶ + 2τ⁵ + 4τ⁴ + 8τ³ + 9τ² + 4τ + 1)/(4τ²(τ + 1)²) for some τ ∈ ℚ ∖ {0, −1}; the cycle is x₁ = (τ³ + 2τ² + τ + 1)/(2τ(τ + 1)) ↦ x₂ = (τ³ − τ − 1)/(2τ(τ + 1)) ↦ x₃ = −(τ³ + 2τ² + 3τ + 1)/(2τ(τ + 1)) ↦ x₁, and τ = x₁ + x₂. The at-most-one rational 3-cycle conclusion is owned separately by [3.88 Reduction excluding two rational 3-cycles](#388-reduction-excluding-two-rational-3-cycles).

### 4.6 The analytic projective line at a place of a number field, with its kernel, circle measures and weight

The analytic line at v is the compact Hausdorff space P¹_v^an equal to the Riemann sphere P¹(ℂ) when v is infinite and to the Berkovich projective line over C_v when v is finite, together with: (i) the inclusion P¹(K̄) → P¹_v^an of type I points, x ↦ ι_v(x), ∞ ↦ ∞; (ii) the kernel δ_v on A¹_v^an × A¹_v^an, equal to |x − y| on ℂ at an infinite place and to the Hsia kernel relative to ∞ at a finite place (δ_v(x, y) = diam(x ∨ y), the diameter of the smallest disc point above x and y; Favre–Rivera-Letelier's sup{x, y}), so that δ_v(ι_v x, ι_v y) = |x − y|_v for x, y ∈ K̄; (iii) for a ∈ K̄ and r > 0 the circle measure `m_{a,r,v},` the normalised arc-length probability measure on {z : |z − ι_v a| = r} at an infinite place and the Dirac mass at the point `ζ_{ι_v a, r}` (the sup-norm on the disc D(ι_v a, r)) at a finite place; (iv) the weight r_v = [K_v : ℚ_v]/[K : ℚ].

### 4.7 Generic sequences of algebraic points

Let X be an integral scheme of finite type over K. A sequence (x_n) of points of X with values in K̄ (viewed as points of the underlying space of X) is generic if for every Zariski-closed Z ⊊ X only finitely many n satisfy x_n ∈ Z; equivalently, no infinite subsequence is contained in a proper closed subvariety of X. On a curve (in particular on P¹) a sequence is generic iff every point occurs for only finitely many n. A sequence (x_n) is small for a height h with target c if h(x_n) → c; for an adelic metrized line bundle the target is h_L̄(X).

X integral of finite type over K; points with values in K̄.

The proper closed subsets of an integral curve are the finite sets of closed points, which gives the curve criterion. If f : X → Y is a dominant morphism and x_n ∈ X generic, then f(x_n) is generic: f(x_n) ∈ Z ⊊ Y infinitely often would put x_n in the proper closed subset `f^{-1}(Z).` A subsequence of a generic sequence is generic.

*Needs:* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme`; `AlgebraicGeometry.IsIntegral`; `IsClosed`; `Set.Finite`.

([yuan2008](#yuan2008), §1.1, p. 3 — The definition; [yuan2008](#yuan2008), §3.1, p. 34 — Small sequences.)

Prove the following basic API.

- The predicate: for every proper closed Z ⊊ X, {n : x_n ∈ Z} is finite.
- For X of dimension 1: (x_n) is generic iff {n : x_n = x} is finite for every x.
- A subsequence of a generic sequence is generic.
- The image of a generic sequence under a dominant morphism is generic.
- If all x_n lie in a proper closed Z, the sequence is not generic.

**Checks.**

- A constant sequence in a positive-dimensional integral X is not generic.
- An injective sequence of closed points of an integral curve is generic.
- A sequence of distinct points on a line in the affine plane is not generic in the plane.
- If X = Spec K is a point, its only proper closed subset is ∅, so every sequence in X is generic.

**Endpoint checks.** On P¹ the sequence of primitive n-th roots of unity is generic; the constant sequence 0 is not. For f(z) = z^d the exceptional set {0, ∞} is a proper subvariety; the sequence x_n = 0 is small (ĥ_f(0) = 0) but not generic, and [x_n]_v = δ_0 does not converge to λ_v.

Applications include Yuan Theorem 3.1 — the hypothesis of the general equidistribution theorem; DeMarco–Mavraki–Ye §2.4 (Yuan–Zhang) — generic sequences of PCF parameters on S_d; ArithmeticDynamics Layer 4 applications — a sequence in a proper exceptional subvariety is not generic.

### 4.8 The standard measure λ_v at a place

The standard measure at a place v of K is λ_v := `m_{0,1,v}:` the normalised Haar (arc-length) probability measure on the unit circle {|z| = 1} ⊂ ℂ when v is infinite, and the Dirac mass at the Gauss point `ζ_{0,1}` when v is finite. Its logarithmic potential is ∫ log δ_v(z, w) dλ_v(w) = log⁺|z|_v for z ∈ P¹(C_v) ∖ {∞}, extended continuously to A¹_v^an.

v is a place of the number field K; P¹_v^an is The analytic projective line at a place of a number field, with its kernel, circle measures and weight.

Define λ_v as the circle measure `m_{0,1,v}` of The analytic projective line at a place of a number field, with its kernel, circle measures and weight. Its potential is log max(|z|_v, 1) = log⁺|z|_v by the circle-measure potential formula (Jensen's formula at infinite places, Mathlib circleAverage_log_norm_sub_const_eq_log_radius_add_posLog; the Gauss norm at finite places). (λ_v, λ_v)_v = −∫ log⁺|z|_v dλ_v = 0 and ([x]_v, λ_v)_v = −log⁺|x|_v follow from the Fubini formula for the mutual energy supplied by Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions.

### 4.9 Galois-stable finite sets and their probability measures [F]_v

A finite set F ⊂ P¹(K̄) is Galois-stable if σ(F) = F for every σ ∈ Gal(K̄/K); the Galois orbit Gal(K̄/K)·x of x ∈ P¹(K̄) is the smallest Galois-stable set containing x, of cardinality [K(x) : K] (1 for x = ∞). For a nonempty finite F ⊂ P¹(K̄) and a place v, [F]_v := `|F|^{-1}` `Σ_{x∈F}` `δ_{ι_v x}` is the equidistributed probability measure on the image of F in P¹_v^an. If F is Galois-stable, [F]_v does not depend on the embedding ι_v.

F finite; for independence of ι_v, F Galois-stable.

The orbit of x ∈ K̄ is the set of roots of its minimal polynomial over K, finite of size [K(x) : K] (minpoly). The elements of C_v algebraic over K form an algebraic closure of K. Both embeddings ι_v and ι'_v map K̄ isomorphically onto that same field, so ι'_v = ι_v ∘ σ for a K-automorphism σ of K̄. Thus the images of a Galois-stable finite set, and their uniform measures, agree. Under a finite extension L/K and a place w of L above v, a Galois-stable set over K is Galois-stable over L and [F]_w = [F]_v on P¹_w^an = P¹_v^an.

### 4.10 Continuous functions are uniformly approximated by their circle averages

For every place v and every continuous g : P¹_v^an → ℝ, the regularisation modulus ω_g(r) := `sup_{x∈K̄}` |∫ g `dm_{x,r,v}` − g(ι_v x)| tends to 0 as r → 0⁺. If g is κ-Hölder for the chordal metric (0 < κ ≤ 1), then ω_g(r) ≤ C r^κ.

g continuous on the compact space P¹_v^an.

Infinite place: P¹(ℂ) is a compact metric space for the chordal metric, g is uniformly continuous, and every point of the circle |z − x| = r is within chordal distance ≤ r of x; so ω_g(r) ≤ `sup_{d(z,z')≤r}` |g(z) − g(z')| → 0. At a finite place, argue by compactness with convergent subnets, rather than assuming sequential compactness. Along a bounded subnet, factor every polynomial over C_v and compare Π max(|x−a_i|,r) with Π|x−a_i| as r→0: the evaluation seminorms and `ζ_{x,r}` have the same limit. If the limit is ∞, use the reciprocal chart; r→0 and |x|→∞ put both points in every sufficiently small neighbourhood of ∞. The weak topology of Layer 2 Nonarchimedean potential theory and local degrees then forces the same limit, contradicting a fixed positive difference of g-values. The Hölder bound: the chordal distance between ι x and `ζ_{x,r}` (FRL §4.7) is at most r.

*Needs:* [The analytic projective line at a place of a number field, with its kernel, circle measures and weight](#46-the-analytic-projective-line-at-a-place-of-a-number-field-with-its-kernel-circle-measures-and-weight); Layer 2, Nonarchimedean potential theory and local degrees; `CompactSpace.uniformContinuous_of_continuous`.

**Endpoint checks.** For g(z) = min(log⁺|z|_v, 1): ω_g(r) ≤ r at an infinite place (g is 1-Lipschitz in |z|) and ω_g(r) = 0 for r < 1 at a finite place `(log⁺|ζ_{x,r}|_v` = log⁺|x|_v). For g constant, ω_g ≡ 0.

Let X be a projective variety of dimension n ≥ 1 over a number field K and L̄ = (L, (‖·‖_v)_v) an ample line bundle with a semipositive adelic metric (at every place a uniform limit of semipositive model metrics, and the model metric of one integral model at almost all places; §4.1a local curvature measures and model functions). Put h_L̄(X) := `ĉ₁(L̄)^{n+1}/((n` + 1) deg_L X) and h_L̄(x) := ĉ₁(L̄|_x̄)/deg x. If (x_m) is a generic sequence in X(K̄) with h_L̄(x_m) → h_L̄(X), then for every place v the Galois-orbit probability measures `µ_{v,x_m}` converge weakly on X_v^an to c₁(L̄_v)^n / deg_L(X), a probability measure because c₁(L̄_v)^n has total mass deg_L X.

X projective, dim X = n ≥ 1; L ample with semipositive adelic metric; (x_m) generic and small.

Reduce to the geometric case over `X_{C_v}^an` and to test functions f that are smooth (infinite v) or model functions (finite v; the model-function density theorem stated in Yuan §3.3, §4.1a local curvature measures and model functions), by Stone–Weierstrass (Yuan §3.1–3.3). Variational principle: for ε > 0 twist the metric at v by `e^{−εf},` L̄(εf); then `h_{L̄(εf)}(x_m)` = h_L̄(x_m) + r_v ε ∫ f `dµ_{v,x_m}.` Write O(f) as a difference of two ample metrized line bundles and apply Yuan's arithmetic Siu inequality and adelic Minkowski to the perturbed section lattices. For large N obtain a nonzero section whose weighted logarithmic sup norms have sum at most N(−h_L̄(εf)(X)+O(ε²))+o(N); the constant in O(ε²) is independent of N. A generic sequence eventually avoids its divisor, so computing point heights with that section gives liminf_m `h_{L̄(εf)}(x_m)` ≥ `ĉ₁(L̄(εf))^{n+1}/((n+1)deg_L` X) + O(ε²). This step applies to the perturbed integrable metric without assuming it remains semipositive (Yuan Lemma 3.3 and the argument following it, pp.36–38). Expand `ĉ₁(L̄(εf))^{n+1}` = `ĉ₁(L̄)^{n+1}` + (n+1)r_v ε ∫ f c₁(L̄_v)^n + O(ε²); divide by ε and let ε → 0⁺, then replace f by −f. The global inputs (adelic intersection numbers, heights of subvarieties, arithmetic Siu, successive minima) are HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §§5.17a–f together with §4.3 arithmetic Siu; the local measures and model approximation come from §4.1a, the analytification X_v^an from §4.1 and deg_L X from SchemeAndStackFoundations Layer 5.

### 4.12 Adelic measures on the projective line

An adelic measure ρ over the number field K is a family `(ρ_v)_{v∈M_K}` of probability measures ρ_v on P¹_v^an such that (i) ρ_v = λ_v for all but finitely many places v, and (ii) each ρ_v has a continuous potential: there is a continuous `g_{ρ,v}` : P¹_v^an → ℝ with `g_{ρ,v}(z)` = ∫ log δ_v(z, w) dρ_v(w) − log⁺|z|_v for z ∈ A¹_v^an (equivalently ρ_v − λ_v = Δ `g_{ρ,v}` for the Laplacian of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions, normalised by Δ log⁺|z|_v = λ_v − δ_∞); the continuous extension satisfies `g_{ρ,v}(∞)` = 0. N(ρ) denotes the finite set of places with ρ_v ≠ λ_v. For a finite extension L/K an adelic measure over K defines one over L by ρ_w := ρ_v for w | v.

K a number field; P¹_v^an, δ_v and λ_v as in The analytic projective line at a place of a number field, with its kernel, circle measures and weight and The standard measure λ_v at a place. The Laplacian, potentials and the class of measures with continuous potential are those of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions.

The data are the measures ρ_v; condition (ii) is stated through the logarithmic potential, which needs only the kernel δ_v. A measure with continuous potential charges no type I point (the potential of a point mass at a type I point is −∞ there), in particular not ∞; hence `g_{ρ,v}(z)` → 0 as z → ∞ (FRL, proof of Proposition 2.6), which is the normalisation `g_{ρ,v}(∞)` = 0. Base change: for L/K and w | v, P¹_w^an = P¹_v^an (the same C_v) and λ_w = λ_v, so `(ρ_v)_{w|v}` is an adelic measure over L.

### 4.13 Adelic metrics on `O_{P¹}(1)`

In the local P¹ energy theory, an adelic metric means a finite-support model-admissible metric: a family φ = `(φ_v)_{v∈M_K}` of continuous functions φ_v : P¹_v^an → ℝ with φ_v = 0 for all but finitely many v. It defines at each place the continuous metric ‖·‖_v := `‖·‖_{st,v}` `e^{−φ_v}` on O(1) over P¹_v^an, where the standard metric is `‖s(x)‖_{st,v}` = |s(x₀, x₁)|_v / max(|x₀|_v, |x₁|_v) for a linear form s, extended continuously to P¹_v^an. With affine coordinate z = x₀/x₁ and ∞ = (1 : 0): −log‖x₁‖_v(z) = log⁺|z|_v + φ_v(z) (the section x₁ has divisor ∞) and −log‖x₀‖_v(z) = `log⁺|z^{-1}|_v` + φ_v(z) (divisor 0). Retain these local metric families without a descent condition. Define local Galois invariance of an adelic metric by invariance of every φ_v under §4.6’s local Galois action. For that subclass, the pair Ō=(O(1),(‖·‖_v)_v) is a descended adelically metrized line bundle in Zhang’s sense. On arbitrary families the height in §4.34 is the K-orbit average, with the same ground-field dependence as §4.18. The quasi-projective adelic completion used in the general-variety endpoint is broader and has its own approximation conditions.

K a number field; the metrics on O(1)^an over P¹_v^an are those of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions, described on P¹ by the function φ_v.

The standard metric is continuous on P¹_v^an: at a finite place −log‖x₁‖_st(S) = log⁺|S| is continuous on the Berkovich line (Layer 2 Nonarchimedean potential theory and local degrees). Two continuous metrics on the same line bundle differ by `e^{−φ}` with φ continuous (the ratio of norms of a nowhere-vanishing local section), so every continuous metric has the stated form; this is the P¹ case of the correspondence of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions. The finiteness condition is Zhang's adelic condition: at all but finitely many places the metric is the model metric of the standard model `P¹_{O_K}.`

### 4.14 Regularisation of a finite set by circles of radius r

For a place v, a nonempty finite set F ⊂ K̄ and r > 0, the regularised measure is [F]`_{v,r}` := `|F|^{-1}` `Σ_{x∈F}` `m_{x,r,v}:` the average of the normalised arc-length measures on the circles |z − x| = r (v infinite) or of the Dirac masses at the points `ζ_{x,r}` (v finite). Its potential is ∫ log δ_v(z, w) d[F]`_{v,r}(w)` = `|F|^{-1}` `Σ_{x∈F}` log max(|z − x|_v, r) for z ∈ K̄, it has a continuous potential in the sense of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions, and for x, y ∈ K̄ the mutual energy satisfies `(m_{x,r,v},` `m_{y,r,v})_v` ≤ −log max(|x − y|_v, r). Equality holds at finite places; at infinite places it holds when x = y or |x − y| ≥ 2r.

F ⊂ K̄ finite nonempty (∞ ∉ F); r > 0.

The potential formula for one circle measure is AnalyticLine.potential_circle; average over F. At an infinite place the potential z ↦ `|F|^{-1}Σ` log max(|z − x|, r) is continuous on ℂ and log|z| + o(1) at ∞, so [F]`_{v,r}` − λ_v has a continuous potential on P¹(ℂ); at a finite place [F]`_{v,r}` is a finite combination of Dirac masses at type II/III points, which has continuous potential (FRL §4.3; Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions). Integrate the potential of `m_{x,r}` against `m_{y,r}.` At a finite place the ultrametric disc formula gives exactly −log max(|x−y|,r). At an infinite place write log max(|z−x|,r) as the average of log|z−w| over w on the x-circle; Fubini and the circle-potential formula give its average over the y-circle at least log max(|x−y|,r). If |x−y| ≥ 2r, both circles are separated and the mean-value formula gives equality; for x = y the value is −log r. Overlapping distinct circles generally give a strict inequality. As r → 0, `m_{x,r,v}` → `δ_{ι_v x}` weakly, hence [F]`_{v,r}` → [F]_v.

### 4.18 The height h_ρ attached to an adelic measure

For an adelic measure ρ over K and a nonempty finite Galois-stable set F ⊂ P¹(K̄), h_ρ(F) := ½ `Σ_{v∈M_K}` r_v ([F]_v − ρ_v, [F]_v − ρ_v)_v, where (·,·)_v is the mutual energy of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions (the diagonal of type I points omitted, so ([F]_v, [F]_v)_v = `−|F|^{-2}` `Σ_{x≠y∈F∖{∞}}` log|x − y|_v); for x ∈ P¹(K̄), `h_{ρ,K}(x)` := h_ρ(Gal(K̄/K)·x). - `f_*µ_{f,v}` = `µ_{f,v}` and `f^*µ_{f,v}` = `d·µ_{f,v}` (Layer 2).

**Checks.**

- `ρ_{z^d}` = λ for every d ≥ 2.
- `ρ_{f∘f}` = ρ_f.
- For σ_α(z) = α − (α − z)² and a finite place v with |α|_v > 1, `ρ_{σ_α,v}` = `δ_{ζ_{α,1}}.`
- For f(z) = (z² − z)/p over ℚ, `ρ_{f,p}` ≠ λ_p.

**Endpoint checks.** `ρ_{z^d}` = λ for every d ≥ 2. For f(z) = (z² − z)/p over ℚ, `µ_{f,p}` is supported on a Cantor set of type I points in ℤ_p, so `ρ_{f,p}` ≠ λ_p.

Applications include Favre–Rivera-Letelier Theorem 4 / Theorem 8 and Corollary 1.5 — the canonical height is the adelic height of ρ_f, so the equidistribution theorem applies to dynamics; Petsche–Szpiro–Tucker Theorems 1–3 — ⟨ϕ, ψ⟩ = ⟨ρ_ϕ, ρ_ψ⟩ and equality of canonical measures; Baker–Rumely Theorem 2.3 — the limit measures of dynamical equidistribution; ArithmeticDynamics Layer 6 — canonical measures of Lattès maps in the Legendre family.

### 4.20 The adelic Multibrot measure

Fix D ≥ 2 and put P_c(z) = z^D + c. For a place v of ℚ (or of K ⊇ ℚ) let `G_{M,v}(c)` := `lim_{n→∞}` `D^{−(n−1)}` log⁺|P_cⁿ(0)|_v. At a finite place `G_{M,v}(c)` = log⁺|c|_v; at the infinite place G_M is continuous on ℂ, harmonic off the Multibrot set M_D = {c : (P_cⁿ(0))_n bounded}, zero on M_D, and G_M(c) = log|c| + o(1) as c → ∞ (M_D has logarithmic capacity 1). The family `µ_{M_D}` := (λ_v + `Δ(G_{M,v}` − log⁺|c|_v))_v — the harmonic (equilibrium) measure of M_D at the infinite place and λ_v at finite places — is an adelic measure with Hölder potentials, and ∫ log|c − w| `dµ_{M_D,∞}(w)` = G_M(c).

D ≥ 2; the normalisation `D^{−(n−1)}` corrects FRL Lemma 6.3 ([Correction 25](#correction-25)).

Finite place: if |c|_v ≤ 1 all P_cⁿ(0) are v-integral; if |c|_v > 1, |P_cⁿ(0)|_v = `|c|_v^{D^{n−1}}` by induction, so `G_{M,v}(c)` = log⁺|c|_v and `µ_{M,v}` = λ_v. Infinite place: G_M(c) = `G_{P_c}(c)` = `D·G_{P_c}(0)` for the escape rate of P_c (The homogeneous escape rate `G_{F,v});` the telescoping estimate `|D^{-n}` `log⁺|P_c^{n+1}(0)|` − `D^{−(n−1)}` log⁺|P_cⁿ(0)|| ≤ `D^{-n}` log(1 + |c|) gives locally uniform convergence and continuity. G_M = 0 on M_D, G_M > 0 and harmonic off M_D (a locally uniform limit of harmonic functions where P_cⁿ(0) → ∞), and G_M(c) − log|c| → 0 at ∞ (|P_cⁿ(0)| = `|c|^{D^{n−1}}(1` + o(1))). Hence ΔG_M = `µ_{M,∞}` − δ_∞ with `µ_{M,∞}` a probability measure on ∂M_D (Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions, archimedean Laplacian); the potential u(c) = ∫ log|c − w| `dµ_{M,∞}(w)` has the same Laplacian, so u − G_M is constant, and the constant is 0 because both are log|c| + o(1) at ∞: `µ_{M,∞}` is the equilibrium measure of M_D and M_D has capacity 1. Hölder continuity of G_M: G_M(c) = `D·G_{P_c}(0)` and the escape rate is jointly Hölder in (c, z) on compact sets by the argument of FRL Proposition 6.5 (Lipschitz one-step estimate for (c, z) ↦ z^D + c, then optimisation of the truncation).

- `G_{M,v}(c)` = `G_{P_c,v}(c)` = `D·G_{P_c,v}(0).`

### 4.21 Curvature measures and semipositivity of an adelic metric on O(1)

For an adelic metric φ on O(1) over K, the curvature at v is initially the distribution `µ_{φ,v}` := λ_v + Δφ_v, with total mass 1 = deg O(1) (Laplacian of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions, Δ log⁺|z|_v = λ_v − δ_∞), characterised by Δ(−log‖s‖_v) = `µ_{φ,v}` − `δ_{div s}` for every linear form s; φ is semipositive if every curvature distribution is positive; in this case it is represented by a positive Radon measure. For semipositive φ, µ_φ = `(µ_{φ,v})_v` is an adelic measure: `µ_{φ,v}` = λ_v when φ_v = 0, and ∫ log δ_v(z, w) `dµ_{φ,v}(w)` − log⁺|z|_v = φ_v(z) − φ_v(∞), so the potential of `µ_{φ,v}` is `g_{µ_φ,v}` = φ_v − φ_v(∞). This is the P¹ case of the Chambert-Loir measure c₁(Ō_v) of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions.

φ an adelic metric on O(1) over K. An arbitrary continuous metric need not have a measure-valued Laplacian; only the semipositive case asserts curvature is a measure. The archimedean distribution and its positive-measure representation are part of the Riesz-measure construction contract below.

Δ(−log‖x₁‖_v) = Δ log⁺|z|_v + Δφ_v = λ_v + Δφ_v − δ_∞ (Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions normalisation), so `µ_{φ,v}` := λ_v + Δφ_v; total mass: Δφ_v has mass 0. For another linear form s = a x₀ + b x₁, −log‖s‖_v − (−log‖x₁‖_v) = −log|a z + b|_v + (log of the constant part), whose Laplacian is δ_∞ − `δ_{div s};` this gives the characterisation for every s. For semipositive φ, the positive curvature distribution is represented by a Radon measure of mass 1; its potential g(z) = ∫ log δ_v(z, w) dµ(w) − log⁺|z|_v satisfies Δg = µ − λ = Δφ_v, so g − φ_v is constant (Laplacian kernel = constants, Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions), and g(∞) = 0 fixes the constant. At the places with φ_v = 0, `µ_{φ,v}` = λ_v; these are all but finitely many.

Prove the following basic API.

- Every curvature measure `µ_{φ,v}` is positive.
- For semipositive φ, the adelic measure µ_φ = (λ_v + Δφ_v)_v.
- `g_{µ_φ,v}` = φ_v − φ_v(∞).
- µ of the standard metric is λ.
- `µ_{φ+c}` = µ_φ for constants c.
- `µ_{φ,v}(P¹_v^an)` = 1 = deg O(1).
- `µ_{φ,v}` is the Chambert-Loir measure c₁(Ō_v) of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions.

**Checks.**

- The curvature of the standard metric is the standard adelic measure.
- For φ_v = log max(|z|_v, R) − log⁺|z|_v (R ≥ 1) the curvature at v is `m_{0,R,v}.`
- Adding a constant c_v to φ_v does not change the curvature.
- For R > 1 the metric −(log max(|z|_v, R) − log⁺|z|_v) is not semipositive.

**Endpoint checks.** Standard metric: µ_v = λ_v at every place. The metric φ_v(z) = log max(|z|_v, R) − log⁺|z|_v (R ≥ 1) has curvature `m_{0,R,v}` (the circle of radius R at an infinite place, `δ_{ζ_{0,R}}` at a finite place): semipositive. The metric −φ_v with R > 1 has curvature 2λ_v − `m_{0,R,v},` which is not positive: not semipositive.

For every place v, every nonempty finite F ⊂ K̄ and every r > 0: ([F]`_{v,r},` [F]`_{v,r})_v` ≤ ([F]_v, [F]_v)_v + (−log r)/|F|, where ([F], [F])_v = `−|F|^{-2}` `Σ_{x≠y∈F}` log|x − y|_v (the diagonal omitted).

F ⊂ K̄ finite nonempty, r > 0.

Expand bilinearly: ([F]_r, [F]_r)_v = `|F|^{-2}` `Σ_{x,y∈F}` `(m_{x,r},` `m_{y,r})_v.` For x ≠ y use `(m_{x,r},m_{y,r})_v` ≤ −log max(|x−y|_v,r) ≤ −log|x−y|_v; the first inequality may be strict at an infinite place. For x = y, `(m_{x,r},` `m_{x,r})_v` = −log r; there are |F| diagonal terms, contributing `|F|^{-2}·|F|·(−log` r) = (−log r)/|F|.

### 4.23 Regularising a finite set changes its energy against a measure with continuous potential by little

Let v be a place, ρ a probability measure on P¹_v^an with continuous potential, and g the continuous function with g(z) = ∫ log δ_v(z, w) dρ(w) − log⁺|z|_v off ∞ (a potential of ρ − λ_v). For every nonempty finite F ⊂ K̄ and 0 < r < 1: |([F]_v, ρ)_v − ([F]`_{v,r},` ρ)_v| ≤ ω_g(r) + ε_v(r), with ε_v(r) = r if v is infinite and ε_v(r) = 0 if v is finite.

ρ a probability measure with continuous potential (Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions); 0 < r < 1.

By the Fubini formula for the energy (Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions; FRL Lemmas 2.5 and 4.4), (µ, ρ)_v = −∫ g_ρ dµ for µ = [F]_v and µ = [F]`_{v,r},` where g_ρ(z) = ∫ log δ_v(z, w) dρ(w) = log⁺|z|_v + g(z). So ([F], ρ) − ([F]_r, ρ) = `|F|^{-1}` `Σ_{x∈F}` (∫ g_ρ `dm_{x,r}` − g_ρ(ι x)). The g-part is bounded by ω_g(r) (Continuous functions are uniformly approximated by their circle averages). The log⁺-part: at an infinite place |log⁺|x + `re^{it}|` − log⁺|x|| ≤ r since log⁺ is 1-Lipschitz; at a finite place `log⁺|ζ_{x,r}|` = log⁺ max(|x|_v, r) = log⁺|x|_v because r < 1.
