### 4.24 Decomposition of the adelic height into local potentials

For an adelic measure ρ over K: h_ρ(∞) = ½ Σ_v r_v (ρ_v, ρ_v)_v, and for every nonempty finite Galois-stable F ⊂ K̄ (∞ ∉ F), h_ρ(F) = h_ρ(∞) − Σ_v r_v (ρ_v, [F]_v)_v = h_ρ(∞) + Σ_v r_v `|F|^{-1}` `Σ_{x∈F}` ∫ log δ_v(ι_v x, w) dρ_v(w). These two identities determine h_ρ; consequently h_ρ(F) = `|F|^{-1}` `Σ_{x∈F}` h_ρ(x) for every nonempty Galois-stable finite F ⊂ P¹(K̄).

ρ adelic; F Galois-stable finite. All finite sets to which the height-average identities are applied are nonempty.

[∞]_v pairs to 0 with every measure (pairs involving ∞ are excluded from the energy), so ([∞] − ρ, [∞] − ρ)_v = (ρ_v, ρ_v)_v. Expand ([F] − ρ, [F] − ρ)_v = (ρ, ρ)_v − 2(ρ, [F])_v + ([F], [F])_v (bilinearity, Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions) and sum with weights; the last terms sum to 0 by Product formula for the energy of a Galois-stable finite set. (ρ_v, [F]_v)_v = `−|F|^{-1}` `Σ_{x∈F}` ∫ log δ_v(ι_v x, w) dρ_v(w) by the Fubini formula for the energy (Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions). The right-hand side is affine in [F]_v, so for F a disjoint union of Galois orbits O_i, h_ρ(F) = Σ_i (|O_i|/|F|) h_ρ(O_i); for ∞ ∈ F use the first identity for the orbit {∞}.

### 4.25 The local dynamical energy of two rational maps

For rational maps f, g of degree ≥ 2 over K and a place v, E_v(f, g) := `½(µ_{f,v}` − `µ_{g,v},` `µ_{f,v}` − `µ_{g,v})_v.` Equivalently E_v(f, g) = ½(∫ `(λ_{f,v}` − `λ_{g,v})` `dµ_{g,v}` + ∫ `(λ_{g,v}` − `λ_{f,v})` `dµ_{f,v})` for local canonical heights `λ_{f,v},` `λ_{g,v}` (any normalisation). E_v(f, g) ≥ 0 with equality iff `µ_{f,v}` = `µ_{g,v},` E_v = 0 for all but finitely many v, and ⟨f, g⟩ = Σ_v r_v E_v(f, g).

f, g of degree ≥ 2 over K; v a place.

`λ_{f,v}` − `λ_{g,v}` is a continuous potential of `µ_{f,v}` − `µ_{g,v}` up to an additive constant (The canonical measure `µ_{f,v}` on the Berkovich line), so (µ_f − µ_g, µ_f − µ_g)_v = −∫ (λ_f − λ_g) d(µ_f − µ_g) (Fubini, Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions), which is the displayed formula; constants integrate to 0 against a mass-zero measure. Positivity and nondegeneracy: Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions (FRL Propositions 2.6, 4.5). Where both maps have good reduction, µ_f = µ_g = λ_v.

### 4.26 The normalised adelic metric of an adelic measure

For an adelic measure ρ over K, the normalised adelic metric Ō^ρ is φ^ρ_v := `g_{ρ,v}` + ½(ρ_v, ρ_v)_v, where `g_{ρ,v}` is the potential of ρ_v (normalised by `g_{ρ,v}(∞)` = 0). It is semipositive with curvature ρ, φ^ρ_v = 0 for v ∉ N(ρ) (since (λ_v, λ_v)_v = 0), and φ^ρ_v(∞) = ½(ρ_v, ρ_v)_v. Every semipositive adelic metric with curvature ρ is φ^ρ + c for a unique family of constants c = (c_v).

ρ an adelic measure over K.

φ^ρ_v is continuous `(g_{ρ,v}` is) and vanishes where ρ_v = λ_v. Its curvature is λ_v + `Δg_{ρ,v}` = ρ_v (Curvature measures and semipositivity of an adelic metric on O(1)). Two semipositive metrics with the same curvature differ at each place by a function with zero Laplacian, hence a constant (Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions).

### 4.31 Local energy criterion for weak convergence of [F_n]

Let v be a place and ρ a probability measure on P¹_v^an with continuous potential. Let F_n ⊂ P¹(K̄) be nonempty finite sets with |F_n| → ∞ and limsup_n ([F_n ∖ {∞}]_v − ρ, [F_n ∖ {∞}]_v − ρ)_v ≤ 0. Then [F_n]_v → ρ weakly: ∫ f d[F_n]_v → ∫ f dρ for every continuous f : P¹_v^an → ℝ.

Removing ∞ from F_n changes [F_n]_v by a measure of total variation ≤ 2/|F_n| → 0, so assume ∞ ∉ F_n. Let `ν_{n,r}` := [F_n]`_{v,r}` − ρ, of mass 0 with continuous potential. By Lower bound for the local energy of [F] − ρ, `(ν_{n,r},` `ν_{n,r})_v` ≤ ([F_n] − ρ, [F_n] − ρ)_v + 2(ω_g(r) + ε_v(r)) + (−log r)/|F_n|, so limsup_n `(ν_{n,r},` `ν_{n,r})_v` ≤ 2(ω_g(r) + ε_v(r)), which tends to 0 as r → 0. For a test function φ in the dense class D_v of Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions (smooth at infinite places; locally constant off a finite subtree and C¹ on its edges at finite places) the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality |∫ φ dν|² ≤ ⟨φ, φ⟩_v (ν, ν)_v (Layer 2 Local mutual energy and test functions; FRL (32)–(33) with the squares restored, [Correction 23](#correction-23)) gives limsup_n |∫ φ `dν_{n,r}|` ≤ (⟨φ, φ⟩_v · 2(ω_g(r) + `ε_v(r)))^{1/2}.` |∫ φ d([F_n]`_{v,r}` − [F_n]_v)| ≤ ω_φ(r) uniformly in n (Continuous functions are uniformly approximated by their circle averages); letting n → ∞ then r → 0 gives ∫ φ d[F_n]_v → ∫ φ dρ for φ ∈ D_v. D_v is dense in C(P¹_v^an) for the sup norm and all measures involved are probability measures, so the convergence holds for every continuous f (MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_iff_forall_integral_tendsto).

The [uniform periodic-multiplicity contract](#471-periodic-point-averages-counted-with-multiplicity-petscheszpirotucker-theorem-2) gives only finitely many parabolic cycles (Fatou), so e_n is bounded and the excess points carry boundedly many values of ĥ_f; hence the multiset average differs from the set average by `O(d^{-n}),` and |Fix(gⁿ)| → ∞ so every set occurs finitely often. For power maps the canonical adelic measure agrees with the standard adelic measure and the corresponding energy comparison vanishes. Distinct-point equidistribution does not by itself justify an average counting algebraic multiplicity; the uniformly bounded excess target supplies that passage.

## Layer 5: Arboreal Galois representations

Build finite preimage levels with noncollision and separability hypotheses, compatible Galois actions, the rooted-tree inverse limit and continuity. Selected maximality and index theorems follow from their exact irreducibility/ramification criteria. The all-level x²+1 example is the selected endpoint; broader density and wild-characteristic theorems remain outside its scope.

### 5.1 Level towers and rooted trees

A level tower T is a sequence of sets `(V_n)_{n≥0}` (the vertices at level n) with parent maps π_n : `V_{n+1}` → V_n. The ancestor map at level k of a vertex at level k + j is π_k ∘ ⋯ ∘ `π_{k+j−1}` (the identity for j = 0); the children of v ∈ V_n are the elements of `π_n^{-1}(v).` T is a rooted tree when V_0 is a single point; its vertices are ⊔_n V_n and its edges join x ∈ `V_{n+1}` to π_n(x). T is d-regular (d ∈ ℕ) when V_0 has exactly one element, every V_n is finite, and every vertex has exactly d children. A morphism T → T' is a family of maps V_n → V'_n commuting with the corresponding maps; an isomorphism is a family of bijections commuting with the corresponding maps.

No hypotheses: any family of types and maps is a level tower. Regularity is a separate predicate. Pinned convention: levels are indexed from the root, V_0 being the root level; the corresponding map goes down one level.

Structure with two fields (V, parent); ancestor by recursion on j; children as a fibre; IsRegular as the conjunction of the three conditions; Hom and Iso as structures of levelwise maps with the commutation field. card_level_of_isRegular: induction on n, `V_{n+1}` is the disjoint union over v ∈ V_n of the children of v (the fibres of π_n), each of cardinality d, so Nat.card `V_{n+1}` = d · Nat.card V_n. parent_surjective_of_isRegular: a fibre of cardinality d ≥ 1 is nonempty.

*Needs:* `Nat.card`.

([jones-arboreal-survey](#jones-arboreal-survey), §1.1, p. 3 — The survey's tree: vertices graded by n, edges given by φ; the level tower is this grading with edges as parent maps; [jones-density-2008](#jones-density-2008), §2, p. 6 — Rooted forests graded by level; d-regularity. (The printed 'connected to precisely d others' counts children, not neighbours: each non-root vertex also has a parent.).)

Prove the following basic API.

- For k, j ∈ ℕ, the ancestor map `V_{k+j}` → V_k, π_k ∘ ⋯ ∘ `π_{k+j−1}.`
- The ancestor map with j = 0 is the identity.
- ancestor k (j + 1) x = ancestor k j `(π_{k+j}` x).
- The children of v ∈ V_n: the subset `π_n^{-1}(v)` of `V_{n+1}.`
- T is d-regular: Nat.card V_0 = 1, every V_n is finite, and every vertex has exactly d children.
- If T is d-regular then Nat.card V_n = dⁿ for every n.
- If T is d-regular with d ≥ 1, every parent map π_n is surjective.
- Morphisms of level towers: levelwise maps commuting with the corresponding maps.
- Isomorphisms of level towers: levelwise bijections commuting with the corresponding maps.
- The identity isomorphism of T.
- The inverse of an isomorphism (levelwise inverse bijections).
- The composite of two isomorphisms.

**Checks.**

- If T is 2-regular then Nat.card V_3 = 8.
- If T is 1-regular then every level has exactly one element.
- The tower with V_n = Fin (n + 1) and every parent map constant equal to the last vertex is not d-regular for any d (vertex 0 of level 1 has no children, the last vertex of level 1 has three).
- The ancestor one level down is the corresponding: ancestor k 1 x = π_k x.

**Endpoint checks.** A 2-regular tower has 8 vertices at level 3; a 1-regular tower has one vertex at each level. The tower with levels Fin (n + 1) and every vertex sent to the last vertex below is regular of no degree.

Applications include Jones, arboreal survey, §1.1, p. 3 — the preimage tree T_∞(α) with vertex set ⊔ `φ^{-n}(α)` and edges given by φ is a rooted tree graded by level; Aut(T_n) and Aut(T_∞) are automorphisms of such trees; Jones 2008, §2, p. 6 (rooted forests) — rooted forests graded by the distance to a root carry the Galois action; a level tower with arbitrary V_0 is exactly a graded rooted forest; The preimage tree T_∞(g, α) of a point under a self-map and The complete rooted d-ary tree T^d — both are level towers; [5.20 Every d-regular level tower is isomorphic to T^d](#520-every-d-regular-level-tower-is-isomorphic-to-td) compares them.

### 5.3 Capelli's lemma

Let K be a field, g, h ∈ K[x] with g ≠ 0 and deg h ≥ 1, and let β be a root of g in some field extension L of K. Then g(h(x)) is irreducible over K if and only if g is irreducible over K and h(x) − β is irreducible over K(β).

deg h ≥ 1 (if h is constant, g ∘ h is constant and the statement degenerates). β is any root of g in any extension; when g is irreducible all roots are conjugate, so the condition does not depend on the choice.

For the reverse implication, choose a root γ of h − β over K(β). Irreducibility gives [K(β):K] = deg g and [K(γ):K(β)] = deg h, while β = h(γ) implies K(β,γ) = K(γ). The tower law gives [K(γ):K] = deg g · deg h = deg(g ∘ h). Since g ∘ h annihilates γ, it is a nonzero scalar multiple of its minimal polynomial and is irreducible. This works for arbitrary leading coefficients; Polynomial.irreducible_comp supplies the already formalized monic special case. ⇒, g irreducible: a factorization g = g₁g₂ into non-units gives g ∘ h = (g₁ ∘ h)(g₂ ∘ h) into non-units since deg h ≥ 1. ⇒, h − β irreducible: let γ be a root of h(x) − β in an extension; then γ is a root of g ∘ h, so [K(γ) : K] = deg g · deg h (g ∘ h irreducible), while K(β) ⊆ K(γ) because β = h(γ), [K(β) : K] = deg g (g irreducible) and [K(γ) : K(β)] ≤ deg h (IntermediateField.adjoin.finrank, Module.finrank_mul_finrank). Equality forces [K(γ) : K(β)] = deg h, so h − β, of degree deg h with root γ, is the minimal polynomial of γ over K(β) up to a unit, hence irreducible.

*Needs:* `Polynomial.irreducible_comp`; `IntermediateField.adjoin.finrank`; `Module.finrank_mul_finrank`; `IntermediateField.AdjoinSimple.gen`.

([jones-density-2008](#jones-density-2008), §4, Lemma 4.2, p. 13 — The statement with f and g renamed h and g; the hypothesis deg h ≥ 1 is implicit in the source.)

**Endpoint checks.** g = x² + 1, h = x² over ℚ: g ∘ h = x⁴ + 1 is irreducible, and x² − i is irreducible over ℚ(i). g = x² − 2, h = x² over ℚ: x⁴ − 2 irreducible, and x² − √2 irreducible over ℚ(√2).

### 5.4 Invariant vectors of 2-groups in permutation modules

Let G be a finite 2-group acting transitively on a finite set X, and let W ⊆ (X → F_2) be a nonzero F_2-subspace stable under the permutation action (w ↦ w ∘ `g^{-1}).` Then the constant function 1 lies in W.

G a finite 2-group (IsPGroup 2 G); the action transitive.

W is a finite set of cardinality a power of 2 with a G-action; |W| ≡ |W^G| (mod 2) (IsPGroup.card_modEq_card_fixedPoints), and 0 ∈ W^G, so W^G contains a nonzero w (IsPGroup.exists_fixed_point_of_prime_dvd_card_of_fixed_point). A G-invariant function on X is constant on G-orbits; X is one orbit, so w is constant and nonzero, i.e. w = 1.

### 5.10 The automorphism group Aut(T) of a level tower and its profinite topology

For a level tower T, Aut(T) is the group of families `(σ_n)_{n≥0}` with σ_n a permutation of V_n and π_n ∘ `σ_{n+1}` = σ_n ∘ π_n for all n, under levelwise composition; it is a subgroup of ∏_n Perm(V_n). It acts on each level through levelHom n : Aut(T) → Perm(V_n). Its topology is the subspace topology from the product ∏_n Perm(V_n) with each factor discrete (for finite levels this equals pointwise convergence on vertices). When every V_n is finite, Aut(T) is a compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected topological group, i.e. a profinite group, and finite intersections of kernels of levelHom form a basis of open neighbourhoods of 1; if every parent map is surjective, the individual level kernels form such a basis.

Profiniteness (compactness) needs every level finite; the topological group structure, Hausdorffness and total disconnectedness hold for every T.

autSubgroup: the compatibility condition is closed under composition, identity and inverses (for inverses apply `σ_n^{-1}` to both sides). Topological group: induced from the product of discrete groups, a topological group (Pi.topologicalSpace with the discrete topology on each Perm(V_n)). Hausdorff and totally disconnected: the product of discrete spaces is, and so is any subspace. Compactness for finite levels: the compatibility conditions are closed (each is an equality of values in a discrete space depending on finitely many coordinates), and ∏_n Perm(V_n) is compact by Tychonoff (finite discrete factors). Aut.ext_iff': equality of families is levelwise equality. Iso.autCongr: conjugation by the levelwise bijections of an isomorphism. A basic neighbourhood in the product fixes finitely many level permutations. When all parents are surjective, fixing the highest of those levels fixes its ancestors; without that condition use the finite intersection, or the kernel of truncation, rather than a single level kernel.

### 5.12 Non-collision: fⁿ − α is separable iff no critical point reaches α

Let K be a field, f ∈ K[x] with deg f ≥ 1, α ∈ K and n ≥ 1. Then fⁿ(x) − α is separable if and only if for every c ∈ K̄ with f'(c) = 0 and every 1 ≤ k ≤ n, f^k(c) ≠ α. Hence fⁿ − α is separable for all n ≥ 1 iff α does not lie in the forward orbit {f^k(c) : k ≥ 1, f'(c) = 0} of the critical points (the non-collision condition). If f' = 0 (f inseparable) every c ∈ K̄ is critical and both sides fail.

deg f ≥ 1. Critical points are the roots of f' in an algebraic closure, with the convention that every point is a root of the zero polynomial.

fⁿ − α splits over K̄ with roots z (f^n(z) = α); it is separable iff its roots are simple (Polynomial.nodup_roots_iff_of_splits), iff no root z has (fⁿ)'(z) = 0. By derivative-of-iterate, (fⁿ)'(z) = `∏_{i<n}` f'(fⁱ(z)); it vanishes iff c := fⁱ(z) is critical for some i < n, and then `f^{n−i}(c)` = α with 1 ≤ n − i ≤ n. Conversely if f'(c) = 0 and f^k(c) = α with 1 ≤ k ≤ n, choose z ∈ K̄ with `f^{n−k}(z)` = c (K̄ algebraically closed, deg f ≥ 1); z is a multiple root.

Let g ∈ ℤ[x] be even (g(−x) = g(x)), and let `(γ_n)_{n≥1}` be integers with γ_1 = ±g(0), `γ_{n+1}` = g(γ_n) and all γ_n ≠ 0; put β_n = `∏_{d∣n}` `γ_d^{μ(n/d)}.` Suppose that for every n ≥ 1 there is m ∈ ℕ with m ∣ γ_n + `γ_{2n},` m coprime to γ_n, and −1 not a square in ℤ/mℤ. Modulo m the factor with t = 1 is `γ_k^{μ(n')}` ≡ `(−A)^{μ(n')}` and every other factor is `A^{μ(n'/t)};` since μ(n') = ±1 and `Σ_{t∣n'}` μ(n'/t) = 0, splitting the divisors of n' by the sign of μ(n'/t) (two sets of equal size) writes β_n = P/Q with P ≡ −Q (mod m) and Q a unit mod m. If P/Q = (u/v)² in ℚ, clearing denominators and reducing modulo m (Q invertible, P ≡ −Q) makes −1 a square in ℤ/mℤ, a contradiction.

### 5.23 Preimage trees of rational maps of P¹ and their Galois action

For a polynomial φ = f and α ∈ K (α ≠ ∞) it is T(f, α; K^sep) of The preimage tree T_∞(g, α) of a point under a self-map, since ∞ is totally invariant.

Topology: the map Aut(T) → ∏_n Aut(T_n) is a continuous injective group homomorphism from a compact space (Aut.compactSpace) to a Hausdorff space, with image the compatible families, hence a homeomorphism onto the inverse limit. ### 5.45 Juul's disjoint ramification lemma

Let k be algebraically closed of any characteristic, f a separable rational map of degree d≥2 with a critical point a such that fᵐ(a) ≠ `f^{m'}(b)` for all critical points b and 1 ≤ m' ≤ m ≤ N unless (m', b) = (m, a). For n < N let α_1, …, `α_{dⁿ}` be the roots of fⁿ(x) − t, M_i the splitting field of f(x) − α_i over k(α_i), and M̂_i the compositum of K_n and the M_j, j ≠ i. Then the prime (f(a) − α_i) of k[α_i] does not ramify in M̂_i.

Use a coordinate chart in which the marked critical images through N are finite. No tameness assumption is needed for this nonramification statement. Use AlgebraicCurves Layer 8, Composita, Stichtenoth Corollary 3.9.3, for finite separable extensions in every characteristic.

The prime (f(a)−α_i) lies above f^[n+1](a)−t. By the iterated branch-support bound (§5.6a), the latter point is not a branch point of the earlier splitting tower: the orbit-separation hypothesis excludes every earlier critical image. If a prime above it ramified in another next-level factor M_j, it would force α_j=f(b) for a critical point b. Projecting to the t-line gives f^[n+1](a)=f^[n+1](b), hence b=a. Two distinct roots α_i,α_j would then specialize to f(a), contradicting the already proved absence of earlier ramification. Apply the unramified-compositum theorem to all other factors (Juul Lemma 3.3, p.9). This uses branch-support containment, not an e−1 discriminant formula at wild points.

### 5.50 A square root of c_n in K_n, transformed by the level-n sign

Then s_n² = c_n, and for every σ ∈ Gal(K^sep/K), σ(s_n) = sign(σ|V_n) · s_n, where sign(σ|V_n) is the sign of the permutation of level n induced by ρ(σ). In particular c_n is a square in K_n, and K(√c_n) ⊆ K_n is the fixed field of the kernel of χ_n ∘ ρ.

s_n² = ∏_β (y_β − γ)² = ∏_β (β − δ) = c_n (shifted-root-product). The two children of β are γ ± (y_β − γ). σ sends y_β to a child of σβ, so σ(y_β − γ) = ε_β `(y_{σβ}` − γ) with ε_β = ±1, and σ(s_n) = (∏_β ε_β) s_n. The permutation of V_n induced by σ is the composite of the 'label-preserving' permutation y_β ↦ `y_{σβ},` 2γ − y_β ↦ 2γ − `y_{σβ}` (two copies of the permutation of `V_{n−1},` hence even) with the transpositions {y_β, 2γ − y_β} for ε_β = −1; its sign is ∏ ε_β.

### 5.53 The index of G_∞ in Aut(T_∞)

Assume deg f = d ≥ 1 and fⁿ − α separable for all n. Then G_∞(f, α) has finite index in Aut(T_∞) iff the sequence [Aut(T_n) : G_n] is bounded, iff [`K_{n+1}` : K_n] = `(d!)^{dⁿ}` for all sufficiently large n; and then [Aut(T_∞) : G_∞] = sup_n [Aut(T_n) : G_n] = lim_n [Aut(T_n) : G_n]. In particular [Aut(T_∞) : G_∞] = 1 iff G_n = Aut(T_n) for all n.

deg f ≥ 1; all fⁿ − α separable.

G_∞ is closed and is the inverse limit of the G_n (arboreal-image-inverse-limit); Aut(T_∞) = lim Aut(T_n) (tree-automorphism-inverse-limit). For a closed subgroup H of a profinite group lim Γ_n with images H_n, the maps of coset sets Γ/H → Γ_n/H_n are surjective. Any finite collection of distinct cosets of H is separated at some common finite level: closedness separates each pair, and finitely many pairs admit a common larger level. Consequently the finite-level indices are bounded iff Γ/H is finite. In that bounded case the natural-valued Subgroup.index is the largest finite-level index, hence their supremum. The unbounded case is expressed by infinitude of Γ/H; a cardinal-valued supremum then lies in ℕ ∪ {∞}, whereas Subgroup.index returns 0. Boundedness of their non-decreasing integer sequence is eventual constancy; level-index-recursion translates constancy into maximal relative degrees.

### 5.57 Jones's ramification criterion for maximality

Let f = x² + bx + c with b, c ∈ ℤ, γ = −b/2, α ∈ ℤ and n ≥ 1, with fⁿ − α irreducible over ℚ. If there is an odd prime p with `v_p(c_{n+1})` odd and v_p(c_k) = 0 for 1 ≤ k ≤ n, then [`K_{n+1}` : K_n] = `2^{2ⁿ},` i.e. `H_{n+1}` = `Gal(K_{n+1}/K_n)` is maximal (the whole kernel of `Aut(T_{n+1})` → Aut(T_n)). In words: a primitive prime divisor of the adjusted critical orbit appearing to odd multiplicity forces a new maximal Kummer layer.

`c_{n+1}` ≠ 0 (odd valuation), so `f^{n+1}` − α is separable; fⁿ − α is separable (irreducible over ℚ). p is unramified in K_n (unramified-outside-critical-orbit); so `c_{n+1}` is not a square in K_n (odd-valuation-nonsquare). stoll-kummer-step gives [`K_{n+1}` : K_n] = `2^{2ⁿ}.`

### 5.59 Odoni's theorem: the generic polynomial has full arboreal image

Let d≥2 and k be any field with (d,char k)≠(2,2), and let s_0, …, `s_{d−1}` independent indeterminates, F = k(s_0, …, `s_{d−1})` and G(x) = x^d + `s_{d−1}x^{d−1}` + ⋯ + s_0 ∈ F[x]. Then for every n, G_n(G, 0) = Aut(T^d_n): the Galois group of Gⁿ(x) over F is the full iterated wreath product [S_d]^n; hence G_∞(G, 0) = Aut(T^d_∞).

For the polynomial conclusion assume (d,char k)≠(2,2). For the generic rational function `Φ(X)=(X^d+s_{d−1}X^{d−1}+⋯+s₀)/(u_dX^d+⋯+u₀)`, with all coefficients independent, prove the generic rational-map arboreal theorem over k(s,u) for every field k and d≥2: Gal(Φ^[n](X)/k(s,u))=[S_d]^n at each n. The polynomial theorem is the generic polynomial arboreal theorem with the stated exception.

Separability: Gⁿ is separable over F (it specializes to separable polynomials), so the tree is d-regular. Reduce to k algebraically closed: G_n over k̄(s) is contained in G_n over k(s) (level-image-base-change), so it suffices to prove maximality over k̄(s). ### 5.60 Stoll's maximality criterion

Let K be a field of characteristic ≠ 2, f = (x − γ)² + δ ∈ K[x], α ∈ K and n ≥ 0 with fⁿ − α separable. Then G_n(f, α) = Aut(T_n) (equivalently [K_n : K] = `2^{2ⁿ−1})` if and only if c_1, …, c_n are 2-independent in K: no nonempty subproduct `∏_{i∈S}` c_i, S ⊆ {1, …, n}, is a square in K (equivalently, the classes of c_1, …, c_n in Kˣ/Kˣ² are F_2-linearly independent: TauCeti.linearIndependent_squareClass_iff).

char K ≠ 2; f monic quadratic (any quadratic reduces to this by affine-conjugation-invariance); fⁿ − α separable.

Induction on n; n = 0 is trivial. Assume the equivalence at n. (Stoll Lemma 1.4) `G_{n+1}` = `Aut(T_{n+1})` iff G_n = Aut(T_n) and [`K_{n+1}` : K_n] = `2^{2ⁿ},` since `|Aut(T_{n+1})|` = |Aut(T_n)| · `2^{2ⁿ}` ([5.29 The order of Aut(T_n)](#529-the-order-of-autt_n)), `|G_{n+1}|` = |G_n| [`K_{n+1}` : K_n] (arboreal-image-finite-level) and [`K_{n+1}` : K_n] ≤ `2^{2ⁿ}.` If c_1, …, `c_{n+1}` are independent, each c_i is a non-square, so (f, α) is stable up to n + 1 (quadratic-stability-criterion) and stoll-kummer-step applies: [`K_{n+1}:K_n`] = `2^{2ⁿ}` iff `c_{n+1}` is not a square in K_n. (Stoll Lemma 1.5) If G_n = Aut(T_n) and c_1, …, c_n are independent then for c ∈ Kˣ: c is a square in K_n iff c_1, …, c_n, c are dependent. ⇐: c ≡ `∏_{i∈S}` c_i mod squares and each c_i is a square in K_n (square-root-of-adjusted-critical-value). ⇒: K(√c_1, …, √c_n) ⊆ K_n has degree 2ⁿ (independence, multiquadratic degree formula), and every subfield of K_n generated by square roots of elements of K has degree ≤ #Hom(Gal(K_n/K), ±1) = 2ⁿ (binary-tree-sign-characters, as G_n = Aut(T_n)); so √c ∈ K(√c_1, …, √c_n) and square descent (TauCeti.Multiquadratic.squareClass_of_sq_mem_fintype) gives c `∏_{i∈S}` c_i ∈ Kˣ². Combine: `G_{n+1}` maximal iff c_1..c_n independent and `c_{n+1}` not a square in K_n iff c_1, …, `c_{n+1}` independent. The equivalence of square-free subproducts with linear independence of square classes is TauCeti.linearIndependent_squareClass_iff.

### 5.64 Stoll's theorem: surjective arboreal representations for x² + a over ℚ

The headline `stoll_integer_family_card_gal` states the finite-level theorem on the native polynomial splitting-field Galois group: for every integer a in the three families below and every n ≥ 0, the Galois group of the n-fold compositional iterate of X² + a over ℚ has order 2^(2^n − 1). The inequalities, congruences and nonsquare condition are explicit hypotheses; at n = 0 the polynomial is X and the order is 1.

Let a ∈ ℤ with (a) a > 0 and a ≡ 1 (mod 4), or (b) a > 0 and a ≡ 2 (mod 4), or (c) a < 0, a ≡ 0 (mod 4) and −a not a square. Then for f = x² + a over ℚ and α = 0, G_n(f, 0) = Aut(T_n) for every n ≥ 1; equivalently the arboreal representation ρ : Gal(ℚ^sep/ℚ) → Aut(T²_∞) is surjective.

One of (a), (b), (c).

In all cases −a is not a square. Rescale: g := |a| x² + sgn(a), an even integer polynomial; with γ_1 := 1 its iteration sequence satisfies γ_n |a| = |c_n| for n ≥ 1 (induction), so γ_n > 0 (critical-orbit-positivity) and β_n = |b_n| for n ≥ 2 (the Möbius exponents sum to zero for n ≥ 2, so the factors |a| cancel). Case (a): g(0) = 1, g(1) = a + 1 ≡ 2 (mod 4); cases (b), (c): g(1) = |a| ± 1 ≡ 3 (mod 4). By even-sequence-congruence-criterion no |b_n|, n ≥ 2, is a square. stoll-mobius-criterion (2) gives G_n = Aut(T_n) for all n; the tree is regular (c_n ≠ 0, adjustedCriticalOrbit_ne_zero_iff) and surjectivity follows from arboreal-surjectivity-criterion / arboreal-image-inverse-limit.

### 6.3 The Lattès map of multiplication by n on a Weierstrass curve

Let F be a field, E a Weierstrass curve over F (Mathlib WeierstrassCurve) with discriminant Δ(E) ≠ 0, and n ∈ ℤ with n ≠ 0. The Lattès map `f_{E,n}` : ℙ¹_F → ℙ¹_F is the rational map (Rational self-maps of ℙ¹ over a field) given by the forms (Φ_n^h(X, Z), ΨSq_n^h(X, Z)), the homogenisations in degree n² (Mathlib Polynomial.homogenize) of Mathlib's division polynomials WeierstrassCurve.Φ n and WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq n. In the affine coordinate x it is x ↦ Φ_n(x)/ΨSq_n(x), with `f_{E,n}(x)` = ∞ when ΨSq_n(x) = 0 and `f_{E,n}(∞)` = ∞. It is the descent of [n] : E → E through the x-coordinate x : E → ℙ¹ (the quotient by P ↦ −P, with x(O) = ∞): `f_{E,n}` ∘ x = x ∘ [n] (The Lattès map semiconjugates multiplication by n). For |n| ≥ 2 it has degree n².

F any field; E any Weierstrass curve over F with Δ(E) ≠ 0 (no characteristic hypothesis: the coprimality of Φ_n and ΨSq_n holds in every characteristic). n ≠ 0 (ΨSq_0 = 0); `f_{E,±1}` is the identity and the dynamical statements assume |n| ≥ 2. Δ(E) ≠ 0 is necessary: for the cuspidal cubic y² = x³ the forms Φ_2 = X⁴ and ΨSq_2 = 4X³ share the root 0.

Degrees: Φ_n has degree n² and leading coefficient 1 (WeierstrassCurve.natDegree_Φ, WeierstrassCurve.leadingCoeff_Φ) and ΨSq_n has degree at most n² − 1 (WeierstrassCurve.natDegree_ΨSq_le); ΨSq_n ≠ 0 (WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_ne_zero_of_Δ_ne_zero). Φ_n and ΨSq_n are coprime (WeierstrassCurve.isCoprime_Φ_ΨSq, using Δ ≠ 0), so the degree-n² homogenisations have no common zero on ℙ¹ over an algebraic closure: at Z ≠ 0 by coprimality, at [1 : 0] because Φ_n^h(1, 0) = 1. They therefore define a Layer 0 rational map of degree n². `f_{E,n}(∞)` = [Φ_n^h(1, 0) : ΨSq_n^h(1, 0)] = [1 : 0] since deg ΨSq_n < n². n = 2: Φ_2 = X⁴ − b₄X² − 2b₆X − b₈ and ΨSq_2 = Ψ₂Sq = 4X³ + b₂X² + 2b₄X + b₆ (WeierstrassCurve.Φ_two, WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_two, WeierstrassCurve.Ψ₂Sq); their resultant is Δ(E)² (a direct computation), so for an integral Weierstrass model over a valuation ring with unit discriminant, this lift has good reduction, including residue characteristic 2. For an abstract elliptic curve with good reduction, use the coordinates of a good integral model.

### 6.4 Translation by a 2-torsion point acts on the x-line by a Möbius involution

Let F be a field of characteristic ≠ 2, E/F a Weierstrass curve with Δ(E) ≠ 0 and T = (e, y_T) ∈ E(F) a point of order 2 (so Ψ₂Sq(e) = 0 and y_T = −(a₁e + a₃)/2). Let τ_T be the Möbius transformation τ_T(x) = e + Ψ₂Sq′(e)/(4(x − e)), with τ_T(e) = ∞ and τ_T(∞) = e, where Ψ₂Sq′(e) = 12e² + 2b₂e + 2b₄ ≠ 0. Then x(P + T) = τ_T(x(P)) for every P ∈ E(F), and τ_T ∘ τ_T = id. For T = O set τ_O = id.

char F ≠ 2; Δ(E) ≠ 0 (so e is a simple root of Ψ₂Sq and Ψ₂Sq′(e) ≠ 0); T of exact order 2.

2T = O means y_T = negY(e, y_T), i.e. 2y_T + a₁e + a₃ = 0, and substituting in the curve equation gives Ψ₂Sq(e) = 0 (Ψ₂Sq = (2y + a₁x + a₃)² on the curve). For P = (x, y) with x ≠ e, Mathlib's addition formula (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.add_of_X_ne, WeierstrassCurve.Affine.addX, WeierstrassCurve.Affine.slope) gives x(P + T) = λ² + a₁λ − a₂ − x − e with λ = (y − y_T)/(x − e); reducing modulo the curve equation (a polynomial identity checked symbolically) gives e + Ψ₂Sq′(e)/(4(x − e)). P = T gives O (x = ∞ = τ_T(e)); P = O gives T (τ_T(∞) = e); P = −P′ with x(P′) = e only for P′ = T. Ψ₂Sq′(e) ≠ 0 because a double root of Ψ₂Sq would make Δ = 0 (Ψ₂Sq has discriminant 16Δ); τ_T is an involution because translation by T is.

### 6.5 Postcritically finite rational maps

Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and f a rational map of degree d ≥ 2 over K. The postcritical set of f is PC(f) = `⋃_{n ≥ 1}` fⁿ(supp Crit(f)) ⊆ ℙ¹(K̄). The map f is postcritically finite (PCF) if every critical point of f is preperiodic, equivalently if PC(f) is finite.

char K = 0; d ≥ 2.

supp Crit(f) is finite (The critical points of a rational map, with multiplicity), so PC(f) is finite iff every critical orbit is finite iff every critical point is preperiodic.

### 6.7 Specialisation of a one-parameter family of rational maps and of its points

Let k be a field with algebraic closure k̄ and f a rational map of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 1 over k(t) (Rational self-maps of ℙ¹ over a field). Choose forms F, G ∈ k[t][X, Y] of degree d representing f whose coefficients have no common factor in k[t] (a primitive representative; unique up to k^×). For t₀ ∈ k̄ let `F_{t₀},` `G_{t₀}` ∈ k̄[X, Y] be obtained by evaluating the coefficients at t₀. The good set is T⁰(f) := {t₀ ∈ k̄ : Res(F, G)(t₀) ≠ 0}, where Res(F, G) ∈ k[t] (The resultant of a pair of binary forms); it is cofinite. For t₀ ∈ T⁰(f) the specialisation `f_{t₀}` := [`F_{t₀}` : `G_{t₀}`] is a rational map of degree d over k(t₀). For P ∈ ℙ¹(k(t)) written P = [p : q] with p, q ∈ k[t] coprime, its specialisation is `P_{t₀}` := [p(t₀) : q(t₀)] ∈ ℙ¹(k(t₀)), defined for every t₀ ∈ k̄.

k any field; the family is a map over the rational function field k(t) (base curve the t-line). Specialisation of maps is defined on T⁰(f); specialisation of points is defined everywhere since p and q have no common root.

Primitive representatives exist and are unique up to k^×: clear denominators and divide by the gcd of the coefficients (k[t] is a UFD). Res(F, G) ∈ k[t] is nonzero because F, G have no common zero over the algebraic closure of k(t); resultants commute with the evaluation map k[t] → k̄ (the Sylvester determinant is a polynomial in the coefficients), so `Res(F_{t₀},` `G_{t₀})` = Res(F, G)(t₀) and `f_{t₀}` has degree d exactly on T⁰(f). T⁰(f) is cofinite: its complement is the set of roots of the nonzero polynomial Res(F, G). For independence of representatives, write a second pair as a rational-function scalar times the primitive pair. At a good parameter, the primitive pair has at least one unit coefficient in the local DVR. If the second pair has a nonzero specialization, its scalar has valuation zero, so the specialized pairs differ by a nonzero scalar. Multiplying both forms by t−t₀ gives a zero pair and is excluded.

### 6.8 The critical height of a rational map

### 6.14 Finite unions of arithmetic progressions in ℕ

A set S ⊆ ℕ is a finite union of arithmetic progressions if there are finitely many pairs (a_i, b_i) ∈ ℕ² with S = ⋃_i {a_i k + b_i : k ∈ ℕ}; the case a_i = 0 contributes the singleton {b_i}, so finite sets qualify. Equivalently, S is eventually periodic: there are N ∈ ℕ and p ≥ 1 with n ∈ S ↔ n + p ∈ S for all n ≥ N.

Arithmetic progressions are one-sided (k ≥ 0) and may have difference 0.

Equivalence: a union of progressions {a_i k + b_i} is periodic with period lcm of the nonzero a_i for n ≥ 1 + max b_i (use maximum 0 for an empty family and period 1 if all steps are zero); conversely an eventually periodic S is the union of the finite set S ∩ [0, N) and the progressions {pk + b} for b ∈ S ∩ [N, N + p). The class is closed under finite unions, intersections and complements (eventually periodic sets form a Boolean algebra).

### 6.30 Preperiodic and periodic points of the power map

Let K be a field and d ≥ 2. A point x ∈ ℙ¹(K) is preperiodic for P_d if and only if x ∈ {0, ∞} or x is a root of unity. It is periodic if and only if x ∈ {0, ∞} or x is a root of unity whose order is prime to d; a root of unity of order N prime to d has exact period the multiplicative order of d modulo N.

K any field; d ≥ 2.

0 and ∞ are fixed. If x ≠ 0, ∞ and P_d^m(x) = P_d^n(x) with m < n, then `x^{d^m}` = `x^{d^n},` so `x^{d^m(d^{n−m} − 1)}` = 1 with a positive exponent; x has finite order (isOfFinOrder_iff_pow_eq_one). Conversely if x has finite order N, all iterates `x^{dⁿ}` lie in the finite group generated by x, so two coincide and x is preperiodic. x (of order N) is periodic iff `x^{dⁿ}` = x for some n ≥ 1 iff N | dⁿ − 1 for some n ≥ 1 (orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one); this forces gcd(N, d) = 1, and conversely gcd(N, d) = 1 gives `d^{φ(N)}` ≡ 1 (mod N) (Nat.ModEq.pow_totient). The least such n is the order of d in (ℤ/N)^×.

### 6.32 Dynatomic polynomials of the power map are products of cyclotomic polynomials

Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and d ≥ 2. Every root has multiplicity one, and the points of formal period n (Formal period versus exact period) are exactly the points of exact period n.

char K = 0 (so that the cyclotomic polynomials are separable and d is a unit). d ≥ 2, n ≥ 1.

For k ≥ 1, `z^{d^k}` − z = z `(z^{d^k − 1}` − 1) = z `∏_{m | d^k − 1}` Φ_m(z) (Polynomial.prod_cyclotomic_eq_X_pow_sub_one). In the Möbius product Φ*_n = `∏_{k | n}` `(z^{d^k}` − `z)^{μ(n/k)}` the exponent of z is `Σ_{k|n}` μ(n/k) = [n = 1], and the exponent of Φ_m is `Σ_{k | n, r | k}` μ(n/k) with r = ord_m(d) (since m | d^k − 1 iff r | k); this sum is [n = r] (Möbius inversion, ArithmeticFunction.moebius). The cyclotomic factors are pairwise coprime and separable in characteristic 0, so all roots are simple; a simple root of Φ*_n has exact period n (Formal period versus exact period).

### 6.33 The preimage tree of the power map and its Kummer Galois action

Let K be a field of characteristic 0, d ≥ 2 and a ∈ K^×. The n-th level of the preimage tree (The preimage tree T_∞(g, α) of a point under a self-map) of P_d at a is `P_d^{−n}(a)` = {β : `β^{dⁿ}` = a}, of size dⁿ. Choose a compatible system (β_n) with `β_{n+1}^d` = β_n, β_0 = a, and a compatible system `(ζ_{dⁿ})` of primitive dⁿ-th roots of unity with `ζ_{d^{n+1}}^d` = `ζ_{dⁿ};` then level n is `{ζ_{dⁿ}^i β_n : i ∈ ℤ/dⁿ},` and every σ ∈ Gal(K̄/K) acts by `ζ_{dⁿ}^i` β_n ↦ `ζ_{dⁿ}^{χ(σ) i + b_n(σ)}` β_n, where χ is the cyclotomic character mod dⁿ and σ(β_n) = `ζ_{dⁿ}^{b_n(σ)}` β_n. Hence the arboreal representation (The arboreal Galois representation ρ : Gal(K^sep/K) → Aut(T_∞(f, α))) of (P_d, a) takes values in the affine group {i ↦ u i + b : u ∈ ℤ_d^×, b ∈ ℤ_d} of the tree lim ℤ/dⁿ, a subgroup of infinite index in the tree automorphism group for d ≥ 2.

char K = 0 (so that `x^{dⁿ}` − a is separable for a ≠ 0). a ≠ 0 (at a = 0 the tree collapses).

`x^{dⁿ}` − a is separable (its derivative `dⁿx^{dⁿ−1}` vanishes only at 0, not a root), so level n has dⁿ points, and they are ζ^i β_n for the dⁿ-th roots of unity ζ^i. `σ(ζ_{dⁿ})` = `ζ_{dⁿ}^{χ(σ)}` and σ(β_n) is again a root of `x^{dⁿ}` − a, so σ(β_n) = `ζ_{dⁿ}^{b_n(σ)}` β_n; multiplicativity gives the displayed formula. Compatibility of the β_n and `ζ_{dⁿ}` under x ↦ x^d makes (χ(σ), b_n(σ)) compatible in n, giving the affine group over ℤ_d = lim ℤ/dⁿ. At level n the affine group has order dⁿφ(dⁿ), at most d²ⁿ. The full rooted tree group has order `(d!)^{(dⁿ−1)/(d−1)}` (The order of Aut(T_n)), so the indices of the images tend to infinity. Do not assert strict containment at every n≥2: for d=2,n=2 both groups have order 8. Use the preceding order comparison at arbitrarily large levels to conclude infinite index. Binary depth two is an equality case, so a claim of strict containment at every depth n ≥ 2 would be false.

### 6.43 The dynamical Mordell–Lang conjecture (statement)

For a quasi-projective variety X over ℂ, a morphism Φ : X → X, a closed subvariety V ⊆ X and a point α ∈ X(ℂ), let S(X, Φ, V, α) = {n ∈ ℕ : Φⁿ(α) ∈ V(ℂ)}. ### 6.44 The dynamical Mordell–Lang statement fails in positive characteristic (Ghioca Example 1.4)

Let p be prime, K = 𝔽_p(t), V ⊂ 𝔾_m² the curve tx + (1 − t)y = 1, Φ(x, y) = `(t^{p²−1}x,` (1 − `t)^{p²−1}y)` and α = (1, 1). Then {n ∈ ℕ : Φⁿ(α) ∈ V} = `{(p^{2j} − 1)/(p² − 1) : j ∈ ℕ},` which is infinite but not a finite union of arithmetic progressions.

Φⁿ(α) = `(t^{n(p²−1)},` (1 − `t)^{n(p²−1)})` lies on V iff t^m + (1 − t)^m = 1 with m = n(p² − 1) + 1. If m = p^k then t^m + (1 − t)^m = (t + 1 − `t)^{p^k}` = 1 (Frobenius, add_pow_char_pow). Conversely write m = p^k m′ with p ∤ m′; if m′ > 1, then with u = `t^{p^k}` the polynomial `u^{m′}` + (1 − `u)^{m′}` − 1 has coefficient −m′ ≠ 0 at u¹, so it is nonzero and t^m + (1 − t)^m ≠ 1. m = p^k ≡ 1 (mod p² − 1) iff k is even (p ≢ 1 mod p² − 1), giving n = `(p^{2j}` − 1)/(p² − 1). The gaps between consecutive elements are unbounded, so the set contains no infinite arithmetic progression with positive difference and is not a finite union of arithmetic progressions (Finite unions of arithmetic progressions in ℕ).

### 6.45 Common iterates from synchronized affine intersections

Let K have characteristic zero, f(X)=aX+b and g(X)=cX+e with a,c nonzero. If the set of common values fⁿ(x₀)=gⁿ(y₀), with the same n≥0, is infinite, then `f^{∘m}=g^{∘m}` for some m≥1. Together with conjugating a nonvertical line to the diagonal, this supplies the linear case of the polynomial-lines DML target.

Infinitude concerns distinct common values, not merely infinitely many time indices. Both slopes are nonzero; constant maps have finite synchronized image.

Reduce to the finitely generated characteristic-zero subfield containing the coefficients and initial points, embed it in C, and shift to a first common value. A nontrivial root-of-unity slope has a finite orbit and is excluded by distinct-value infinitude. If both slopes differ from 1, write the two iterates using their fixed-point translations. If the translated starting values differ, their equality becomes A aⁿ+B cⁿ=1 with A,B nonzero. The finitely generated multiplicative subgroup generated by a,c meets the DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §2.4 two-variable specialization of its finite-rank nondegenerate unit-equation theorem after embedding in an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field; distinct n give distinct solutions because a is not a root of unity. Thus the translated starting values coincide, forcing equal fixed points and aⁿ=cⁿ at a return, hence equality of the corresponding affine iterates. If both slopes are 1, equality after shifting to a common start forces the two translation increments to coincide. If exactly one slope is 1, the nontrivial translation grows linearly along the common-return subsequence. A slope of complex modulus at most 1 gives a bounded other orbit; one of modulus greater than 1 grows exponentially. Either contradicts infinitely many returns (GTZ Proposition 5.3). GTZ Lemma 5.1 handles nonvertical lines by affine conjugation; a vertical or horizontal line with infinitely many distinct orbit points is periodic because the relevant coordinate is periodic. Use the finite-union-of-progressions contract for time sets.

### 6.52 Benedetto zero-height criterion for nonisotrivial polynomials

Let F be any field, K/F a finite extension of F(T), and f∈K[z] a polynomial of degree d≥2 which is not affine-conjugate over a finite extension of K to a polynomial over the algebraic constant field. For every x∈P¹(K̄), its geometric canonical height is zero if and only if x is preperiodic.

The height uses geometric places trivial on F; this is not the number-field Northcott argument. Isotriviality allows a finite extension and an affine change of coordinates.

Over any fixed finite extension containing x, zero local escape rates place its forward orbit in every local filled Julia set. The rational zero-height set is forward-invariant. If it has at most two points it is already finite. Otherwise, if all places have potentially good reduction, normalize two finite zero-height points to 0 and 1; the product formula forces the leading coefficient to have norm 1 everywhere and then forces all coefficients to be constants (Benedetto Proposition 6.1). Nonisotriviality therefore supplies a bad place in this remaining case. At a bad place the filled Julia set is covered by at most d² open discs of radius `|a_d|^{-1/(d−1)};` at good places it lies in a closed disc of that radius. Two rational points in the same choices of bad-place discs violate the product formula. Thus the rational zero-height set is finite and forward-invariant. Apply this argument in a finite extension containing any algebraic x. Nonisotriviality persists under that extension.

### 6.54 Flexible Lattès maps and the flexible Lattès locus

Let K be a field of characteristic 0 with algebraic closure K̄, and d ≥ 2. A rational map f of degree d over K is a flexible Lattès map if there exist an elliptic Weierstrass curve E over K̄, an integer n with |n| ≥ 2, a point T ∈ E(K̄) with 2T = O, and a Möbius transformation φ ∈ PGL₂(K̄) such that φ ∘ f ∘ φ⁻¹ = τ_T ∘ `f_{E,n}` over K̄ (Translation by a 2-torsion point acts on the x-line by a Möbius involution, τ_O = id), i.e. f is conjugate to the descent of P ↦ nP + T through x. Then d = n². The flexible Lattès locus L_d ⊂ M_d(K̄) (The moduli space M_d(K) of degree-d maps) is the set of conjugacy classes of flexible Lattès maps of degree d; it is empty unless d is a perfect square.

char K = 0 (the sources work over ℂ and ℚ̄; the translation τ_T needs char ≠ 2). The Möbius transformation and the curve may be defined only over K̄. Rigid Lattès maps (quotients of complex-multiplication endomorphisms, or by the groups of order 3, 4, 6) are not flexible and are not constructed in Layer 6.

x(nP + T) = τ_T(x(nP)) = `τ_T(f_{E,n}(x(P)))` (Translation by a 2-torsion point acts on the x-line by a Möbius involution, The Lattès map semiconjugates multiplication by n), so τ_T ∘ `f_{E,n}` is the descent of P ↦ nP + T; its degree is n² since τ_T is Möbius. The predicate is invariant under conjugation by PGL₂(K̄) by construction, so it descends to conjugacy classes (Conjugation of rational maps by PGL₂) and defines L_d ⊆ M_d(K̄). Milnor's Lemma 5.5: a Lattès map is flexible iff it is a quotient by ±1 of τ ↦ aτ + b with a ∈ ℤ; commuting with −1 forces 2b ∈ Λ, so b is a 2-torsion point and the map is τ_b ∘ `f_{E,a}` with E(ℂ) = ℂ/Λ.

For a field F of characteristic ≠ 2 and t ∈ F ∖ {0, 1}, with A(z, w) = (w − z, w) and B(z, w) = (z, tw): A ∘ F_t = `−F_{1−t}` ∘ A and B ∘ F_t = `F_{1/t}` ∘ B as maps F² → F², and more generally A ∘ F_tⁿ = `−F_{1−t}ⁿ` ∘ A and B ∘ F_tⁿ = `F_{1/t}ⁿ` ∘ B for all n ≥ 1. On ℙ¹: `f_{1−t}` = α ∘ f_t ∘ α⁻¹ with α(z) = 1 − z, and `f_{1/t}` = β ∘ f_t ∘ β⁻¹ with β(z) = z/t.

### 6.57 Standard projections of an elliptic curve

On the native Weierstrass point carrier, define `ellipticStandardProjection` for W over ℂ and A ∈ GL₂(ℂ) by applying A to `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.xRep` and taking the ratio of its two coordinates, with infinity when the second coordinate is zero. Its source is W.toAffine.Point and its target is `OnePoint ℂ`; it is a standard projection when W is elliptic. The matrix acts on column vectors from the left, so [[a,b],[c,d]] gives (ax+b)/(cx+d). Invertibility and nonvanishing of the native x-representative exclude the zero transformed vector. All standard projections are obtained this way, since they differ from the x-coordinate quotient by an automorphism of the projective line (demarco-krieger-ye-2020, §1, p. 2, and Corollary 8.2, pp. 44–45).

Its basic API consists of compatibility with projective coordinate changes, invariance under multiplying A by a nonzero scalar, and equality of fibres precisely for pairs P,−P on a smooth curve. The ramification points are exactly the four two-torsion points, with simple ramification.

**Checks.**

- For A = [[0,1],[1,0]], infinity maps to 0, 0 maps to infinity, and the affine x-value 2 maps to 1/2. The inverse-ratio convention would give 2 instead.
- Replacing the identity matrix by twice the identity leaves an affine x-value 2 equal to 4/2 = 2 and leaves infinity fixed; the projection depends on the projective class of A.
- For the Legendre curve at t = 2 and A = 1, the zero point maps to infinity and (0,0) maps to 0; these distinct points must not be identified.
- The zero matrix is excluded by invertibility; otherwise every vector would map to infinity under the total formula. At t = 0 the Legendre model is singular, so the smooth four-branch-value assertion does not apply.

Let E be an elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic ≠2. A standard projection is π=φ∘x for φ∈PGL₂(k), where x(O)=∞. Equivalently it is a degree-two quotient identifying P and −P, followed by a projective coordinate choice. Translating by any e∈E[2] gives another map of this form because x∘τ_e=ι_e∘x for a Möbius map ι_e. The branch set π(E[2]) has four points, and π(E^tors)=φ(x(E^tors)); precomposing by τ_e leaves the torsion-image set unchanged.

k algebraically closed, char k ≠ 2. Over ℂ these are exactly the degree-two quotients π with π(P) = π(−P) composed with 2-torsion translations.

x ∘ τ_e(P) = τ_e-image of x(P) (Translation by a 2-torsion point acts on the x-line by a Möbius involution), so π is φ ∘ τ_e′ ∘ x with τ_e′ a Möbius map; it identifies Q and −Q + 2e = −Q. Branch set: x is ramified exactly at E[2] (x(P) = x(−P), P = −P iff P ∈ E[2]), so π(E[2]) = φ(τ_e(x(E[2]))) has four points. π(E^tors) = φ(τ_e(x(E^tors))) = φ(x(E^tors + e)) = φ(x(E^tors)) since E^tors + e = E^tors.

- π=φ∘x for φ∈PGL₂(k); the alternative φ∘x∘τ_e with e∈E[2] is obtained by absorbing ι_e into the Möbius parameter.
- π(−P + 2e) = π(P), i.e. π(−P) = π(P) for e ∈ E[2] (2e = O).
- The points of ℙ¹ with exactly one preimage under π are the four points of π(E[2]); π is two-to-one elsewhere.
- π(E^tors) = φ(x(E^tors)).
- A Möbius transformation ψ moves the branch set π(E[2]) to {0, 1, t, ∞} for some t ≠ 0, 1; after translating by a 2-torsion point so that π(O) = ∞, E is in Legendre form E_t.

**Checks.**

- For E_t and e = O, φ = id, the standard projection is x, with branch set {0, 1, t, ∞}.
- Translating by e ∈ E[2] does not change the set of torsion images: π^e(E^tors) = π(E^tors).
- The branch set π(E[2]) has exactly four points (the roots of Ψ₂Sq and ∞ for π = x, Mathlib WeierstrassCurve.Ψ₂Sq).
- The map E → ℙ¹ given by the y-coordinate of y² = x³ + 1 has degree 3, is not a quotient by P ↦ −P, and is not a standard projection.

**Endpoint checks.** For E_t, x itself is a standard projection with branch set {0, 1, t, ∞}.

### 6.61 An unramified map returns to the residue class to first order (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Propositions 2.4 and 2.6)

In the setting of Power-series coordinates on a residue disc (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Propositions 2.1–2.2, Remark 2.3), write F(β⃗) = C⃗ + L β⃗ + (higher order terms). If Φ is unramified at x, then L is invertible modulo p, and there is n ≥ 1 with Fⁿ(β⃗) ≡ β⃗ (mod p) for all β⃗ ∈ ℤ_p^g.

Φ unramified at the fixed point x.

In the local ring A of the special fibre at x, unramifiedness gives the extended-ideal equality Φ*(m)A=m, with ideal extension understood as `Ideal.map`. Apply `Algebra.FormallyUnramified.map_maximalIdeal` to the local algebra structure defined by Φ*. Since x is 𝔽_p-rational and Φ is over 𝔽_p, its residue-field map is the identity. Reducing coefficients of the extended-ideal equality modulo m therefore makes the induced linear map on m/m² surjective, hence an isomorphism of this finite-dimensional 𝔽_p-vector space; this map is the reduction of Lᵀ, hence L mod p is invertible. β⃗ ↦ C⃗ + Lβ⃗ mod p is then a bijection of the finite set 𝔽_p^g, so some power is the identity; the higher order terms vanish mod p (Power-series coordinates on a residue disc (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Propositions 2.1–2.2, Remark 2.3) (c)).

### 6.62 Simple-root primes for a family with prescribed denominator exclusions

Let n ≥ 0, R = ℤ[T₁,…,Tₙ], and H ∈ R[Y] have positive natural degree and separable image in (FractionRing R)[Y]. Let D be a finite set of nonzero parameter polynomials. For every N ∈ ℕ there exist a ∈ ℤⁿ, a prime p > N and b ∈ ℤ such that Hₐ = H(Y,a) has the same natural degree as H, p ∤ lc(H)(a), p ∤ q(a) for all q ∈ D, p ∣ Hₐ(b), and p ∤ Hₐ′(b).

The prime and integral parameter specialization are chosen together; the conclusion does not apply to every prime or every specialization. No algebraic independence of a is asserted: a is only the integral residue-box centre for the later p-adic perturbation. Nonconstant H is essential; p = 2 is not forbidden here, while N = 3 forces p ≥ 5 when the analytic consumer needs it.

Apply Integral specialization preserving separability and marked denominators to obtain A,B,c,a with c(a), lc(H)(a) and all q(a) nonzero, and the degree equality. Set m = lc(H)(a)·∏q∈D q(a), a nonzero integer (empty product one). Map AH + BH′ = C c along evaluation at a; Polynomial.derivative_map gives the exact derivative required by Simple roots modulo primes from an integral Bézout certificate. Apply that existing prime-selection target to Hₐ, Aₐ, Bₐ, c(a), m and N. It gives p > N with p ∤ m and a simple residue root b. Each excluded factor divides m, so p divides neither lc(H)(a) nor any q(a). No Chebotarev or Hilbert irreducibility is used. The output is the exact residue data consumed by the remaining algebraically independent p-adic perturbation and Hensel steps of Embedding a finitely generated field into ℚ_p with prescribed integral elements (Lech–Cassels). Producing H and D from the original field, and extending the eventual root to a field embedding, remain separate gaps.

### 6.63 Preperiodic points of a Lattès map are the torsion images

Let F be a field, E/F a Weierstrass curve with Δ(E) ≠ 0 and n ∈ ℤ with |n| ≥ 2. For P ∈ E(F), the point x(P) ∈ ℙ¹(F) is preperiodic for `f_{E,n}` if and only if P has finite order. If F is algebraically closed, the set of preperiodic points of `f_{E,n}` in ℙ¹(F) is exactly x(E(F)_tors) (which contains ∞ = x(O)).

Δ(E) ≠ 0; |n| ≥ 2; no characteristic hypothesis.

By The Lattès map semiconjugates multiplication by n and Composition of Lattès maps: `f_{E,m}` ∘ `f_{E,n}` = `f_{E,mn},` `f_{E,n}^k(x(P))` = x(n^k P) for all k. If P has finite order N, the points n^k P lie in the finite group generated by P, so the forward orbit of x(P) is finite. Conversely, if f^a(x(P)) = f^b(x(P)) with a < b, then x(n^a P) = x(n^b P). Points with the same x-coordinate are equal or opposite (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Y_eq_of_X_eq for affine points; only O has x = ∞), so n^b P = ±n^a P and (n^b ∓ n^a)P = O with n^b ∓ n^a ≠ 0 because |n^b| > |n^a|; hence P has finite order (the additive form of isOfFinOrder_iff_pow_eq_one). Over an algebraically closed F, every a ∈ F is x(P) for some P (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.exists_point_on_curve, nonsingular by WeierstrassCurve.Affine.equation_iff_nonsingular_of_Δ_ne_zero), which gives the description of all preperiodic points.

### 6.65 Flexible Lattès maps are postcritically finite

Let K be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, E/K elliptic, |n| ≥ 2, T ∈ E[2] and g = τ_T ∘ `f_{E,n}.` Every critical point of g (The critical points of a rational map, with multiplicity) is x(P) for some P with nP ∈ E[2], and g(x(E[2])) ⊆ x(E[2]). Hence the postcritical set of g is contained in the four points x(E[2]) = {∞} ∪ {roots of Ψ₂Sq}, g is postcritically finite (Postcritically finite rational maps), and so is every flexible Lattès map. Precisely, the critical points of `f_{E,n}` are the 2n² − 2 points x(P) with nP ∈ E[2] and P ∉ E[2], each of multiplicity one.

char K = 0 (so that [n] is separable and τ_T is defined); K algebraically closed.

Invariant differential: [n]*ω = n ω for ω = dx/η, η = 2y + a₁x + a₃ (TauCeti.Isogeny.pullbackDifferential_mulByIntIsogeny_invariantDifferential), and the pullback of x along [n] is `f_{E,n}(x)` (TauCeti.Isogeny.fieldPullback_mulByIntIsogeny_X). Comparing the two sides gives `f_{E,n}′(x)` · η = n · (η ∘ [n]) in K(E). Evaluating at an affine P with nP affine and P ∉ E[2] (both sides regular; η(P) ≠ 0): `f_{E,n}′(x(P))` = n η(nP)/η(P), which vanishes iff η(nP) = 0 iff nP ∈ E[2]. If P ∈ E[2] then nP ∈ E[2] anyway. The poles x(P) with nP = O also satisfy nP ∈ E[2]. So every critical point c = x(P) has nP ∈ E[2], and g(c) = x(nP + T) ∈ x(E[2]). x(E[2]) is forward invariant: g(x(Q)) = x(nQ + T) with nQ + T ∈ E[2] for Q ∈ E[2]. Counting (for the multiplicities): #[n]⁻¹(E[2]) = 4n², of which the 4 points of E[2] are not critical (the local degrees satisfy e_f(x(P))·e_x(P) = e_x(nP) with e_x = 2 exactly on E[2]), leaving 4n² − 4 points and 2n² − 2 = 2 deg g − 2 simple critical points. Conjugation by φ preserves postcritical finiteness, giving the statement for every flexible Lattès map.

### 6.66 Affine-torus Lattès maps

Use complex elliptic uniformization and the finite torus-quotient classification, including translation and cyclic quotient data (Milnor Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.5 and Theorem 5.1). For multiplier finiteness require McMullen stable-family rigidity, its Thurston and holomorphic-motion inputs, and the Noetherian finite-spectrum adapter. The elementary fixed-degree lattice argument is conditional on the classification, with flexibility characterized by Milnor Lemma 5.5. No imaginary-quadratic class-number theorem is required for that finite bound.

A complex rational map f of degree ≥2 is an affine-torus Lattès map if there exist a rank-two lattice Λ⊂C, the torus T=C/Λ, an affine endomorphism L(z)=az+b with aΛ⊂Λ and |a|²>1, and a finite holomorphic quotient Θ:T→P¹ such that f∘Θ=Θ∘L. The classification normalizes Θ to T/G_n for n∈{2,3,4,6}, with ω_nΛ=Λ and (1−ω_n)b∈Λ. Flexibility is equivalent to n=2 and a an integer.

Λ has rank two; cylinder quotients give power/Chebyshev maps and are excluded. Finite quotient is essential. The translation b is allowed; the multiplication-only Lattès map is a special case.

Use the quotient-of-affine-map notion of Milnor Definition 2.1 restricted to a torus. The semiconjugacy determines degree |a|². Milnor Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.5 give the cyclic quotient normal form; Theorem 5.1 fixes the conjugacy invariants. Lemma 5.5 identifies flexibility. Elliptic uniformization and the cyclic-quotient classification are the affine-quotient classification contract below; do not identify the whole notion with multiplication-only maps.

Let n ≥ 0, H ∈ ℤ[T₁,…,Tₙ][Y] have positive natural degree and separable image over Frac(ℤ[T₁,…,Tₙ]), and let D be a finite set of nonzero parameter polynomials. For every N ∈ ℕ there are a prime p > N, ξ ∈ ℤ_pⁿ with algebraically independent image in ℚ_p over ℚ, and η ∈ ℤ_p such that F = H(Y,ξ) satisfies F(η) = 0, F′(η) is a unit, deg F = deg H, lc(H)(ξ) is a unit, and every q(ξ), q ∈ D, is a unit.

H is supplied integral polynomial data; it need not be monic or irreducible. This is not a presentation of an arbitrary finitely generated field. The independence of ξ makes evaluation on ℚ[T] injective, but extending across an arbitrary field presentation is a separate contract.

Apply Simple-root primes for a family with prescribed denominator exclusions to H, D and N. It chooses the prime p and integral residue data a,b with exactly the root, derivative, leading-coefficient and denominator exclusions required by Hensel specialization preserving degree and denominator units. Apply Independent p-adic parameters in prescribed residue classes to this p and a. The resulting ξ is integral, independent in ℚ_p and has the same residues; choosing merely ξ = a would destroy independence whenever n > 0. Apply Hensel specialization preserving degree and denominator units to obtain η and all asserted root, degree and unit conclusions. Retain the independence proof from the preceding step; η is algebraic over the evaluated parameter field and is not asserted independent of ξ. The finite-field-presentation adapter and extension of the induced fraction-field map to the primitive extension are not conclusions of this target. Embedding a finitely generated field into ℚ_p with prescribed integral elements (Lech–Cassels) consumes this parameter/root output and retains those two exact gaps.

### 6.83a Specialization preserving polynomial degrees and a wandering point

Let L/ℚ be finitely generated as a field, f,g∈L[X] with deg f≥2 and deg g≥1, x,y∈L with x wandering for f, and T⊂L× finite. Prove that there exist a finitely generated ℚ-subalgebra R⊂L with fraction field L containing x,y, the coefficients of f,g and every t,t⁻¹ for t∈T, a number field M, and a ℚ-algebra homomorphism α:R→M such that deg f_α=deg f, deg g_α=deg g and x_α is wandering for f_α. For every n≥0, α(f^[n](x))=f_α^[n](x_α) and α(g^[n](y))=g_α^[n](y_α). Thus any infinite set of synchronized equalities f^[n](x)=g^[n](y) remains an infinite set of distinct diagonal orbit points after specialization. The map α is defined on R, not on the whole field L.

The specialization is obtained by induction on trdeg(L/ℚ), with no equality-of-degrees hypothesis. At a one-variable function-field step L/E, realize L as the function field of a smooth projective curve over its algebraic constant field. Remove the finitely many poles of the marked data and zeros of the leading coefficients and elements of T. For positive geometric canonical height, the general-base curve specialization limit of §6.24 gives a positive specialized height and hence a wandering specialized point. For a nonisotrivial polynomial, §6.52 supplies this positivity. In the isotrivial zero-height case, after a finite extension and affine conjugation the polynomial and marked point are constant (GTZ Lemma 6.8); retain the nonzero conjugating slope and its inverse, so their constant wandering orbit survives specialization without a positive geometric height. A finite map of the base curve to ℙ¹ gives points of bounded residue degree and arbitrarily large chosen base height; these avoid the finite excluded set. Iterate the reduction of transcendence degree. These are the wandering-point and finite-mark parts of GTZ §6; the no-common-iterate condition of Proposition 6.1 is unnecessary for this target.

Deduce the arbitrary-degree comparison: over every characteristic-zero field K, if the synchronized orbit of (x,y) under (f,g) has infinitely many distinct points on the diagonal, then deg f=deg g>0. Descend the finite coefficients and starting points to a finitely generated subfield. A constant polynomial makes the diagonal intersection finite. If both degrees are one there is nothing to compare; otherwise interchange the coordinates to put a nonlinear polynomial first, apply the specialization just stated, and use GTZ Lemma 5.7 over M. There the nonlinear wandering orbit has positive absolute canonical height: its height grows at least δd^n for some δ>0. A degree-e nonlinear orbit has height at most Ce^n; a linear orbit has height at most Cn+C′. If d>e, these bounds exclude all sufficiently large synchronized equalities. This includes the mixed linear/nonlinear case. No positivity of geometric height over K is inferred.

Construct the divisor D_P on the smooth base curve with degree equal to the generic Néron–Tate height. Compare specialized local Néron functions with the local Weil functions of D_P by bounded errors whose adelic sum is O(1), using Néron models over the base's local rings. The specialization limit alone gives only an o(h(t)) error and is insufficient for this contract.

There is a constant C(E, P) such that `|ĥ_{E_{t₀}}(P_{t₀})` − `ĥ_{E/K(t)}(P)` · h(t₀)| ≤ C(E, P) for all t₀ ∈ ℚ̄ with Δ(E)(t₀) ≠ 0 (absolute Néron–Tate heights normalised to (O), as in Silverman's specialisation theorem for elliptic surfaces over the t-line). (For a general base curve X, `ĥ_{E_t}(P_t)` = `h_{D}(t)` + O(1) for a ℚ-divisor D of degree ĥ_E(P); for X = ℙ¹ this is the displayed statement.)

K a number field; base the t-line; Δ(E)(t₀) ≠ 0.

The parameter-divisor and local-height construction contract below strengthens Silverman's specialisation theorem for elliptic surfaces over the t-line from o(h(t₀)) to O(1).

### 6.90 The dynamical Mordell–Lang theorem for lines under split polynomial maps (Ghioca–Tucker–Zieve Theorem 1.4)

The named signature `polynomialLine_returnTimes` states the return-set conclusion for A·f^[n](x)+B·g^[n](y)=C, with A≠0 or B≠0. Both polynomials may be constant.

Let K be a field of characteristic 0, f, g ∈ K[X] and x₀, y₀ ∈ K. If {(fⁿ(x₀), gⁿ(y₀)) : n ∈ ℕ} meets a line L ⊂ 𝔸²_K in infinitely many points, then L is periodic under (f, g). Consequently {n : (fⁿ(x₀), gⁿ(y₀)) ∈ L} is a finite union of arithmetic progressions: DML(𝔸², (f, g)) holds for lines.

char K = 0; f, g arbitrary polynomials (possibly of different degrees or linear).

For a vertical or horizontal line, repeated occurrences of the fixed coordinate make its one-variable orbit eventually periodic; the return times are finitely many progressions. For a line Y=aX+b with a≠0, GTZ Lemma 5.1 conjugates the second polynomial by ℓ(X)=aX+b and replaces y₀ by ℓ⁻¹(y₀), reducing to the diagonal. A constant polynomial gives only finitely many distinct diagonal points. For nonconstant polynomials, first apply the arbitrary-degree comparison of §6.83a: specialize the finitely generated coefficient field while preserving degrees and a wandering coordinate, then apply Lemma 5.7 only over the resulting number field. Both degrees are consequently equal. If they are one, use Common iterates from synchronized affine intersections with its S-unit/Siegel input. If they exceed one, §6.84 gives a common positive iterate; conjugating back makes L periodic. The equal-degree theorem is applied after this comparison.

If an infinite orbit meets a periodic line of period k, each first return in a residue class modulo k generates its entire subsequent progression; there are at most k such first returns. The first assertion counts distinct orbit points, not indices. A finite orbit has an eventually periodic time sequence, giving the return-set conclusion even when L is not periodic. An infinite orbit has no repeated points, so a finite intersection with L gives only finitely many return times. Zero-step progressions encode those singletons. These cases prove the return-set assertion for arbitrary degrees, including constant polynomials.

### 6.101 The dynamical Mordell–Lang theorem for étale maps (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker)

Let X be a quasi-projective variety over ℂ, Φ : X → X an étale endomorphism (Mathlib AlgebraicGeometry.Etale), V ⊆ X a closed subvariety and α ∈ X(ℂ). Then V(ℂ) ∩ O_Φ(α) is a union of finitely many orbits `O_{Φ^N}(Φ^ℓ(α))` (N, ℓ ∈ ℕ); equivalently {n ∈ ℕ : Φⁿ(α) ∈ V(ℂ)} is a finite union of arithmetic progressions. That is, DML(X, Φ) holds (The dynamical Mordell–Lang conjecture (statement)).

Characteristic 0 (over ℂ); Φ étale (for smooth irreducible X, unramified suffices: Theorem 4.1).

Reduce using the finite directed graph of irreducible components under Φ: components need not be permuted globally, but each component followed by the orbit is eventually in a cycle. Pass to a suitable iterate on a cyclic component and split the time set into residue classes and a finite prefix. Induct on dimension on the singular locus; étaleness preserves regularity in both directions, and on a component’s smooth open locus apply the smooth irreducible case. Finite unions and affine preimages preserve finite unions of arithmetic progressions. Smooth irreducible case: choose a finitely generated ℤ-algebra R carrying X, Φ, V, α; spread out to a smooth quasi-projective model with unramified Φ over a dense open of Spec R (Spreading out an unramified endomorphism (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Proposition 4.3)) and embed R into ℤ_p for a prime p ≥ 5 (A p-adic model of an unramified endomorphism (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Proposition 4.4)). Replace α by an iterate whose residue class is Φ-periodic of period N; on each residue disc, Φ^N is given by power series F_j (Power-series coordinates on a residue disc (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Propositions 2.1–2.2, Remark 2.3)) and some `F_j^{M_j}` ≡ id mod p (An unramified map returns to the residue class to first order (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Propositions 2.4 and 2.6)); by p-adic analytic interpolation of orbits (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Theorem 3.3) there are analytic `U_{j,ℓ}` : ℤ_p → ℤ_p^g with `U_{j,ℓ}(k)` = `ι_j(Φ^{N(M_j k + ℓ) + j}(α)).` For each polynomial h in the ideal of V, h ∘ ι_j⁻¹ ∘ `U_{j,ℓ}` is analytic on ℤ_p; by the imported restricted-series zero theorem it has finitely many zeros or vanishes identically. Hence each subprogression either meets V finitely often or lies in V.

### 6.106a The archimedean Legendre measure determines the parameter

For every t∈ℂ∖{0,1}, prove that the archimedean equilibrium measure μ_t of the Legendre Lattès map f_t has affine density C_t/|z(z−1)(z−t)| against Euclidean area, with C_t>0 chosen to give total mass one. The density is locally bounded off {0,1,t} and has an integrable inverse-distance singularity at each of these three points; in the reciprocal chart infinity has the same kind of singularity. Thus the measure recovers the four-point branch set {0,1,t,∞}. In the fixed standard coordinate, for s,t∈ℂ∖{0,1}, prove μ_s=μ_t if and only if s=t (demarco-krieger-ye-2020, §2.6 after (2.7), p.10).

Put p_t(z)=z(z−1)(z−t). The explicit duplication formula of §6.35 gives (f′_t(z))²p_t(z)=4p_t(f_t(z)) where the affine denominators are nonzero; use reciprocal charts at poles. The complex change-of-variables formula makes the pullback of the displayed atomless probability four times itself. The Layer 2 uniqueness theorem identifies it with μ_t. This gives the density directly on the sphere; it is the density described through Haar pushforward in the cited source. Equality of measures gives equality almost everywhere of densities; continuity off the branch sets and their unbounded local behavior then recovers those sets. Nondegeneracy of mutual energy supplies E∞(s,t)=0 iff μ_s=μ_t, and this parameter recovery supplies the additional implication s=t.

**Checks.**

- At t=2 and z=2+u, density times |u| tends to C_2/2>0, while at t=3 it tends to 0 because the density is bounded near 2. The two measures differ even though both have full support ℙ¹(ℂ).
- At t=2,z=3, f_t(z)=49/24, f′_t(z)=−35/144 and p_t(z)=6; both sides of (f′_t(z))²p_t(z)=4p_t(f_t(z)) equal 1225/3456. The pullback factor is 4, not 2.
- At s=t=2 the measures coincide and E∞(2,2)=0. The six Legendre parameters with the same j-invariant are not identified in the fixed x-coordinate: t=3 and 1−t=−2 have different fourth branch values.
- At t=0 or 1 the cubic has a repeated root; near that root the candidate density has order |u|⁻² and is not locally integrable. Smoothness excludes these parameters.

### 6.111 Uniform common torsion images for pairs of Legendre curves (DeMarco–Krieger–Ye Theorem 1.4; published Theorem 1.5)

Define `legendreTorsionImages` at t ∈ ℂ as the image of the finite-additive-order points of the Weierstrass coefficient model (0, −(1+t), 0, t, 0) under `ellipticStandardProjection` with the identity matrix. It is a subset of `OnePoint ℂ`, with an affine point (x,y) sent to x and the zero point sent to infinity. The headline `uniformLegendreCommonTorsion` asserts one B ∈ ℕ for all distinct t₁,t₂ ∈ ℂ ∖ {0,1}, with both finiteness of their common projected torsion set and cardinality at most B (demarco-krieger-ye-2020, Theorem 1.4, p. 3).

Its basic API consists of the following facts.

- Membership means that a finite-additive-order point has the given standard projected x-coordinate.
- The zero point maps to infinity, so infinity belongs to every projected torsion set.
- Negating a point preserves its projection; the smooth fibres have branch values 0, 1, t and infinity.

**Checks.**

- At t = 2, the coefficient tuple is (0,−3,0,2,0), the discriminant is 64, and (0,0) is a nonzero point of order two whose projection is 0; the zero point instead maps to infinity.
- At t₁ = 2 and t₂ = 3, the branch values common to the two fibres are exactly 0, 1 and infinity. Thus the full common torsion set has at least three elements, and omitting infinity changes the count.
- At t₁ = t₂ = 2 the common projected torsion set is infinite: the 2^m-torsion has 4^m points and projection has fibres of size at most two. The distinct-parameter hypothesis excludes this case; a cardinal bound without finiteness would be vacuous for an infinite set because its natural cardinal is zero.
- At t = 0 and t = 1 the discriminant is zero; the smooth-curve assertion excludes both fibres.

There is a uniform constant B such that `|π(E_{t₁}^tors)` ∩ `π(E_{t₂}^tors)|` ≤ B for all t₁ ≠ t₂ in ℂ ∖ {0, 1}, where E_t : y² = x(x − 1)(x − t) and π(x, y) = x (with π(O) = ∞).

t₁ ≠ t₂ complex, ≠ 0, 1.

Over ℚ̄ this is Uniform bound on joint small points over ℚ̄ (DeMarco–Krieger–Ye Theorem 8.1). Suppose a complex pair has more than B common torsion images. Choose B+1 distinct witnesses, separating the possible witness ∞ from the finite x-coordinates. For each finite witness and each of the two maps choose r<s with f_t^r(x)=f_t^s(x), using Preperiodic points of a Lattès map are the torsion images. Iteration of the homogeneous Legendre forms makes this a polynomial cross-product identity in t and x, with rational coefficients. Include t₁,t₂, all finite witnesses and the inverses of t_i(t_i−1), t₁−t₂ and every difference of finite witnesses in a finitely generated ℚ-domain. Apply Specialising a finitely generated domain to ℚ̄ while keeping finitely many elements nonzero. The inverted elements stay nonzero; the specialized maps have degree four and every evaluated iterate remains a nonzero projective pair because its resultant is nonzero. The cross-product identities therefore preserve preperiodicity and hence torsion images. The possible point ∞ stays ∞, giving B+1 distinct common torsion images over ℚ̄, a contradiction. Neither a division-polynomial converse nor a claim that an algebraic witness belongs to every Legendre fibre is needed.

**Endpoint checks.** The common images {0,1,∞} give B≥3. The genus-two torsion-intersection constant obtained in §9.3 of the source is 16B, so Stoll's 34-point example gives 34≤16B, not B≥34. For B=3 these numerical constraints read 3≤3 and 34≤48; the proof gives no explicit upper value of B (demarco-krieger-ye-2020, §9.3, p.47).

### 6.112 The Bogomolov–Fu–Tschinkel bound with three common branch values (DeMarco–Krieger–Ye Corollary 8.2)

The headline `uniformThreeBranchCommonTorsion` uses arbitrary smooth Weierstrass models W₁,W₂ over ℂ and arbitrary invertible matrices A₁,A₂ defining their standard projections. If the intersection of the projected two-torsion sets has exactly three elements, then their projected torsion intersection is finite and has cardinality at most a single B ∈ ℕ independent of the curves and matrices. The two ellipticity instances are explicit binders in the statement.

There is a uniform B such that |π₁(E₁^tors) ∩ π₂(E₂^tors)| ≤ B for all elliptic curves E₁, E₂ over ℂ and standard projections π₁, π₂ (Standard projections of an elliptic curve) with |π₁(E₁[2]) ∩ π₂(E₂[2])| = 3.

E_i elliptic over ℂ; exactly three common branch values.

Apply a Möbius map to send the three common branch values to {0, 1, ∞} (standardProjection_normalize). Replace π_i by `π_i^{e_i}` for suitable e_i ∈ E_i[2] so that π_i(O_i) = ∞; the torsion images are unchanged (Standard projections of an elliptic curve). Then each π_i is the x-coordinate of a Legendre model `E_{t_i}` with t₁ ≠ t₂ (the fourth branch values differ), and Uniform common torsion images for pairs of Legendre curves (DeMarco–Krieger–Ye Theorem 1.4; published Theorem 1.5) applies.

*Needs:* [Uniform common torsion images for pairs of Legendre curves (DeMarco–Krieger–Ye Theorem 1.4; published Theorem 1.5)](#6111-uniform-common-torsion-images-for-pairs-of-legendre-curves-demarcokriegerye-theorem-14-published-theorem-15); [Standard projections of an elliptic curve](#657-standard-projections-of-an-elliptic-curve).

([demarco-krieger-ye-2020](#demarco-krieger-ye-2020), Corollary 8.2, p. 44; proof p. 45 (arXiv v2) — The cited result supplies The Bogomolov–Fu–Tschinkel bound with three common branch values (DeMarco–Krieger–Ye Corollary 8.2) under the stated hypotheses; the target fixes its conventions and lists the precise inputs used in the proof.)

**Endpoint checks.** If the four branch values coincide, E₁ ≅ E₂ and the intersection is infinite: the hypothesis "exactly three" is needed.

### Examples

The marked set {0,1/6}⊂ℚ tests zero marks and denominators in the parameter ring in Lech–Cassels. A progression of step zero is a singleton, so finite hitting sets are allowed. The maps z³ and −z³ have equal second iterates; z² and −z² do not. These distinguish the root-of-unity and parity conditions in the equal-iterate classification.

### Dependencies

Layers 0–5 as specified per target; elliptic geometry and heights; SchemeAndStackFoundations §0.9 `spreading_out_models` and the relative Cohen contract; HeightsRationalPointsAndObstructions §§0.16, 4.8 heights and Siegel; Layer 2 The native analytic projective line hybrid geometry; the stated complex-dynamics, polynomial-decomposition and rigidity inputs.

## Downstream consumers

The canonical-height and equidistribution theories feed arithmetic specialization
and unlikely-intersection problems. The preperiodic predicates and critical-height
comparisons support bifurcation and rigidity. The certified dynatomic reductions
feed effective arithmetic, while the preimage tower supplies explicit examples of
profinite Galois images. General probability, potential theory and moduli theory
are used through their specified interfaces.
